title: UNHCR Middle East Situation: Emergency Update #23 as of 9 September 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

REGIONAL CONTEXT

Since late February 2026, hostilities in Iran and Lebanon have caused significant harm for civilians directly affected, while generating humanitarian consequences and elevated protection risks across the region, including refugee returns in adverse circumstances to Afghanistan and Syria. While diplomatic efforts have contributed to periods of reduced military activity, renewed hostilities have resulted in continued reports of attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure across contexts, including in Yemen. Prior to the escalation, there were more than 31 million forcibly displaced people and recent returnees already across the region, alongside host communities facing significant economic and social pressures.

Inter-agency emergency response efforts are underway in directly affected countries. In Iran, the Refugee Response Plan supports refugees and others in need of international protection alongside affected host communities. In Lebanon, a Flash Appeal extended through August 2026 complements the Lebanon Response Plan, while in Afghanistan, support for returnees is reflected under the Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan. UNHCR and partners continue to focus on the wider consequences of the situation, including returns under adverse circumstances, economic deterioration and pressure on national systems affecting growing protection risks facing refugees and vulnerable populations across the region. Preparedness arrangements remain in place, including border monitoring, reception and protection readiness, but continue to depend on flexible and predictable funding in an increasingly constrained resource environment.

A cross-regional protection analysis of the consequences of the escalation of hostilities is available in the recently-published InterAgency Protection Advocacy Brief (February – September 2026).

title: Disease Outbreak News: Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus, Democratic Republic of the Congo (10 September 2026)
content:
Since the last Disease Outbreak News was published on 28 August 2026, the Bundibugyo virus outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has expanded to one additional health zone, Kayna, in North Kivu. This increase brings the total number of affected health zones to 61 across six out of 26 provinces of the country: Bas-Uélé, Haut-Uélé, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, and Tshopo. As of 7 September 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo has reported 6757 confirmed cases, including 3267 deaths, resulting in a crude case fatality ratio (CFR) of 48.3%. The transmission dynamics remain variable across affected locations, with evidence of ongoing geographical expansion and sustained increase in cases in some health zones. The continuously high CFR highlights the seriousness of the disease and persistent challenges in timely case detection, access to early and adequate patient care, and effective interruption of transmission. Delayed detection of cases continues to increase the risk of further spread within households, communities, and healthcare settings.

Since the publication of the previous Disease Outbreak News on 28 August 2026, additional confirmed cases and deaths of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) have been reported only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

As of 7 September 2026, a cumulative total of 6778 confirmed cases has been reported: 6757 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (including two cases diagnosed in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and subsequently treated in Germany), 20 cases in Uganda and one case in France. Overall, 3269 deaths have been reported, including two in Uganda. As of 7 September, at least 1611 patients have recovered, including 1590 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, 18 in Uganda, two in Germany and one in France.

The sustained level of transmission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues to pose a risk of cross-border spread. Health screening and surveillance activities remain operational at airports, ports, and official land border crossings; however, travel through informal crossing routes persists and may facilitate virus exportation, importation, and subsequent transmission. In this context, strengthened cross-border coordination, together with ongoing surveillance and preparedness efforts, remains critical to limiting further regional spread and supporting an effective public health response.

Figure 1. Distribution of cumulative confirmed cases of Bundibugyo virus disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as of 7 September

Democratic Republic of the Congo

Since the previous Disease Outbreak News was published on 28 August 2026, an additional 963 confirmed cases, including 481 confirmed deaths, have been reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. While part of this increase may be attributable to strengthened surveillance activities, enhanced laboratory testing, improved diagnostic capacity, and reconciliation of previously unreported data, the continued growth in both cases and deaths also reflects sustained community transmission and significant geographic expansion of the outbreak. As of 7 September, the Democratic Republic of the Congo has reported a total of 6757 confirmed cases, including 3267 deaths (CFR 48.3%). A total of 1590 patients have recovered to date.

Confirmed cases have been reported from 61 health zones (HZ) across six provinces, with 51 HZ from five provinces reporting at least one case in the last 21 days. Ituri remains the most affected province, with 28 of its 36 health zones reporting cases, followed by North Kivu (16/34), Tshopo (7/23), Haut-Uélé (6/13), Bas-Uélé (3/11), and South Kivu (1/34). No new cases have been reported from South Kivu province since 29 May 2026. Kayna HZ in North Kivu province is the most recently affected area. As of 7 September, 71 new confirmed cases had been reported in the preceding 24 hours from 17 health zones located in Ituri, North Kivu, and Haut-Uélé provinces.

Ituri continues to be the epicentre of the outbreak, accounting for 5406 confirmed cases since the start of the outbreak, including 1114 new confirmed cases reported in the previous 21 days, as of 7 September. North Kivu is the second most affected province, with a cumulative number of 1066 confirmed cases, including 453 reported in the last 21 days, as of 7 September. One of the highest CFR (65.4%) observed in this outbreak has been reported from North Kivu province; and investigations are ongoing to better understand the factors contributing to this elevated mortality rate.

The number of individuals requiring follow-up as contact has also risen considerably with the expansion of the outbreak. As of 7 September, 85.3% of identified contacts were successfully monitored during the previous 24 hours with 21 359 contacts seen out of 24 719 requiring follow up. The large volume of contacts under surveillance highlights the extent of potential exposure within affected communities and the substantial demands placed on response operations.

The outbreak continues to unfold within a complex humanitarian setting characterized by insecurity, armed conflict, and widespread population displacement. More than 26 million people are experiencing acute food insecurity, while approximately one million internally displaced persons reside in Ituri Province alone. Ongoing insecurity and displacement limit access to healthcare and essential services, constrain the ability of response teams to reach affected areas, and impede surveillance, case investigation and contact tracing activities. Overcrowding, limited water, sanitation and hygiene services, and restricted access to healthcare in mining communities, informal settlements and sites for internally displaced persons further undermine early case detection, infection prevention and control measures, and the provision of timely care. These conditions also reduce the effectiveness of response interventions and outreach efforts.

Figure 2: Number of confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, by date of notification, as of 7 September 2026

Figure 3: Number of deaths among confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo by date of notification, as of 7 September 2026.

Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) is a severe Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, one of the Orthoebolavirus species. It is a zoonotic disease, with fruit bats suspected to be the natural reservoir.

Human infection is thought to occur through close contact with the blood or secretions of infected wildlife, such as bats or non-human primates, and it subsequently spreads from person-to-person through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs, or other bodily fluids of infected individuals or contaminated surfaces and materials. Transmission is particularly amplified in health-care settings when IPC measures are inadequate and during unsafe burial practices involving direct contact with deceased individuals.

The incubation period for BVD ranges from two to 21 days, and infected individuals are not infectious until symptom onset. Early symptoms such as fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache, and sore throat are non-specific, which complicates clinical diagnosis and can delay detection. These symptoms then progress to gastrointestinal symptoms, organ dysfunction, and, in some cases, haemorrhagic manifestations.

The historical CFR from the past two BVD outbreaks, reported in Uganda and in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2007 and 2012, were 30% and 50%, respectively.

Differentiating BVD from other endemic febrile illnesses such as malaria is challenging without laboratory confirmation using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or antigen- or antibody-based assays. Outbreak control relies on rapid case identification, isolation and care, contact tracing, safe burials and strong community engagement, as no approved vaccines or specific treatments currently exist for BVD.

Since first detected in May 2026, this BVD outbreak has rapidly evolved into a large and geographically expanding epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with sustained transmission, high mortality and an increasing risk of further international spread. The current outbreak is the second documented Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the country, after the 2012 outbreak, and the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo irrespective of Ebola virus species. The population at greatest risk of exposure is concentrated in communities living in and moving through the health areas with active transmission.

For detailed information about the ongoing public health response actions by the Ministry of Health, WHO and partners please refer to the latest situation reports published by the WHO Regional Office for Africa: Ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo | WHO | Regional Office for Africa

Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in collaboration with WHO and partners, are continuing to implement and coordinate extensive public health measures, including disease surveillance, laboratory testing, infection prevention and control, clinical care, community engagement, research, logistics and support for response interventions and essential health services, engaging donors and mobilizing additional resources to address critical funding gaps and sustain response operations across affected and at-risk areas. A substantial scale-up is ongoing across all response pillars to get ahead of the outbreak.

On 14 August 2026, WHO reassessed the risk of the outbreak of BVD, incorporating newly available information on the evolving situation. The risk for countries sharing land borders with the Democratic Republic of the Congo was separated from the risk for other countries in the African Region.

The risk in the Democratic Republic of the Congo was assessed as very high, the risk for countries sharing land borders with the Democratic Republic of the Congo was again assessed as high, and the risks for the rest of the African region and at the global level was again assessed as low.

For further information, please see WHO Rapid Risk Assessment-Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus, Democratic Republic of the Congo v4

Based on the currently available information, WHO advises against any restriction of travel to, or trade with, affected countries. WHO continues to closely monitor and, where necessary, verify travel and trade measures in relation to this event.

The updated Temporary Recommendations issued to States Parties on 24 August 2026 underscore the importance of coordinated outbreak control, strengthened cross‑border collaboration, and sustained surveillance and preparedness to prevent further regional spread and ensure an effective public health response. Rapid recognition of cases, testing and optimized supportive care can reduce mortality, and improve community perceptions and acceptance of health care within the response.

On 7 August, the WHO Technical Advisory Group on candidate vaccine prioritization released a report regarding possible candidate vaccines for Bundibugyo virus disease. The members recommended that Ervebo, the only licensed Ebola vaccine (previously known as ebolavirus Zaire), be prioritized for inclusion in a randomized clinical trial in the context of the ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Following a review of additional evidence on 19 August 2026, the WHO Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization (SAGE) concluded that available evidence remains insufficient to support the programmatic use of Ervebo for the prevention of BVD, and that its efficacy against BVD in humans remains unknown. WHO therefore recommends that Ervebo be used for BVD only within the context of a research protocol. Ervebo vaccination of healthcare and frontline workers is now underway. As of 6 September 2026, a total of 2007 people had been vaccinated across six health zones in three provinces: Tshopo, Bas-Uélé and Ituri.

On 2 July, a clinical trial to find effective treatments against BVD began patient enrollment on 2 July. The trial, known as the PARTNERS trial, is now open in five different clinical management facilities in Ituri province, and has enrolled over 300 people who are confirmed cases.

title: BGD: Epidemic - 09-2026 - Dengue in Bangladesh (2026-09-09)
content:
Description

The current dengue outbreak is placing substantial pressure on Bangladesh's health system, particularly in high-burden districts and urban centres. As of 8 September 2026, more than 45,000 dengue cases and 130 deaths had been reported nationwide, with over 1,500 new cases recorded in a single day and admissions continuing to rise. The surge in severe and hospitalized cases is increasing demand for hospital beds, clinical staff, diagnostics, blood transfusion services, and essential treatment supplies. Health facilities are reporting shortages of dengue NS1 rapid diagnostic kits, intravenous fluids, bedside ultrasound equipment, hematocrit testing capacity, blood bags, and apheresis kits, which may affect timely diagnosis, monitoring, and management of severe dengue cases. Reuters also reported growing strain on hospitals and bed shortages as admissions reach their highest levels of the year. The outbreak is also having significant secondary impacts on affected populations. Households face increased health risks and financial burdens associated with hospitalization, transportation, caregiving responsibilities, and loss of income during illness. The rapid geographic spread of cases across all eight divisions, combined with gaps in community awareness and vector-control activities, increases the risk of continued transmission and additional severe cases. Shortages of information, education and communication (IEC) materials and reduced community engagement activities may further limit preventive actions at household level. Experts cited by Reuters warn that favourable weather conditions, including heavy rainfall, high humidity, and warm temperatures, are likely to sustain mosquito breeding and transmission in the coming weeks, while WHO has previously highlighted these environmental factors as key drivers of large-scale dengue outbreaks in Bangladesh. Consequently, vulnerable populations, including low-income households, children, older persons, and those with limited access to healthcare, remain at heightened risk of illness, economic hardship, and adverse health outcomes during the peak transmission period

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: No

NS Requests International Assistance: No

Information Bulletin Published

No

Actions taken by National Society

Health

Clinical case management for epidemic disease

Community-based surveillance (CBS)

General

Volunteer Support

Summary

BDRCS has undertaken a range of preparedness and response activities to support the national dengue response. To strengthen diagnostic capacity and clinical management, BDRCS provided 23,000 dengue NS1 rapid testing kits to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) and 50 apheresis kits to the BDRCS Dhaka Blood Bank through the ASEF-funded Stockpile Project. A further 44,375 NS1 testing kits were handed over to DGHS Disease Control in July 2026 with support from the Takeda Fund, Swiss Red Cross, and Danish Red Cross. BDRCS mobilized volunteers to conduct dengue prevention and vector-control activities, including cleaning canals and water bodies and removing stagnant water from identified breeding sites. The National Society has also continued Community-Based Surveillance (CBS) activities in Puthia and Godagari upazilas of Rajshahi, monitoring suspected dengue cases and mosquito breeding risks to support early warning and timely community action. In parallel, BDRCS continues to closely monitor the evolving dengue situation and maintain coordination with national health authorities to inform preparedness and response measures. BDRCS is supporting the Government of Bangladesh's nationwide three-month dengue prevention campaign, commencing on 12 September 2026 following its announcement by the Prime Minister. Through its extensive volunteer network, BDRCS will participate in community-based clean-up and awareness activities in coordination with Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief, DGHS, district administration and relevant stakeholders. These efforts aim to eliminate mosquito breeding sites, strengthen community awareness, and promote preventive behaviours to reduce dengue transmission.

Actions taken by Federation

Summary

IFRC is closely monitoring the evolving dengue outbreak in Bangladesh and maintaining regular coordination with BDRCS, national health authorities, and Red Cross Red Crescent Movement partners. Through ongoing situation monitoring, information sharing, and preparedness planning, IFRC is supporting evidence-based decision-making, assessing emerging humanitarian needs and response gaps, and ensuring readiness for a potential scale-up of assistance should the outbreak continue to intensify.

Actions taken by RCRC

Summary

The Swiss Red Cross, Danish Red Cross supported the procurement and delivery of dengue NS1 rapid test kits to DGHS, while Swiss Red Cross continues to support Community-Based Surveillance (CBS) activities in Rajshahi Division to strengthen early warning and risk monitoring.

Actions taken by others

The Government of Bangladesh has announced a three-month nationwide dengue prevention campaign, led by the Prime Minister, focusing on intensified community clean-up activities and public awareness to reduce mosquito breeding sites and dengue transmission. The campaign will be implemented through a coordinated government structure, with city corporations leading activities in metropolitan areas, Deputy Commissioners overseeing district-level interventions, and Upazila Nirbahi Officers (UNOs) coordinating activities at the upazila level. The initiative will engage volunteers from the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief, Bangladesh National Cadet Corps (BNCC), Rover Scouts, BDRCS, as well as school and college students. To strengthen clinical case management capacity, the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), in collaboration with the Bangladesh Society of Medicine and with support from UNICEF, conducted a divisional-level Training of Trainers (ToT) on Clinical Management of Dengue on 31 August 2026. title: DSWD DROMIC Report #78 on the Combined Effects of Enhanced Southwest Monsoon and Tropical Cyclones “Luis”, “Maymay”, “Neneng”, and “Pilandok” as of 10 September 2026, 6AM
content:
I. Situation Overview

On 30 July 2026 at 4:00 PM, the trough of a Low Pressure Area (LPA 07f) affected the eastern sections of Visayas and Mindanao. On the same day, the trough of the LPA brought continuous heavy rainfall, resulting in flash floods in Zamboanga City.

On 01 August 2026, the LPA located east of Infanta, Quezon developed into Tropical Depression (TD) Luis.

On 02 August 2026, TD Luis brought moderate to heavy rainfall, strong winds, and rough sea conditions across Northern and Central Luzon, resulting in flooding in low-lying and flood-prone areas, particularly in the Cagayan Valley Region. Continuous moderate to heavy rainfall was also experienced in parts of La Union and Pangasinan.

The effects of TD Luis also extended to the Bicol Region, where a Yellow Rainfall Warning was raised over Camarines Norte due to the risk of flooding in low-lying areas and communities near river channels. Moderate to heavy rainfall also affected parts of Masbate, Camarines Sur, and Sorsogon. Meanwhile, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) suspended sea travel for all types of vessels in the Province of Catanduanes and the eastern portion of Camarines Norte due to hazardous sea conditions.

On 03 August 2026, TD Luis brought rains accompanied by gusty winds over the Province of Aurora, while the rest of Central Luzon experienced cloudy skies with scattered rain showers and thunderstorms associated with the tropical cyclone (TC). At 11:00 PM on the same day, TD Luis weakened into a LPA while in the vicinity of Peñablanca, Cagayan.

On 04 August 2026, the LPA west of La Union developed into TD “Maymay”. The TD remained over the sea west of La Union, intensified into a Tropical Storm (TS), and gradually moved northward and east-northeastward toward the Ilocos area on the following day.

On 06 August 2026, “Maymay” made landfall near Magsingal, Ilocos Sur, traversed Northern Luzon and then moved over the Philippine Sea while weakening into a TD. By 07 August 2026, “Maymay” had weakened into an LPA over the Philippine Sea.

On 08 August 2026, the effects of the Southwest Monsoon (SWM) continued to affect the country, bringing heavy rains, flooding, and strong winds in several areas. In Western Visayas, flooding and strong winds were reported in Antique, Aklan, and Iloilo City, while sea trips were cancelled, leaving passengers stranded in several ports. A tornado also struck parts of Iloilo City, damaging roofs, power lines, and trees. Flooding was likewise reported in several areas in the National Capital Region (NCR).

On 18 August 2026, the LPA located 1,025 km East of Extreme Northern Luzon (20.4°N, 131.8°E) developed into TD “Neneng”.

On 19 August 2026, TD “Neneng” slightly intensified as it moved northwestward over the sea east of Batanes.

On 20 August 2026, TD “Neneng” weakened into a LPA and exited the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).

On 28 August 2026, an LPA was estimated based on all available data at 720 km East of Itbayat, Batanes.

On 30 August 2026, the LPA located 1,225 km East of Extreme Northern Luzon developed into TD “Pilandok”.

On 01 September 2026, 8:00 AM, Tropical Depression "PILANDOK" intensified into a Tropical Storm with the international name "KROVANH" .

On 03 September 2026, 4:30 AM. Tropical Storm "PILANDOK" exited PAR.

In response, the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), through its Field Offices (FOs) Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR), I, II, III, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, V, VI, VIII, IX, and NCR, is in close coordination with the affected Local Government Units (LGUs), to monitor the situation and ensure the provision of necessary assistance to the affected population.

Meanwhile, the DSWD FOs NCR, CAR, I, II, III, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, V, VI, VIII and IX have already provided relief assistance to address the immediate needs of the affected families and individuals.

Additionally, the DSWD ensures the protection of Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) through Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) and dedicated IDP Protection mechanisms, while continuously working with affected LGUs to support response and recovery efforts.

content:

title: WFP Philippines Country Brief, September 2026
content:
KEY MESSAGES

• WFP continues to work with the Government in strengthening national and subnational systems for disaster risk reduction and management, social protection, and food systems – enabling faster and more scalable government-led solutions for vulnerable households and communities before, during and after shocks.

• Through technical assistance, policy support and strategic partnerships, WFP helps embed innovations such as anticipatory action, home-grown school feeding, rice fortification, and asset creation into government systems, ensuring sustainability and impact beyond direct assistance.

CONTEXT

• A Southeast Asian archipelago home to 116 million people, the Philippines has made significant progress in reducing poverty and improving food security, despite the impacts of unprecedented levels of climate shocks, inflationary pressures, and sporadic conflict.

• In July 2026, the Philippines was designated an upper-middle income country. However, intensifying El Niño effects and the impact of the Middle East conflict have slowed the country’s growth outlook.

• For three consecutive years, the Philippines has had the highest disaster risk worldwide (World Risk Index) due to exposure to extreme weather events and geologic hazards combined with low coping mechanisms and fragmented geography.

• While the poverty incidence dropped to a historic low of 9.7 percent in 2025, chronic malnutrition remains a critical issue. Stunting prevalence among Filipino children aged 0 to 5 years old increased to 25.3 percent in 2025, the first increase since 2013.

• Against this backdrop, WFP’s Country Strategic Plan 2024-2028 prioritizes supporting the Government in achieving food and nutrition security. Improving disaster risk reduction and management (DRRM), enhancing the delivery of social protection, and strengthening resilience to shocks remain key priorities.

• WFP uses a conflict-sensitive approach particularly in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), where the poverty incidence and food insecurity remain highest.

title: Flow Monitoring of Afghan Returnees — Bi-Weekly Report (1–15 August 2026)
content:
Highlights

  • Cumulatively, from 15 September 2023 to 15 August 2026, 2,682,993 individuals have returned.

• During the reporting period, the number of returns (-43%) and deportations (-41%) decreased significantly compared to the previous reporting period (16–31 July 2026). The decrease in returns and deportations is likely linked to reduced arrest and enforcement operations during this reporting period.

• Fear of arrest (96%) remained the most important reason among respondents to return to Afghanistan.

title: Syrian Arab Republic — Emergency Mobility Tracking and Cross Border Monitoring Situation Update — Round 21 (07 September 2026)
content:
OVERVIEW

Following the ceasefire in Lebanon announced on 17 April 2026, cross-border movements from Lebanon into the Syrian Arab Republic (hereafter referred to as Syria) have continually declined. Observed cross-border mobility is increasingly characterised by more gradual and stabilised patterns. From 02 March to 07 September, DTM identified 127,788 arrivals across 1,177 communities in all 14 governorates in Syria. Syrian nationals accounted for the overwhelming majority of arrivals, with Lebanese nationals representing less than 1 per cent. Flow monitoring at four assessed Syrian-Lebanese border crossings recorded 761,319 movements into Syria over the same period, of which approximately 98 per cent were Syrian nationals and 2 per cent Lebanese nationals. In addition, 3,870 Lebanese nationals were recorded transiting through Syria towards Jordan, highlighting the continued use of Syria as a route for onward regional movement. The Arida border crossing remains closed following the temporary closure from 6 August due to technical works on the Lebanese side. Consequently, Arida movement figures are available only up to 5 August. Key informants (KIs) cited persistent access constraints for travellers, with those previously using Arida having to rely on alternative crossings located further from Tartous Governorate, increasing travel times and associated costs. The situation remains fluid, and DTM continues to monitor development

title: HeRAMS Ukraine health services across oblasts August 2026 - legal entities [EN/UK]
content:
Overview

The Health Resources and Services Availability Monitoring System (HeRAMS) aims to provide decision-makers and health stakeholders with vital, up-to-date information. This system is dedicated to monitoring the availability of critical health resources and services, thus playing a crucial role in identifying existing gaps and establishing intervention priorities.

HeRAMS has been operational in Ukraine since November 2022. This report provides an oblast-level overview of health services across government-controlled areas, focusing on 2087 legal entities, based on data reported as of 01 August 2026. For a comprehensive overview of health services across all 11 099 health facilities monitored by HeRAMS, see HeRAMS Ukraine health services across oblasts August 2026 - all divisions.

Of the 2087 legal entities reporting, 4% were non-operational due to damage, non-functioning status, or inaccessibility, with the highest concentrations in Donetska and Kharkivska oblasts. Key infrastructure gaps include 3% of facilities lacking sufficient water, 2% lacking sufficient electricity, and 5% of inpatient facilities reporting insufficient bed capacity. Health service availability ranges from 53% for communicable disease services to 31% for non-communicable disease and mental health services.

While this HeRAMS deployment remains ongoing and data verification and validation are continuing, the analysis presented here is not final and has been produced solely to inform operations.

title: Nepal Landslides & Flash Floods: Situation Report #4 September 8, 2026
content:
Project HOPE has established five mobile medical units (MMUs) in Nepal, in coordination with local partners Volunteer Corps Nepal and Partnership for Sustainable Development Nepal. Access to healthcare continues to be strained along the Trishuli River, but Project HOPE’s teams have reached increasingly remote locations as roads are cleared, including at least one community where Project HOPE and our partners were the first to reach families since the disaster.

Situational Context

Health needs remain high in affected communities and Nepal’s health system is under significant strain as access to communities is still challenging and families are trying desperately to begin recovery while search-and-rescue efforts continue. Damaged infrastructure — including 41 destroyed bridges and blocked highways — is limiting the delivery of available relief supplies in remote communities. Rain in the region has also made passage along some roadways difficult. Tens of thousands have been displaced, affected families require consistent access to healthcare, and

At the time of this report, estimates show at least 1,331 dead and 4,996 missing in Nepal. Chinese authorities report at least 40 fatalities and 541 missing people missing in Tibet. In the coming months, those displaced, recovering families, and affected communities will need support to meet nearly every basic need across the health; water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH); mental health and psychosocial (MHPSS); food; essential non-food (NFI) item; and other humanitarian sectors.

title: Aid in Danger Bi-Monthly News Brief (19-31 August 2026)
content:
Armed drones are an escalating threat in humanitarian settings, with their use expected to grow. Once rare, they are now a defining feature in modern conflicts. Adapting to the growing threat of drones means rethinking security risk measures in high-risk contexts. This practical guide by Insecurity Insight brings together current best practice and is available in Arabic, Burmese, English, Spanish and French.

Individual resources:

  • Outside When a Drone is Spotted: Arabic; Burmese; English; French; Spanish
  • Inside a Building During a Drone Attack: Arabic; Burmese; English; French; Spanish
  • Responding to Drone Attacks on Aid Work: Arabic, Burmese; English; French; Spanish
  • Traveling in High-Risk Areas: What to Know About Drones: Arabic; Burmese; English; French; Spanish

Adapted for the protection of health services based on case studies on Myanmar in English and Burmese.

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 84, as of 8 September 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • 1,300 households receive 13 tons of fertilizer in Kaga-Bandoro and Mbrès.
  • Insecurity continues to drive population displacement in Nana-Mambéré.

GENERAL CONTEXT

Nana-Mambéré Prefecture, West

  • On 3 September, more than 250 people pre-emptively fled Abba-Bogani village due to ongoing clashes in the area and sought refuge in Bouar. This marks the second wave of internally displaced persons (IDPs) arriving in the town. On 28 July, an initial wave of 203 households, representing 1,015 people, settled with host families in the Ngolo 1, Herman 1 and Herman 2 neighbourhoods. The non-governmental organization All for Peace and Dignity (APADE) provided them with essential household items and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) assistance, including hygiene kits. Resource mobilization is ongoing to address the urgent needs of the newly arrived IDPs, particularly in shelter, essential household items, food assistance and WASH services.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Multi-sector

Lim-Pendé Prefecture, West

  • From 2 to 4 September, CARITAS, an implementing partner of the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), provided multi-sectoral assistance to returnee households in Bézéré, 20 km from Bocaranga, in Kodi Sub-prefecture. The returnees had come back from Cameroon in May, mainly due to difficult living conditions in refugee sites and to resume agricultural activities. A total of 293 households received essential household items, while 190 women-headed households received hygiene kits. In the water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) sector, partners repaired or rehabilitated four water points and revitalized four water management committees comprising 20 community members. Mobile clinics provided curative consultations for 136 children under five and four older persons, mainly for malaria, respiratory infections, diarrhoeal diseases and skin conditions. They identified 10 cases of moderate acute malnutrition (MAM) and 10 cases of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and referred them to Borodoul Hospital for specialized care. In the protection sector, 18 survivors of gender-based violence (GBV) received psychosocial support and tailored case management services. Reported incidents primarily involved sexual violence against minors, child marriage and physical violence.

Food Security

Nana-Gribizi Prefecture, Center

  • From 1 to 4 September, the non-governmental organization Welthungerhilfe (WHH) distributed 13 metric tons of fertilizer to 1,300 returnee and host community households in the sub-prefectures of Kaga-Bandoro and Mbrès. WHH also distributed 2,000 fruit tree seedlings, including avocado, orange, lemon, mango and mandarin trees, to support agricultural production and income diversification. WHH trained 322 members of 20 farmers’ organizations and seed producer groups in post-harvest management techniques. In addition, 30 women received leadership training to strengthen their participation in decision-making processes within community structures and development initiatives.

title: Bolivia Civil Unrest 2026: DREF Operational Update (MDRBO022)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met
02-06-2026
What happened, where and when?

Since early May 2026, Bolivia experienced a period of social unrest characterized by road blockades, demonstrations, and prolonged restrictions on the movement of people and goods across different regions of the country. The protests originated from demands related to fuel supply, the rising cost of living, and the national economic situation, and subsequently incorporated political demands.

The intensity of the demonstrations increased progressively throughout May. By 1 June 2026, 90 active blockade points had been reported across different departments, affecting strategic transport corridors and restricting the movement of people and essential supplies. La Paz, Cochabamba, Oruro, and Potosí were among the most affected departments, with particularly significant disruptions in La Paz and El Alto and along routes connecting the department with other areas of the country and Peru.

The prolonged mobility restrictions disrupted supply chains and affected access to food, fuel, medicines, medical oxygen, and other essential supplies. In response to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation, on 2 June 2026, the Departmental Government of La Paz declared a health and humanitarian emergency based on technical reports from the Departmental Health Service (SEDES), which identified shortages of medical oxygen, medicines, and essential medical supplies. On the same day, the Bolivian Red Cross, in coordination with the Ombudsperson’s Office, facilitated the transportation of a tanker truck carrying medical oxygen from Puente Arce to Sucre through corridors affected by the blockades to support health facilities facing critical supply constraints.

During the first days of June, the national Government promoted dialogue with protesting groups while operations were carried out to restore circulation along the country’s main routes. On 8 June 2026, Law No. 1740 was enacted, regulating the states of exception provided for under the Political Constitution of the State as a mechanism to respond to extraordinary situations affecting public order and the functioning of essential services.

The demonstrations formally concluded during the second week of June following agreements between the parties and the gradual lifting of blockade points. Traffic was progressively restored along the main interdepartmental corridors, allowing logistics and commercial services to resume. However, the prolonged disruption resulted in significant economic losses across transport, trade, industry, tourism, and exports, as well as damage to road infrastructure and reduced household income.

On 25 June 2026, the Departmental Government of La Paz, in coordination with the chambers of industry and commerce, presented an economic recovery plan aimed at supporting sectors affected by more than seven weeks of disruptions. As of the date of this update, the public order situation remains stable and circulation along the main routes has been restored. Nevertheless, the socioeconomic impacts of the crisis persist, particularly among households whose livelihoods and income were affected by the prolonged disruption.

title: Nepal: Rasuwa Flood Situation Report No. 7 (As of 8 September 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • The floods have claimed 1,356 lives. 4,894 people are still missing and 13,396 people have been rescued (NDRRMA, 7 September, 19:00)
  • 3,629 displaced people are living in 37 displacement sites in Nuwakot, Rasuwa, Dhading, and Kathmandu.
  • For the first time in an emergency operation in Nepal, WFP launched cargo drones (Unmanned Aircraft System (USAS) to deliver food assistance to communities in Rawuwa cut off by the floods.
  • UN Women has published the Second Gender Alert, which acts as a companion to the Flash Appeal to inform prioritization, coordination and resource allocation decisions through a gender and social inclusion lens.
  • On 7 September, the UN Resident Coordinator of Nepal, Ms. Lila Pieters Yahia formally launched the Flash Appeal at the UN Member States briefing in Geneva.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Nearly two weeks after the 26 August floods, operations are shifting from search and rescue to relief and recovery, though rescues continue. In Nuwakot, a woman was rescued from a four-storey building after ten days, and Nepali Army and international teams freed a Chinese national from an Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project tunnel. Damaged roads and collapsed bridges continue to isolate upstream communities and severely restrict relief access. In several areas, helicopters remain the only way to reach affected people with life-saving assistance.

On 6 September, the Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Executive Committee amended emergency warehouse procedures, allowing stocks to be released to UN agencies, the Nepal Red Cross Society, and community hospitals during disasters. Recipients must coordinate distribution with district and local disaster committees and report to authorities. The change should speed NDRRMA-led consignment and distribution of relief supplies.

At the UN Member States briefing on Nepal’s Flash Appeal, UN Resident Coordinator Lila Pieters Yahia said the Government is leading the response, supported by humanitarian partners addressing agreed gaps. The appeal seeks US$49.6 million to assist 84,270 people through 31 December. A US$2.5 million CERF allocation funded the initial response, but remaining needs are unfunded. She stressed that the appeal covers targeted humanitarian action—not longer-term recovery or reconstruction—and that access, logistics, coordination, protection, PSEA, and accountability must remain adequately funded.

On 5 September, WFP launched cargo drones to deliver food across difficult last-mile access barriers to flood-isolated communities. With Nepal Red Cross support, Bidur Municipality plans multipurpose cash assistance for 1,500 flood-affected households and NPR 10,000 per month in temporary rent support for households whose homes are uninhabitable.

title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 4 September 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Children continue to be killed by airstrikes and other attacks affecting populated areas in the Gaza Strip.
  • Most of Gaza’s 2.1 million are approaching the rainy season in overcrowded displacement sites, at risk of flooding and disease, while efforts to help them prepare are constrained by funding shortfalls and access restrictions.
  • A water well and desalination plant in Deir al Balah was damaged by a nearby strike, while a temporary suspension of desalination in Israel reduced water provision to 1 million people across the Strip.
  • In the West Bank, settler violence continues at high levels, resulting in Palestinian casualties, damage to property and livelihood assets, and disruptions to access, including to water and other essential infrastructure.
  • More than 2,500 Palestinians have been displaced so far in 2026 due to settler attacks and related access restrictions.
  • Funding shortages continued to constrain humanitarian assistance amid worsening food insecurity, with WFP announcing a reduction in food assistance from 400,000 to 200,000 people in the West Bank.

Overview

Palestinians across the Occupied Palestinian Territory continue to face violence and restrictions with little to no protection. Displacement remains widespread and growing, with more families losing their properties and shelters each day, while humanitarian efforts continue to be constrained.

Gaza Strip

The reporting period for this section is 24-30 August unless otherwise specified.

The humanitarian situation in Gaza remained critical as military activities continued to cause civilian casualties and damage to civilian infrastructure. As the rainy season approaches, concerns are mounting over the vulnerability of displaced people in damaged and makeshift shelters, while the continued deterioration of essential infrastructure – including roads as well as water and sanitation systems – is expected to increase humanitarian needs. Severe access and security constraints as well as funding shortfalls continue to impede humanitarian efforts, particularly preparations for the imminent winter.

According to the Ministry of Health (MoH) in Gaza, which operates under the de facto authorities, 31 Palestinians were reported killed, including those who died of wounds and had their bodies retrieved from under the rubble, and 86 people were injured between 26 August and 2 September. This brings the overall reported casualty toll since the announcement of a ceasefire agreement on 10 October 2025 to 1,334 fatalities and 4,429 injuries, according to MoH.

On 28 August, UNICEF stated that at least four children had been reported killed in the preceding five days and many others injured, including children sustaining life-changing injuries. On 2 September, UNICEF added that three children had reportedly been killed and at least five others injured in the preceding 24 hours with a total of seven children reportedly killed between 23 August and 2 September 2026.

Meanwhile, humanitarian facilities and services continue to be affected by ongoing strikes and general insecurity. On 24 August, a UNICEF-supported water well and desalination facility in Deir Al Balah was severely damaged by a nearby strike, disrupting access to safe drinking water for more than 4,000 people, including about 2,000 children. That day, airstrikes hit close to humanitarian facilities in Ash Shati’ Camp, Al Bureij and two locations in Deir Al Balah, shattering the windows at a guesthouse used by humanitarian partners. Also that day, a humanitarian warehouse in Deir al Balah was destroyed by a nearby strike, which damaged more than US$770,000 worth of UNICEF nutrition supplies intended to support more than 40,500 children, as well as 4,900 pregnant and breastfeeding women. On 27 August, an explosive munition detonated about 30 metres from a UN convoy returning with fuel from the Kerem Shalom crossing, as it crossed the “Yellow Line” in Rafah. The explosion caused a minor mechanical issue involving one of the vehicles in the convoy.

On 29 August, an Israeli drone strike reportedly hit a warehouse within the Al Aqsa Hospital compound in Deir al Balah, according to the hospital director, as reported by the media. Israeli authorities stated that the strike targeted a Hamas commander hiding in the compound.

Water and Sanitation

Water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) conditions remain critical in Gaza amid severe infrastructure constraints. According to the latest Light Touch Monitoring Survey conducted by the WASH Cluster, 91 per cent of assessed households continued to experience moderate-to-high water insecurity in early August, up from 90 per cent in July and 84 per cent in the June round, with overcrowding at water collection points emerging as the most commonly reported barrier to accessing clean drinking and domestic water.

On 31 August, after the reporting period, a temporary halt to desalination in Israel reduced the water available to about 1 million people in Gaza who rely on the Israeli grid. As of 3 September, the problem persisted. Humanitarian partners have used alternative sources to partially compensate for the reduction.

On 24 August, an airstrike damaged a reverse osmosis unit at the J32 well in Deir al Balah, according to the WASH Cluster. After debris clearance, partners repaired the facility, which provides purified drinking water for an estimated 100,000 people.

At the same time, UNICEF and partners are working to restore operations at the Sheikh Ajleen wastewater treatment facility in Gaza city. The facility used to serve about 700,000 people but was damaged extensively in the conflict and is discharging sewage into the Sheikh Radwan Lagoon, originally designed for storm water management. The rehabilitation effort comes against a backdrop of a broader wastewater crisis, with all six wastewater treatment plants currently non-operational and 70 per cent of sewage pumping stations out of service. As a result, more than 150,000 cubic metres of untreated wastewater are discharged into the environment each day, increasing public health risks and the potential for further water contamination.

Preparations for the Winter

With the rainy season approaching, humanitarian actors are increasingly concerned about the heightened risk of flooding and further deterioration of living conditions across Gaza. Urgent preventive and mitigation measures are needed to protect vulnerable communities, critical infrastructure and essential services from the anticipated impact of seasonal rains.

Lessons from last winter underscore the urgent need for additional covered storage and handling space on the Israeli-controlled Palestinian side of the Kerem Shalom crossing, where humanitarian supplies were damaged or spoiled after exposure to rain while awaiting collection. The requirement for additional covered storage space to protect perishable goods at Kerem Shalom has been raised as part of the 2026-27 Winterization Plan developed by the humanitarian community, and WFP as the Logistics Cluster Lead Agency has temporary warehouse structures available in Jordan that may be used to support this requirement, should permission to install them be granted. This issue has been raised with Israeli authorities, so far no way forward has been identified.

At the same time, preparations for the winter remain constrained by depleted humanitarian stocks of shelter materials and non-food items (NFIs), driven by continued access restrictions and funding shortfalls.

During the reporting period, Site Management Cluster partners conducted safety audits across approximately 230 displacement sites hosting at least 187,462 people (31,782 households). The assessments found inadequate lighting around pathways and WASH facilities, deteriorated shelters requiring urgent winterproofing, unsafe latrines and open pits, wastewater hazards, poor drainage in low-lying areas, and overcrowding. Other recurring issues included fire risks, pests and stray animals, limited safe spaces for women and girls, and exposure to security incidents in some locations.

While site-level improvement works like drainage clearance, pathway repairs, pit covering, lighting installation, and community clean-up activities are urgently needed, only limited interventions could thus far be implemented. Where resources, including funding, are available, Site Management partners are undertaking small-scale interventions, including community clean-up and waste removal, very limited manual rubble and debris clearance, minor repairs and basic site maintenance, as well as minor, locally implementable flood mitigation and drainage measures, with some activities implemented through cash-for-work initiatives. However, the shortage of toolkits and related materials, caused by funding shortages hampering the procurement of these supplies and restrictions imposed by the Israeli authorities slowing the entry of the limited available stocks, represents a major impediment to the rapid scale-up of site-level works. As a result, many identified risks are expected to worsen ahead of the winter season.

Efforts are also constrained because most of Gaza’s land remains inaccessible, including areas that are less vulnerable to flooding and could be used to set up tents for temporary and preventive relocation of internally displaced personsat high risks.

Forinformationon delays in securing Israeli approval for the entry of winter-related shelter supplies, see below under “Incoming Supplies.”

Incoming Supplies

According to data collected by the Logistics Cluster, the UN and partners’ aid offloading rate, representing the proportion of truckloads successfully offloaded at Kerem Shalom against those authorized to be manifested each day, stood at 88 per cent, consistent with the previous reporting period. The Egyptian corridor continued to face the highest levels of truck returns and rejections, with an offloading rate of 72 per cent, in line with the previous reporting period. The Ashdod route remained the most utilized entry route for UN and partners’ humanitarian cargo, accounting for 55 per cent of all truckloads entering Gaza. Since the closure of the Zikim Crossing in northern Gaza on 24 May, Kerem Shalom continues to represent the only operational crossing point for cargo.

The entry of items that Israeli authorities label as having humanitarian supplies rated as “dual use” continues to be extremely limited. These goods require a longer approval process that often leads to rejections. Of the approved items labelled as having “dual use,” the Israeli authorities are only allowing 15 truckloads to enter each week. They also limit the offloading of such items at the Kerem Shalom crossing to one day per week.

For example, timber products and tools have often been classified by the Israeli authorities as having “dual use.” On 26 August, the Israeli authorities rejected the entry via the Egypt corridor of 36,960 pieces of timber and 660 Emergency Shelter Kits (ESKs) comprising framing materials and basic construction tools, which had been approved in August. The same cargo was manifested a second time on 2 September, following coordination with the Israeli authorities, but was again rejected. Meanwhile, over 442,000 pieces of timber – representing 80 per cent of all timber available in the Shelter Cluster pipeline – and 15,800 ESKs submitted for entry via the Jordan corridor are pending Israeli customs clearance. These delays are restricting the availability of critical humanitarian supplies: materials needed for emergency shelter repairs and winterization activities.

The Shelter Cluster estimates that at least 400 truckloads would be required to bring into Gaza all urgent and critically needed humanitarian shelter items currently awaiting clearance in the Jordan corridor. These include 141,000 tarpaulins, 7,540 tents, 3,500 sealing-off kits, 2,923 ESKs, as well as over 442,000 pieces of timber, 19,500 toolkits and tens of thousands of pieces of plywood, ropes, tapes, fixing materials and plastic film. Given that most critical shelter inputs – including tents, tarpaulins, timber, ropes and tapes, tools, kitchen sets and solar systems – are classified as having “dual-use,” current restrictions continue to severely limit the scale-up of shelter assistance. At the present rate of entry, many of these materials are unlikely to reach Gaza in time to support an effective 2026-2027 winter response.

On the commercial front, data from the Gaza Chamber of Commerce, shared with the Cash Working Group, indicates that 865 commercial truckloads were collected into the Gaza Strip between 24 and 30 August by the private sector. The composition of cargo remains a concern. According to that data, of the 865 truckloads, shelter materials accounted for 99 truckloads, followed by hygiene items (41), stationery supplies (11), baby care items (3), medicines (3), and animal feed (1). The data further indicates that the remaining trucks were divided roughly equally between food and non-essential commodities, meaning that non-essential goods entering Gaza continue to compete with more critical humanitarian and recovery-related supplies. Overall, in August, a total of 3,627 commercial truckloads were collected into Gaza, exceeding the July total by 116 trucks, according to the Chamber of Commerce. Despite this light improvement, reported supply levels remain very highly insufficient to fully address the scale of needs across the Strip.

According to Cash Working Group market monitoring data, inflation remains high at 206 per cent above pre-October 2023 levels. During the reporting week, the price of several fresh food items, including apples, onions, bananas, cucumbers and tomatoes decreased, while the price of a 25-kg sack of flour rose by 29 per cent compared with the previous week.

The UN is only able to confirm the entry of supplies tracked by UN 2720. For breakdowns of those, see the online UN 2720 Mechanism Dashboard.

For a detailed account of the latest humanitarian operations in Gaza, see Annex 1 below.

West Bank

The reporting period for this section is 25 to 31 August unless otherwise specified.

Humanitarian needs across the West Bank continued to be driven by operations by Israeli forces, settler violence, demolitions and movement restrictions, disrupting population access to essential services and constraining UN and NGO’s operations, amid persistent funding shortages. Food insecurity also continued to worsen, as declining household incomes and high food and fuel prices further constrained families’ ability to meet basic needs.

Israeli authorities continued to maintain a presence at the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) Kalandia Training Centre (KTC) in occupied East Jerusalem, after forcibly entering it on 25 August. Israeli forces vacated the site after more than three days on 28 August but briefly returned to the compound on 30 and 31 August. Upon their departure, UNRWA raised concerns over the protection of its premises and assets after signs of looting were observed inside. The Jerusalem Municipality has indicated it intends to use the KTC premises for educational purposes with municipal workers and a few dozen Palestinian youths observed there in the first days of September. The KTC consists of tens of training workshops, classrooms, dormitories, and administrative buildings, and was preparing for the opening of a new academic year at the time of the forced entry. More than 340 Palestine refugee students from across the West Bank were expected to start their studies there this week.

Elsewhere, in Qusra village in Nablus governorate, three out of 18 Palestinian families remained subject to severe access and movement restrictions for more than 20 days, amid the continued presence of Israeli settlers and Israeli forces in the area following the establishment of a new settlement outpost in Area B near their homes around 9 August 2026. Meanwhile, humanitarian access negotiations enabled partners to reach families with very limited assistance in collaboration with the local municipality.

Meanwhile, funding shortages are increasingly constraining food assistance amid worsening food insecurity. On 1 September, the World Food Programme (WFP) announced that, due to funding shortfalls, it has reduced its food assistance in the West Bank from 400,000 to 200,000 people for the remainder of 2026. This compares with a 2026 Flash Appeal target of 450,000 people, while an estimated 900,000 people are food insecure across the West Bank. As WFP is the largest provider of food assistance within the Food Security Sector, the reduction is expected to significantly constrain overall response coverage and capacity in the coming months. WFP’s latest analysis found that 76 per cent of households experienced a significant decline in income, and one-third could not afford a nutritious diet, with rural areas and southern West Bank governorates particularly affected.

Child protection partners continued to provide mental health, psychosocial and community-based protection services. Since the beginning of 2026, partners have provided mental health and psychosocial support to more than 57,000 children, including over 2,200 children with disabilities, and nearly 25,700 caregivers. Partners have also supported 15 safe spaces and 44 community-based child protection structures, strengthening access to protection services and the identification and referral of children at risk.

Casualties and Settler Violence

On 28 August, an Israeli drone strike on Jenin city killed three Palestinian men who were present in a house under-construction. Israeli forces subsequently withheld the bodies. Local community sources reported that medical access was also obstructed.

Seventy Palestinians, including 13 children and nine women, four Israeli activists and two foreign journalists were injured between 25 and 31 August across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem. More than two thirds (51) of Palestinian injuries occurred in the context of settler attacks, including 35 Palestinians injured by Israeli settlers. In southern Hebron governorate, 17 Palestinians, including at least seven children, were injured on 28 August in two settler attacks in Khallet Al Humus and Khirbet Ghwein al Fauqa. The attacks involved physical assault and pepper spray, including against a nine-month-old infant, and damage to water and electricity infrastructure at one of the affected homes. On 25 August, four Israeli activists were injured and three of their vehicles damaged when settlers attacked them and Palestinian residents in Abu Nujeim, east of Bethlehem, as they attempted to reopen a road reportedly blocked by settlers that provides access to the homes of three Palestinian families. Israeli forces were reportedly present during the incident but did not intervene. In another incident, on 29 August, two Palestinians and two international journalists were injured in Jalud village, south of Nablus, when settlers believed to be from a nearby settlement outpost physically assaulted a Palestinian family and the journalists while they were conducting a media interview. Since the beginning of 2026, 82 Palestinians, including 19 children, have been killed and about 1,900 injured by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank. Of these, 23 Palestinians were killed and over 1,100 injured in the context of settler attacks. The frequency of injuries directly caused by Israeli settlers has risen sharply, from an average of one Palestinian injured every three days in 2020, to two per day in 2025 and more than three per day so far in 2026.

During the reporting period, 39 attacks by Israeli settlers were reported that resulted in Palestinian casualties, property damage or both, including recurrent attacks on some of the same communities that affected Palestinians’ access to homes, agricultural land and key roads, and damaged or disrupted water and electricity infrastructure. In Al Mughayyir, Ramallah governorate, four settler attacks resulted in the injury of 11 Palestinians, including four shot by Israeli forces, and damage to or loss of water infrastructure, property and livelihood assets. Settlers reportedly from a nearby settlement outpost targeted the village’s main water supply point for the second time in August, disrupting water supply to the village’s 3,300 residents for at least three days. Settlers also destroyed four water tanks, took over two agricultural tents and their contents, stole 35 livestock and killed two sheep. Severe movement restrictions imposed by Israeli forces continued for at least three consecutive days, including prolonged closure of the village entrance and restrictions on ambulance access. According to the WASH cluster, settler attacks affecting water access were also reported since 24 August in Tall Al Khashabeh (Nablus), East Tayba Bedouins and Turmus’ayya (Ramallah), including the emptying of cisterns, damage to water connections and repeated attacks on supply lines, further exacerbating water insecurity in affected communities.

Demolitions and Displacement

During the reporting period, 18 Palestinian-owned structures were demolished across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem for lacking Israeli-issued building permits. The demolitions displaced four households comprising 19 people, including nine children, all in a single incident on 31 August where the Israeli Civil Administration, accompanied by Israeli forces, demolished two three-storey residential buildings in area C in Nablus city. Overall, the demolished structures included five residential structures, including two inhabited homes, and 13 livelihood-related, agricultural, and water and sanitation structures.

Across the West Bank, settler attacks and related access restrictions have intensified since January 2023, particularly in Bedouin and herding communities in Area C. Between January 2023 and 31 August 2026, 130 Palestinian communities experienced full or partial displacement. Of these, 48 communities have been fully displaced, including 12 so far in 2026. Overall, more than 6,400 Palestinians, including over 3,100 children, have been displaced in this context since January 2023. Of them, more than 2,500 people, including over 1,200 children, were displaced in 2026 alone. The cumulative impact of repeated displacement, recurrent settler attacks, damage to homes and infrastructure, and restrictions on access to land and essential services continues to increase humanitarian needs while undermining the resilience of affected communities.

More than 3,960 Palestinians have been displaced due to demolitions, evictions, settler attacks and related access restrictions in 2026, averaging more than 16 people per day – nearly double the daily average observed between 2023 and 2025. The increase has been driven primarily by a sharp rise in displacement following recurrent settler attacks and related access restrictions, which has exceeded the annual total recorded in each of the past three years and accounted for over 60 per cent of all displacement recorded so far this year. The figures point to a significant shift in displacement patterns, with settler attacks and related access restrictions emerging as the principal driver of displacement in 2026.

Amid these conditions, WASH Cluster partners continued to provide lifesaving and emergency assistance across the West Bank during August in response to operations by Israeli forces, settler violence, displacement and other acute vulnerabilities. Activities included emergency water trucking and desludging, the distribution of hygiene kits and water storage tanks, the installation of emergency latrines, rehabilitation of household cisterns, and operation and maintenance support to water service providers, alongside hygiene promotion and community engagement activities.

For key figures and additional breakdowns of casualties, displacement, and settler violence between January 2005 and July 2026, please refer to the OCHA West Bank July 2026 Snapshot. title: DSWD DROMIC Report #76 on the Combined Effects of Enhanced Southwest Monsoon and Tropical Cyclones “Luis”, “Maymay”, “Neneng”, and “Pilandok” as of 09 September 2026, 6AM
content:
I. Situation Overview

On 30 July 2026 at 4:00 PM, the trough of a Low Pressure Area (LPA 07f) affected the eastern sections of Visayas and Mindanao. On the same day, the trough of the LPA brought continuous heavy rainfall, resulting in flash floods in Zamboanga City.

On 01 August 2026, the LPA located east of Infanta, Quezon developed into Tropical Depression (TD) Luis.

On 02 August 2026, TD Luis brought moderate to heavy rainfall, strong winds, and rough sea conditions across Northern and Central Luzon, resulting in flooding in low-lying and flood-prone areas, particularly in the Cagayan Valley Region. Continuous moderate to heavy rainfall was also experienced in parts of La Union and Pangasinan.

The effects of TD Luis also extended to the Bicol Region, where a Yellow Rainfall Warning was raised over Camarines Norte due to the risk of flooding in low-lying areas and communities near river channels. Moderate to heavy rainfall also affected parts of Masbate, Camarines Sur, and Sorsogon. Meanwhile, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) suspended sea travel for all types of vessels in the Province of Catanduanes and the eastern portion of Camarines Norte due to hazardous sea conditions.

On 03 August 2026, TD Luis brought rains accompanied by gusty winds over the Province of Aurora, while the rest of Central Luzon experienced cloudy skies with scattered rain showers and thunderstorms associated with the tropical cyclone (TC). At 11:00 PM on the same day, TD Luis weakened into a LPA while in the vicinity of Peñablanca, Cagayan.

On 04 August 2026, the LPA west of La Union developed into TD “Maymay”. The TD remained over the sea west of La Union, intensified into a Tropical Storm (TS), and gradually moved northward and east-northeastward toward the Ilocos area on the following day.

On 06 August 2026, “Maymay” made landfall near Magsingal, Ilocos Sur, traversed Northern Luzon and then moved over the Philippine Sea while weakening into a TD. By 07 August 2026, “Maymay” had weakened into an LPA over the Philippine Sea.

On 08 August 2026, the effects of the Southwest Monsoon (SWM) continued to affect the country, bringing heavy rains, flooding, and strong winds in several areas. In Western Visayas, flooding and strong winds were reported in Antique, Aklan, and Iloilo City, while sea trips were cancelled, leaving passengers stranded in several ports. A tornado also struck parts of Iloilo City, damaging roofs, power lines, and trees. Flooding was likewise reported in several areas in the National Capital Region (NCR).

On 18 August 2026, the LPA located 1,025 km East of Extreme Northern Luzon (20.4°N, 131.8°E) developed into TD “Neneng”.

On 19 August 2026, TD “Neneng” slightly intensified as it moved northwestward over the sea east of Batanes.

On 20 August 2026, TD “Neneng” weakened into a LPA and exited the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).

On 28 August 2026, an LPA was estimated based on all available data at 720 km East of Itbayat, Batanes.

On 30 August 2026, the LPA located 1,225 km East of Extreme Northern Luzon developed into TD “Pilandok”.

On 01 September 2026, 8:00 AM, Tropical Depression "PILANDOK" intensified into a Tropical Storm with the international name "KROVANH" .

On 03 September 2026, 4:30 AM. Tropical Storm "PILANDOK" exited PAR.

In response, the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), through its Field Offices (FOs) Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR), I, II, III, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, V, VI, VIII, IX, and NCR, is in close coordination with the affected Local Government Units (LGUs), to monitor the situation and ensure the provision of necessary assistance to the affected population.

Meanwhile, the DSWD FOs NCR, CAR, I, II, III, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, V, VI, VIII and IX have already provided relief assistance to address the immediate needs of the affected families and individuals.

Additionally, the DSWD ensures the protection of Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) through Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) and dedicated IDP Protection mechanisms, while continuously working with affected LGUs to support response and recovery efforts.
