title: DSWD DROMIC Report #71 on the Combined Effects of Enhanced Southwest Monsoon and Tropical Cyclones “Luis”, “Maymay”, “Neneng”, and “Pilandok” as of 06 September 2026, 6PM
content:
I. Situation Overview

On 30 July 2026 at 4:00 PM, the trough of a Low Pressure Area (LPA 07f) affected the eastern sections of Visayas and Mindanao. On the same day, the trough of the LPA brought continuous heavy rainfall, resulting in flash floods in Zamboanga City.

On 01 August 2026, the LPA located east of Infanta, Quezon developed into Tropical Depression (TD) Luis.

On 02 August 2026, TD Luis brought moderate to heavy rainfall, strong winds, and rough sea conditions across Northern and Central Luzon, resulting in flooding in low-lying and flood-prone areas, particularly in the Cagayan Valley Region. Continuous moderate to heavy rainfall was also experienced in parts of La Union and Pangasinan. The effects of TD Luis also extended to the Bicol Region, where a Yellow Rainfall Warning was raised over Camarines Norte due to the risk of flooding in low-lying areas and communities near river channels. Moderate to heavy rainfall also affected parts of Masbate, Camarines Sur, and Sorsogon. Meanwhile, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) suspended sea travel for all types of vessels in the Province of Catanduanes and the eastern portion of Camarines Norte due to hazardous sea conditions.

On 03 August 2026, TD Luis brought rains accompanied by gusty winds over the Province of Aurora, while the rest of Central Luzon experienced cloudy skies with scattered rain showers and thunderstorms associated with the tropical cyclone (TC). At 11:00 PM on the same day, TD Luis weakened into a LPA while in the vicinity of Peñablanca, Cagayan.

On 04 August 2026, the LPA west of La Union developed into TD “Maymay”. The TD remained over the sea west of La Union, intensified into a Tropical Storm (TS), and gradually moved northward and east-northeastward toward the Ilocos area on the following day.

On 06 August 2026, “Maymay” made landfall near Magsingal, Ilocos Sur, traversed Northern Luzon and then moved over the Philippine Sea while weakening into a TD. By 07 August 2026, “Maymay” had weakened into an LPA over the Philippine Sea.

On 08 August 2026, the effects of the Southwest Monsoon (SWM) continued to affect the country, bringing heavy rains, flooding, and strong winds in several areas. In Western Visayas, flooding and strong winds were reported in Antique, Aklan, and Iloilo City, while sea trips were cancelled, leaving passengers stranded in several ports. A tornado also struck parts of Iloilo City, damaging roofs, power lines, and trees. Flooding was likewise reported in several areas in the National Capital Region (NCR).

On 18 August 2026, the LPA located 1,025 km East of Extreme Northern Luzon (20.4°N, 131.8°E) developed into TD “Neneng”.

On 19 August 2026, TD “Neneng” slightly intensified as it moved northwestward over the sea east of Batanes.

On 20 August 2026, TD “Neneng” weakened into a LPA and exited the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).

On 28 August 2026, an LPA was estimated based on all available data at 720 km East of Itbayat, Batanes.

title: South Sudan Humanitarian Flash Update (Restoring Life-Saving Services: UNICEF Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) – Wiechjol and Waat), August 2026
content:
Overview:

UNICEF and partners completed Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) missions to Wiechjol in Akobo County and Waat in Nyirol County, Jonglei State, restoring immediate access to life-saving health, nutrition and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services for conflict-affected, displaced and returnee communities. After months of disrupted humanitarian access, the missions delivered approximately 8.3 metric tons of critical supplies and provided nutrition screening, primary healthcare, household water-treatment support, hygiene promotion and referrals for children and pregnant and lactating women requiring further care. The intervention provided a critical humanitarian lifeline for communities that had been largely cut off from assistance following months of conflict, population displacement, and disrupted service delivery. Through an integrated package of health, nutrition and WASH interventions, UNICEF and partners delivered immediate life-saving support to conflict-affected, displaced and returnee populations. The missions screened 1,666 children for acute malnutrition, provided 1,241 primary health care consultations, reached 2,075 people with hygiene-promotion messages, and distributed essential hygiene supplies, including soap to 3,250 households and buckets to 948 households. Teams also identified and referred vulnerable children and women requiring additional care, including 146 children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and 58 pregnant and lactating women at nutritional risk. As the first humanitarian assistance delivered in several months to these locations, the missions also generated critical information on humanitarian needs and service gaps, helping inform follow-up actions and the gradual restoration of essential services in hard-to-reach areas of northern Jonglei.

title: Desert Locust Bulletin 575 (5 September 2026)
content:
SOLITARIOUS POPULATIONS IN THE WESTERN REGION

In August, the grouping locust populations declined compared to the previous months in the Western Region. However, a few groups, and mainly isolated adults and hoppers, were present. A few adult groups were seen in southeastern Algeria and southwestern Libya, where transiens hoppers were detected and isolated adults were present. In Mauritania, increasing solitarious adult populations continued to be seen, and isolated hoppers were observed. Solitarious adults were seen at some sites in northern Niger and at many locations in Chad. No locusts were seen in Morocco since mid-July, and no more locusts were reported elsewhere. In the Central Region, there was an unconfirmed report of adult groups in the interior of Yemen, and no locusts were seen in Egypt, Sudan, Saudi Arabia and Oman. In the Eastern Region, no locusts were seen in Iran, Pakistan and India. During the forecast period, increasing populations will appear in the southern part of the Western Region, where summer breeding is expected to increase in Mauritania, southern Algeria, northern Mali, Niger, Chad and southwestern Libya. Hopper and adult groups may form by the end of the forecast period. Surveys should continue at high intensity in the summer breeding areas of these countries, where preventive control operations may be required. In the Central Region, small-scale summer breeding is expected to occur in the summer breeding areas of Sudan, western Eritrea, and the interior of Yemen, and winter breeding may commence on the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden coastal plains, but no significant developments are expected. In the Eastern Region, summer breeding may occur along the Indo-Pakistan border; however, no significant developments are expected.

title: UNICEF Nepal Humanitarian Situation Report No. 2, 4 September 2026
content:
Highlights

• Nepal flash flood has affected an estimated 84,270 people, including 32,021 children and 1,854 persons with disabilities across 17 municipalities in six districts.
• Essential services for children and families are severely disrupted. Fifty water supply systems and 20 schools have been damaged, while four health facilities have been destroyed and two partially damaged.

title: Indonesian Humanitarian Coordination Platform: Flash Update No. 1 - Anak Krakatau Eruption, Volcanic Ashfall and Concurrent Forest Fire & Haze Situation (6 September 2026)
content:
1. Situation Overview

Anak Krakatau remains at Level III (SIAGA/Alert). PVMBG/Badan Geologi reports that the volcano has remained at Level III since 2 July 2026. A series of Strombolian eruptions continued through 5 September, producing incandescent ejecta, volcanic ash and sustained lava-fountain activity. PVMBG recommends that communities, visitors and tourists do not approach or conduct activities within a 3 km radius of the active crater.

Volcanic ash has reached populated areas beyond the immediate vicinity of the volcano. Ashfall has been officially reported in coastal Banten and volcanic ash was detected at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport. In addition, IHCP has received field-confirmed observations of volcanic ash in Jakarta, Depok and Bogor on the morning of 6 September. At the time of this update, IHCP has not identified an official BMKG/PVMBG publication defining the complete ground-level ashfall footprint across these three cities; the geographic extent, concentration and duration of ashfall therefore require continued official verification.

No tsunami threat has been identified under the current eruption scenario. In 2018, a tsunami occurred due to the activity of the volcano. However, BNPB, citing PVMBG's assessment, reported that the post-2018 Anak Krakatau edifice remains relatively small and is not considered capable of a collapse of sufficient scale to generate a tsunami under current conditions. Monitoring continues and coastal communities should continue to follow official instructions.

title: Nepal: deadly flash floods - September 4, 2026, no. 2
content:
Key figures

● 4,521 people in shelters across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading

● 5,053 people missing

● 1,259 deaths recorded

● 12,038 people rescued

Highlights

● Corus teams are on the ground in Rasuwa and Nuwakot, assessing needs and coordinating with local authorities.

● Distribution of 500 hygiene kits and 1,500 sets of clothing is now underway for people affected by the flooding.

● Corus is procuring two 5,000-liter water tanks to help address urgent water storage and distribution needs identified through the WASH cluster in Nuwakot.

Situation Overview

On August 26, 2026, an ice-and-rock avalanche in the upper Bhote Koshi watershed near the ChinaNepal border triggered a massive debris flow and flash flood that swept down the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli river system. The disaster caused extensive loss of life and widespread damage to homes, roads, bridges, hydropower facilities and other critical infrastructure. Rasuwa and Nuwakot are the two most severely affected districts. Local education authorities estimate that approximately 600 students remain unaccounted for across the two districts, although verification is ongoing.

Search, rescue and relief operations continue. Some communities remain isolated because roads and bridges have been damaged or washed away. An alternate road route to Rasuwa has opened, but conditions remain rough and slippery, particularly with continued rainfall. Air transport remains important for reaching communities that cannot be accessed by road and delivering relief supplies.

Authorities continue to monitor upstream water accumulations and debris blockages. Further flooding, landslides and debris movement remain possible.

title: Nepal Flash Flood 2026 Situation Report 2 (4 September 2026)
content:
A major flash flood entered Nepal through the Bhote Koshi River at approximately 9:00 AM on 26 August 2026, causing significant loss and damage across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts. Timure, Rasuwagadhi and Syabrubesi are among the worst affected areas, with impacts reported on communities, markets, roads, bridges and hydropower infrastructure.

The cause of the flood remains under investigation, with authorities assessing the possibility of a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) or another upstream hydrological event. The Government of Nepal has mobilised security forces for search, rescue and relief operations and issued alerts for communities downstream along the Trishuli River corridor.

Our humanitarian response

Plan International Nepal is responding to the flash floods and landslides in the most affected areas, prioritising children and adolescents, girls, young women, pregnant and lactating women, persons with disabilities and other marginalised groups.

Food Security, Non-Food Items and Livelihoods

Response and achievements

● 229 families, approximately 1,000 people, in Nuwakot received food packs through Plan International and partners.

● 125 families at a holding centre in Uttargaya, Rasuwa, received food and NFI packs through coordination with the local government.

● 26 displaced families (104 people) staying at a holding centre in Belkotgadi, Nuwakot, received food packs and 35 blankets.

● 78 food packs were handed over to the local government in Bidur, Nuwakot, to support affected families.

● 300 shelter kits and 300 kitchen kits were distributed in Belkotgadi and Ward 7 of Nuwakot, reaching approximately 2,700 internally displaced people (IDPs).

● Three generator sets and power supplies were provided through the Ministry of Home Affairs to support holding centres and help restore essential communications in Rasuwa.

● Procurement is underway for 1,500 additional food packs through Plan International’s partner DEPROSC Nepal, coordinated with WFP to address identified food gaps and minimise duplication.

title: Syrian Arab Republic Drought 2025 - DREF Operational Update (MDRSY017)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met
08-08-2025
What happened, where and when?

Since the launch of this DREF operation in August 2025, the humanitarian situation in Syria has remained highly complex, with the impacts of severe drought continuing to interact with economic decline, deteriorating public infrastructure, prolonged pressure on basic services, and increasing climate-related hazards. Although parts of the country experienced localized improvements in rainfall during the 2025/2026 rainy season and severe flooding affected sections of the Euphrates Basin between May and June 2026, these events were insufficient to reverse the cumulative impacts of consecutive years of below-average rainfall, depleted groundwater reserves, and years of underinvestment in water infrastructure. Consequently, water insecurity remains a critical humanitarian concern across many governorates.

Throughout the implementation period, water and sanitation services continued to face significant operational challenges. Ageing infrastructure, persistent electricity shortages, limited financial and institutional capacity, rising operational costs, and shortages of essential equipment and spare parts have constrained the ability of water establishments to adequately operate and maintain critical water systems. These factors continue to reduce service reliability and place additional pressure on already fragile water supply networks.

Despite localized rainfall and flood events, the underlying structural drivers of water insecurity remain largely unchanged. Groundwater resources continue to experience increasing pressure due to unsustainable abstraction and unregulated well drilling in some areas, while high levels of non-revenue water resulting from ageing distribution networks and inefficient irrigation practices continue to increase demand on already stressed water resources. These pressures have further reduced the resilience of local water systems and, in some communities, have contributed to increased competition over limited water resources, affecting access to safe and reliable water supplies for vulnerable populations.

Between May and June 2026, flooding along the Euphrates River affected Ar-Raqqa and Deir-ez-Zor governorates, damaging water stations, irrigation infrastructure, and transport routes. While the floods temporarily increased surface water availability in some locations, they also disrupted water services and caused additional damage to critical WASH infrastructure. The simultaneous occurrence of prolonged drought impacts in many parts of the country and flood-related damage in others illustrates the growing variability of climate-related hazards and the increasing vulnerability of Syria's water resources and water service infrastructure.

These evolving conditions demonstrate that improving water security requires not only responding to climate-related emergencies but also strengthening the resilience of essential water systems. These evolving conditions demonstrate that improving water security requires strengthening the resilience of essential water systems through more efficient water resource management, reduced water losses, and sustainable management of available water resources, supported by community participation. Such measures are essential to sustain safe drinking water services, reduce humanitarian risks, and enhance the resilience of vulnerable communities to future climate related shocks.

Communities across Syria remain highly vulnerable to both slow-onset hazards, such as drought, and sudden climate-related events. These overlapping risks continue to undermine reliable access to safe drinking water and sanitation services, reinforcing the need for sustained humanitarian interventions that strengthen essential WASH infrastructure and improve the resilience of affected communities.

title: Nepal, Asia-Pacific | Flash Flood - Emergency Appeal Operational Strategy (MDRNP022)
content:
TIMELINE

26 August 2026: A massive surge of water enters the Bhote Koshi River bordering China. Floodwaters rapidly impact Timure, Rasuwaghadi, and Syafrubeshi towns in Rasuwa District and other towns further downstream in Nuwakot and Dhading Districts. The Government of Nepal issues evacuation orders and mobilises security forces. The Prime Minister’s Office convenes a high-level emergency meeting to assess the evolving situation and coordinate response measures. Additionally, the government holds a second emergency meeting and declares three districts and 15 municipalities as crisis-affected areas for three months while expediting relief and rescue operations.

26 August 2026: The NRCS activates its EOC on 26 August 2026. The NRCS is supporting the response through the mobilisation of staff and volunteers, search and rescue support, first aid and health assistance, emergency relief distributions, shelter and household items, WASH support, and dead body management, including the recovery, safe handling, identification, and dignified management of deceased persons. Other humanitarian partners are supporting complementary food, shelter, health, WASH, and protection activities, while international assistance and funding continue to be mobilised.

26 August 2026: The IFRC allocates CHF 999,934 from its Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) to support the immediate response, targeting 20,000 of the most affected people in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading. A CHF 100,000 Emergency Advance Payment request is signed enabling immediate access to funding.

28 August 2026: The IFRC launches a Federation-wide Emergency Appeal of CHF 25 million (CHF 18 million secretariat) to provide early recovery and recovery support to approximately 28,000 people in three districts.

28 August 2026: Multiple IFRC surge role alerts are issued, and the Regional Operational Coordinator, Communications Coordinator, and WASH Coordinator arrive in Nepal to provide technical support.

DESCRIPTION OF THE EVENT

On 26 August 2026, a major ice–rock avalanche occurred in the upper Bhote Koshi watershed near the China–Nepal border. An estimated 1km2 of ice and rock detached from a slope, picking up loose proglacial sediments downstream and transforming into a highly mobile sediment- and water-laden debris flow. Initial assessments suggest that the resulting outburst flood in the upper watershed was an order of magnitude or more greater than normal seasonal flooding.

A powerful debris flow of sediment moved rapidly downstream, causing widespread destruction across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts. Reports indicate that water levels in the Trishuli River rose up to nine metres above normal levels, inundating settlements and damaging critical infrastructure, including roads, bridges, schools, police stations, markets, health facilities, telecommunication towers, electricity poles, financial institutions, vehicles, hydrometeorological stations, customs infrastructure, and multiple hydropower projects. Timure border market was among the hardest-hit areas. The disaster has disrupted transportation along several key highways and roads, while authorities have restricted accessto river corridors due to ongoing risks. The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) issued a red alert for downstream districts, while the Government of Nepal convened an Emergency Disaster Council meeting chaired by the Prime Minister to coordinate search and rescue operations, damage assessments, and humanitarian response. Relief supplies have been mobilised from the Kathmandu Humanitarian Staging Area, with health response coordination led through national emergency mechanisms and partners. The scale of the physical damage, service disruption, and impacts on communities along the river corridor has created significant humanitarian needs requiring immediate relief and early recovery support.

title: Bosnia & Herzegovina — Migrant Mobility Situation Report (July 2026)

title: Nepal Rasuwa Flood Situation Report No. 6
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

More than a week after the 26 August flood, search and rescue has largely given way to relief operations. NDRRMA reports 1,259 deaths, 5,083 people out of contact and 12,038 rescued. Access remains the principal constraint, with damaged roads and bridges slowing the movement of relief supplies into upper Rasuwa, and several locations reachable only on foot.

Alongside the Government of Nepal, the Humanitarian Country Team launched a Flash Appeal in support of the Government-led response. The appeal seeks US$49.6 million to provide life-saving assistance to 84,270 people (19,284 households) in 17 municipalities across six districts: Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan, Gorkha and Tanahu. All identified affected people are targeted, of whom nearly 40 per cent are children.

Requirements cover ten sectors through the end of 2026, with roughly three quarters concentrated in five: food security (US$7.94 million), WASH (US$7.9 million), health (US$7.6 million), logistics and emergency telecommunications (US$7.33 million) and shelter (US$7.1 million). The appeal complements the Government's Official Disaster Relief Appeal of 27 August and the NDRRMA-led operation. It is a time-bound humanitarian response, not a recovery plan; recovery and reconstruction needs will be addressed through the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment.

To sustain the immediate response ahead of the appeal, the CERF allocation has been recalibrated to US$2.5 million, prioritizing life-saving assistance in the worst-affected districts.

The Logistics Cluster has been activated to support partners with logistics coordination, information management and common services, working with the Ministry of Home Affairs to identify and address transport bottlenecks. With WFP's support, a coordination base for the UN and partners is being established in Bidur, Nuwakot, providing shared operational and office space for agencies and cluster coordinators working closer to affected communities.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Food and non-food items are in sufficient supply in the market areas in Bidur - Nuwakot. Relief supplies continue to build up in Nuwakot, as access challenges hinder the delivery of assistance to many of the most severely affected communities in Rasuwa.

Protection remains a key concern, as women, men, and children continue to share common spaces in displacement centres, raising potential protection risks and limiting privacy for vulnerable groups. Psychological counselling and social and behaviour change (SBC) interventions on personal and menstrual hygiene are needed.
Additional priorities include addressing WASH needs, improving displacement site management and tracking, establishing safe spaces for children, and providing specialized nutritious food to pregnant and breastfeeding mothers and children under five.

title: UNFPA Situation Report: Nepal Floods (28 August – 3 September 2026)
content:
Flooding along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems has caused widespread loss of life, displacement and extensive damage to infrastructure across affected districts of Nepal. Government figures currently put the death toll at 1,204, with approximately 4,216 people still unaccounted for.

An estimated 98,560 women of reproductive age have been affected, including approximately 5,030 pregnant women. Damage to health facilities, impassable roads and disrupted transport have severely constrained routine and emergency maternal health services, increasing risks for pregnant women and newborns.

Displacement, loss of homes and livelihoods, and the breakdown of community support networks are heightening the risks of gender-based violence, sexual exploitation and trafficking, particularly for women and adolescent girls. Many affected families are staying in temporary shelters where overcrowding, limited privacy and inadequate access to safe, gender-segregated facilities are compounding these risks.

In response to the emergency, UNFPA has distributed 2,800 dignity and adolescent kits to women and girls, along with 300 tarpaulins to support privacy and safe spaces. Mobile health teams have provided sexual and reproductive health and gender-based violence services to 146 people and psychosocial support to 419 people.

UNFPA requires US$3.5 million to deliver urgent reproductive health services, prevent and respond to gender-based violence, and provide psychosocial support to flood-affected women, girls and young people in Nepal. Of the total funding required, US$3.2 million is still needed.

title: Sudan Protection Cluster Alert: Blue Nile - Escalating Hostilities and Humanitarian Access Constraints (2 September 2026)
content:
Escalating hostilities in Blue Nile are driving new displacement, increasing protection risks and further constraining humanitarian access. More than 23,000 people have reportedly been displaced from Geissan and Al Kurmuk localities since 11 August 2026, while insecurity and movement restrictions are disrupting humanitarian operations and access to essential services.

The Protection Cluster is concerned that continued hostilities, possible further population movements, explosive ordnance contamination, seasonal flooding and existing pressure on services could further heighten risks for displaced people, refugees and host communities, particularly women, children, older people and persons with specific needs.

The alert reiterates its call on all parties to the conflict to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, facilitate safe, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access and civilian movement, and respect their obligations under International Humanitarian Law. It also calls on humanitarian actors and humanitarian leadership to sustain critical services, strengthen protection monitoring and preparedness, and maintain contingency arrangements for any further deterioration in the security and access environment.

title: Situation Report No.10: Earthquakes in Venezuela 2026 (M7.2 and M7.5), 3 September 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• Just over two months after the two earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026, the response has transitioned into early recovery while sustaining essential emergency operations. Current efforts are focused on ensuring continuity of care across mental health, maternal, perinatal and NCD services and rehabilitation, restoring affected facilities, supporting transitional camps, and strengthening Health Cluster coordination as emergency teams and larger international partners withdraw, while ensuring a continuous, needs-based supply of medicines and essential equipment.

• Health system recovery is advancing, with assessments informing the prioritization of rehabilitation and recovery interventions across affected health areas, while persistent infrastructure, WASH and IPC gaps continue to challenge the safe continuity of essential health services.

• Public health surveillance and prevention remain active, with strengthened epidemiological alert investigation, laboratory confirmation and vaccination activities supporting early detection and response, while environmental risks in transitional camps continue to require sustained vector-control and public health action.

• Demand for continuity of care remains concentrated in Caracas, La Guaira, Miranda and Aragua, with mounting needs for prenatal care and family planning, GBV prevention, and physical rehabilitation and assistive devices, while camp-based services and integrated clinical pathways remain to be established.

• PAHO/WHO continues to support the response with critically needed medical supplies and medicines, having shipped 41.3 metric tons to Venezuela to date, benefiting 40 actors and reaching 70,697 people with treatment through PAHO and partner donations, while reinforcing the second level of care in La Guaira, equipping transitional camps and supporting personnel deployed in strategic areas

title: IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 16 (24-30 August 2026)
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Angola, Burundi
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

According to the Ministry of Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), over 5,900 confirmed cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) had been reported as of 28 August, including more than 2,800 confirmed deaths. This represents an 82 per cent increase in cases reported between July and August and a 99 per cent increase in the number of deaths reported over the same period.

The outbreak is unfolding against the backdrop of a longstanding triple crisis in eastern DRC, where conflict, displacement and health risks converge, leaving internally displaced persons (IDPs) and mobile populations at particular risk. Over 50 IOM-managed IDP sites in eastern DRC are located in areas of Ituri and North Kivu impacted by the outbreak. In such contexts, inadequate water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), health and shelter services accelerate risks of disease transmission and compound vulnerabilities, impacting the safety and protection of displaced, mobile and host communities.

In turn, mobility continues to shape disease transmission. Recent data from IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) highlights that one in two recorded journeys between 17 – 23 August started in an active transmission zone, with 4.5 per cent of the flows originating from active transmission zones leaving Ituri to other provinces within DRC, as well as to neighbouring countries of Uganda and Kenya. At the same time, data reported at points of control (PoCs) indicates a total of 165 case fatalities intercepted at PoCs – highlighting the continued importance of expanding health operations across DRC to effectively detect, prevent and respond to potential new cases.

The spread of the outbreak into Bas-Uélé Province underscores the continued need to comprehensively address the mobility dimensions of the ongoing public health response to prevent regional spillover into the Central African Republic (CAR) and South Sudan. Contact tracing is particularly weak for Bas-Uélé (18.9 per cent as per government sources), underscoring the urgent need for continued disease surveillance and monitoring to ensure a complete epidemiological picture.

In line with the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) systemwide scale-up activation for infectious disease events, IOM has scaled up its response, particularly at points of entry (PoEs), PoCs and in displacement sites, enabling enhanced surge support, operational capacity and coordination across affected countries.

IOM’s response continues to focus on Priority 1a countries, DRC and Uganda, where outbreak response and enhanced preparedness activities remain ongoing, and Priority 1b countries, Burundi, Rwanda and South Sudan, which face an elevated risk of crossborder transmission. Preparedness interventions are also being implemented in other at-risk countries across the region, including Priority 2 countries, Angola, CAR, Ethiopia, Kenya, the Republic of the Congo, the United Republic of Tanzania and Zambia, to strengthen readiness and enhance regional health security, while supporting continent-wide efforts, particularly as co-lead of the PoE technical working group at the continental level.

title: Yemen: Flash Update: Escalation of hostilities and mass displacement in Maqbanah and Jabal Habashi districts, Ta'iz governorate (As of 4 September)
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • Hostilities escalated along the Ta'iz frontlines in the early hours of Thursday, 3 September, with intense shelling and clashes in Maqbanah and Jabal Habashi districts.
  • An estimated 1,790 households have been displaced since 3 September, with movements continuing at the time of reporting.
  • Most displaced families are moving within Maqbanah and Jabal Habashi; others are arriving in Al Ma'afer, Ash Shamayatayn, Mawza and Dubab. Entire IDP sites, including Al-Hajab, Al-Rajehi and Hajjat Gabeh, have reportedly emptied, generating large-scale secondary displacement.
  • Ongoing shelling is restricting the ability of families to move to safer areas, and some households remain stranded in frontline locations.
  • Telecommunications disruptions are hampering information collection, verification and coordination, and emergency stocks are severely depleted, particularly Shelter/NFI and food assistance.

title: Lebanon: Middle East Escalation, LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #9: August 2026
content:
This situation report provides updates on the Middle East escalation, with focus on Lebanon’s security situation. It outlines the telecoms area activities of the Logistics & Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) in support of the humanitarian response1 . The Cluster was formally activated on 16 March 2026 and is led by the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP).

Summary Points

• The security situation in southern Lebanon remained volatile during August, with renewed hostilities and population movements continuing to affect humanitarian access and operational planning.

• Telecommunications services remained largely operational nationwide, but connectivity resilience continued to be constrained by localized disruptions in southern Lebanon, delayed fibre connectivity approvals, and ongoing restrictions affecting Starlink deployment.

• LTC Telecoms launched a nationwide assessment of humanitarian telecommunications needs and engaged partners, UNDSS, and national authorities to identify priority connectivity gaps, strengthen preparedness planning, and support future telecommunications interventions.

Situation Overview

The security situation in southern Lebanon remained volatile throughout August despite ongoing diplomatic engagement and efforts to sustain existing ceasefire arrangements. In early August, renewed Israeli strikes and a displacement order affecting Al-Mansouri prompted further population movements and highlighted the fragility of the security environment. Continued insecurity and periodic hostilities affected humanitarian access, operational planning, and the delivery of assistance in affected areas.

Humanitarian organizations continued to monitor developments closely and support affected populations, particularly in southern Lebanon where displacement and access challenges persisted. The evolving security situation underscores the importance of maintaining operational readiness and ensuring that responders can safely coordinate and deliver humanitarian assistance.

title: Sudan conflict - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms Area) #43 Reporting period: August 2026
content:
The WFP-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) was activated as the Emergency Telecommunications Cluster (ETC) on 25 May 2023 in response to the conflict crisis in Sudan. This Situation Report provides a monthly update on LTC telecoms1 activities.

Summary Points

• Despite ongoing funding and operational constraints, LTC Telecoms maintained connectivity services for approximately 1,700 users across 70 humanitarian locations and expanded shared internet services to 44 sites in Port Sudan, supporting humanitarian coordination and response activities across Sudan.

• LTC Telecoms continued expanding shared connectivity services in Khartoum and Darfur, including preparations for a new connectivity hub in Khartoum and the deployment of services in Geneina and Tawila, helping humanitarian organizations re-establish and sustain operations in priority response areas.

• On 27 August, LTC Telecoms launched connectivity and energy services at the Ald-Aim Community Centre in Khartoum, providing internet access, solar power, charging stations and digital skills support to strengthen access to information and digital services for affected communities.

Situation overview

In August, Sudan’s humanitarian crisis remained severe and highly complex as fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) continued across several parts of the country. Ongoing conflict in Darfur, Kordofan and Blue Nile drove further displacement, disrupted livelihoods and deepened humanitarian needs. Essential infrastructure and services, including health facilities, water systems, power networks and telecommunications infrastructure, remained heavily affected.

Humanitarian needs continue to far exceed available resources. As of late August, Sudan’s 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, which requires nearly USD 3 billion, was only 41 percent funded, with approximately USD 1.2 billion received. Funding shortfalls are forcing humanitarian organizations to scale back critical health, nutrition, protection and food assistance programmes despite growing demand for support.

Without a significant improvement in security conditions and increased donor funding, humanitarian needs are expected to continue rising. UN agencies and humanitarian partners continue to call for an immediate de-escalation of hostilities, the protection of civilians, respect for international humanitarian law, and sustained, unhindered humanitarian access across affected areas.

title: Afghanistan — Flow Monitoring Update (16–29 August 2026)
content: The International Organization for Migration’s (IOM) Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) Afghanistan’s Flow Monitoring (FM) is designed to provide insights into the mobility patterns at Afghanistan’s border points with the Islamic Republic of Iran and Pakistan. This activity involves two interlinked exercises: Flow Monitoring Counting (FMC) which monitors the number of movements across the border, and Flow Monitoring Surveys (FMS) which collect data on the profiles of Afghan nationals crossing the border, including reasons for travel and intentions. The FMS leverages FMC data to determine statistically valid, sex-disaggregated target samples on a daily basis, enabling statistically representative FMS data. It is important to note that DTM collects information on total movements at a given border point, not the number of unique individuals entering or leaving the country. Movements can include returnees, deportees, and circular travellers, including those visiting family or students. DTM FM is operational at four main crossing points connected to Afghanistan’s National Highway as well as two other crossing points with the Islamic Republic of Iran and Pakistan. This flow monitoring update combines information from FM and other IOM sources related to cross-border movement to Afghanistan. For a detailed explanation of the methodology used in gathering various inflow data, the report directs readers to the section titled “IOM Inflow Data” on page 8. Outflow data is collected exclusively through DTM FM.

title: Sri Lanka Dengue Outbreak 2026 - DREF Operational Update (MDRLK024)
content:
Date when the trigger was met

02-06-2026

What happened, where and when?

Sri Lanka is facing a signicant dengue outbreak in 2026, fueled by heavy rains, the onset of the southwest monsoon, and widespread ooding since mid-May. Case numbers climbed sharply from 25,082 in early May to nearly 92,854 by 18 August, marking roughly a 600% increase over the same period last year. The National Dengue Control Unit (NDCU) recorded more than 7,500 new cases in August alone, prompting concern over a potential epidemic. The outbreak was concentrated in the Western, Southern, North Western, Sabaragamuwa, and Central provinces, with the Western Province accounting for nearly half of all cases nationwide and Colombo District alone representing 55.1% of the national total.

During Week 32, Colombo recorded 747 cases, followed by Gampaha (759) and Kalutara (257), with notable numbers also reported in Matara, Kandy, Ratnapura, Galle, Kurunegala, Jana, and Kegalle. On 8 June, a three-day nationwide mosquito control campaign was launched, covering 14 districts and 72 Medical Ocer of Health divisions, alongside strict enforcement measures including "red notice" warnings for properties harboring mosquito breeding sites. In response, the Simplied Early Action Protocol was initially activated on June 3, 2026, covering 23 high-risk zones across ve districts: Colombo, Gampaha, Kalutara, Kandy, and Jana. With the additional 35 highrisk zones identied within the same districts where the sEAP was active, there was an urgent need to expand the intervention throughout the sEAP districts, particularly as the dengue outbreak had spread beyond the originally identied high-risk zones during the sEAP preparedness phase.

Dengue cases in Sri Lanka surged to their highest levels in July. Data from the National Dengue Control Unit (NDCU) as of mid-August 2026 shows that July marked the worst month of the outbreak, with 29,964 cases reported. During mid-July, weekly suspected cases consistently exceeded 7,300 across the country. Overall, the July surge brought the cumulative 2026 caseload to over 92,000, with 69 dengue-related deaths and a case fatality rate of 0.07%.

The geography of the outbreak also shifted: Gampaha district overtook Colombo as the most aected district nationally (13,795 versus 19,068 cases as of 18 August), while the Western Province's overall share eased slightly to around 52.6–52.8% as the Southern Province's contribution grew to roughly 15.6–15.7%, indicating a redistribution of burden rather than a national slowdown. A new and concerning development emerged in mid-July: A cluster of 71 cases, including ve hospitalizations, was identied among University of Colombo students in July, prompting the University of Moratuwa and the University of the Visual and Performing Arts to temporarily close their campuses—the rst institutional clusters recorded in this outbreak.

Separately, disease-monitoring analysis (BEACON) agged that the escalation thresholds it had set out on 3 July had since been breached: high-risk MOH divisions had expanded well beyond the 124 threshold, the case fatality rate had climbed above the historical 0.05% baseline, and case counts had shown no decline through July. Analysts noted that Gampaha's rise to the top of the case burden was signicant given documented insecticide resistance in local Aedes aegypti and Ae albopictus populations, implying that fogging and adulticide measures may be delivering diminishing returns exactly where the burden is now heaviest. The sharp spike in July matches Sri Lanka’s typical post-monsoon dengue pattern, as rainwater creates ideal breeding sites for Aedes mosquitoes. The decline in August is likely due to the rapid rollout of the national "Stop Dengue Now" program, greater community awareness, and targeted surveillance in high-risk areas.

Dengue cases remain highly concentrated in a few areas. During July and August, the Western Province accounted for 52% to 56% of all cases nationwide. Gampaha and Colombo are the national epicenters, mainly due to high population density and urban infrastructure. Kandy is the most aected area outside the Western Province. Other key districts with ongoing transmission include Matara, Kalutara (5,964 cases), Galle (5,063 cases), and Ratnapura (4,946 cases).

The cases over 92,000 recorded by 18 August had already surpassed full-year totals from recent endemic years, including 2025's 51,000 cases, and at the prevailing rate of about 1,100 cases per day, a 100,000-case total was projected to be reached by end-August — well before the October–December northeast monsoon peak — putting the 2019 epidemic total of 105,049 cases within plausible range for the current season alone. The analysis identied the August–September inter-monsoon trough, during which incidence has historically declined, as the critical factor determining whether the health system enters the next monsoon season already saturated.

title: Azerbaijan Population Movement: Imminent DREF Final Report (MDRAZ005)
content:
Update regarding the event’s development

The regional escalation of the conict in the Middle East in February 2026 increased regional tensions and disrupted air trac and regional transport connectivity. The escalation aected commercial aviation, and several countries issued guidance on alternative evacuation routes for their citizens, highlighting the potential risk of restricted mobility and increased reliance on land corridors. Azerbaijan was identied as one of the most likely transit countries for the evacuation of people crossing from the Islamic Republic of Iran. This likelihood was further reinforced by the presence of an estimated 15–23 million ethnic Azerbaijanis in Iran (approximately 16– 24 % of the population), predominantly residing in the north-western provinces bordering Azerbaijan. Iranian Azerbaijanis share close linguistic, cultural and religious ties with the population of Azerbaijan, including a common language, predominantly Shia Muslim identity, and longstanding family and social connections across the border.

Scenario analysis indicated that the humanitarian impact could exceed existing response capacities if 500 or more people crossed into Azerbaijan through the Astara border crossing within a 72-hour period and required humanitarian assistance, or if the authorities conrmed that a comparable number were expected to arrive through coordinated evacuation arrangements in the following days. This threshold reected the point at which existing reception capacity in the southern border districts could become overstretched, creating potential gaps in access to safe drinking water, basic services, First Aid, MHPSS and safe onward transportation. Reaching or exceeding this threshold would have represented a signicant escalation in cross-border movements requiring immediate anticipatory humanitarian action and readiness to scale up the response should arrivals continue.

The anticipated activation period was estimated at two to four weeks, while the situation remained highly dynamic depending on the evolution of hostilities and regional transport disruptions. The main anticipated humanitarian risks included congestion at border crossing points, prolonged travel times, fatigue, dehydration and psychosocial distress among people undertaking extended journeys, as well as temporary pressure on local services and infrastructure, particularly at the Astara border crossing. Additional contingency planning also considered the potential risk of a nuclear incident in the event of attacks aecting nuclear facilities located near the Azerbaijan-Iran border, as well as the possibility of strikes aecting targets within the territory of Azerbaijan.

Overall, the anticipated scenario was characterised by a rapid, short-term and transit-oriented population movement that could generate localized humanitarian pressure at border entry points, with a possibility of subsequent larger-scale internal population movements if the situation further deteriorated.

During the operational period, the Government of Azerbaijan maintained the closure of its land borders, with exceptions granted for cargo trac and humanitarian movements through the Astara border crossing. These movements primarily involved foreign nationals and diplomatic personnel departing the region through Azerbaijan, as well as Azerbaijani citizens returning to the country. Since the beginning of the escalation, more than 3,500 people from 76 countries were evacuated through the Astara border crossing, including more than 600 Azerbaijani nationals.

Overall, cross-border movements remained limited and did not reach the predened trigger thresholds for the activation of large-scale humanitarian assistance. Most travellers continued their onward journey through existing arrangements or evacuation mechanisms coordinated by the Ministry of Foreign Aairs, resulting in only limited humanitarian needs.

As a result, the anticipated escalation scenario did not materialize. The number of people requiring humanitarian assistance remained low and did not place additional pressure on national response capacities. While preparedness measures proved justied and necessary given the uncertainty of the evolving situation, the predened trigger thresholds for activating a large-scale humanitarian response were not reached.

Consequently, the situation remained stable throughout the operational period, and no large-scale humanitarian needs emerged that would have required activation of the planned response.

title: IOM Nepal Flood Response Situation Report #3 | 3 September 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

The 26 August flash floods in central Nepal have caused significant loss of life, displacement and damage to homes, roads, bridges and essential services. Government-led response operations are ongoing, while access constraints and incomplete verification of displacement and housing impacts remain key challenges.

As of 3 September 2026, authorities reported 1,259 bodies recovered and 5,053 people missing. A total of 12,038 people have been rescued, including 583 foreign nationals, with more than 21,402 security personnel mobilized.

Preliminary humanitarian analysis indicates that approximately 84,270 people have been affected across 17 municipalities in six districts. In Nuwakot, initial reports indicate that 1,897 households have been displaced, 1,267 houses completely damaged and 1,253 houses partially damaged.

Health partners continue to assess needs across flood-affected areas and facilities hosting an estimated 5,384 displaced people, while working to maintain essential services, supplies, staffing and referral pathways.

Priority needs include temporary shelter and essential household items, safe water and sanitation, food assistance, health services and referrals, Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS), protection support and access to affected communities.

Damaged roads and bridges, unstable riverbanks and disrupted telecommunications and electricity continue to constrain assessments, logistics and delivery of assistance to hard-to-reach communities.

IOM is supporting the Government-led response through surge support, site assessments, coordination, health, protection, MHPSS, non-food items (NFI), early recovery and Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) activities to help inform targeted assistance to affected and displaced communities.

title: Mozambique | Flood 2026 DREF Operational Update (MDRMZ027)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event
16-01-2026
What happened, where and when?

Mozambique experienced a large-scale flood emergency triggered by persistent and intense rainfall since late December 2025. The situation was compounded by exceptionally high upstream river inflows from South Africa and Zimbabwe and by controlled and emergency discharges from key dams, particularly Massingir Dam, which exceeded 100 per cent of its storage capacity in mid-January 2026.

As the potential impact of the rains and floods became more certain, national hydrological and meteorological authorities (INAM, DNGRH and ARA-Sul/Centro) issued successive high-risk alerts, prompting the Government of Mozambique, through INGD, to activate Anticipatory Actions and initiate evacuations in low-lying areas.

In line with this request, the Mozambique Red Cross (CVM) supported the Government with evacuations, distribution of relief items, and dissemination of early warning messages. This was done through the activation of the Floods Early Action Protocol (EAP) triggered on 27/12/2025 (MDRMZ022EAP2) and other mechanisms.

Despite these efforts, the scope and scale of the emergency exceeded local capacities, and on 16 January 2026, the Government of Mozambique activated a nationwide Red Alert in response to the deterioration of weather conditions and the heightened risk of severe flooding and related hazards across the country. This measure aimed to strengthen national preparedness, accelerate inter-institutional coordination and enable a more effective and timely humanitarian response to the ongoing emergency. The government of Mozambique also requested international assistance.

The humanitarian situation was severe and rapidly evolved, with impacts exceeding national coping capacities. Additional rains and floods continued for months after the initial impact, increasing the impact and limiting access to areas for response.

title: NGA: Population Movement - 08-2026 - Emerging Displacement Crisis in Kebbi State, Nigeria (2026-09-04)
content:
Description

A joint rapid assessment conducted by the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS), SEMA and Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) from 28–31 August 2026 has identified continued and expanding population movements in Danko-Wasagu and Sakaba LGAs in Zuru Emirate, Kebbi State, confirming that the emerging displacement situation extends beyond the initially affected locations. The assessment is part of ongoing efforts to establish the scale and humanitarian needs of displaced and host populations following recent attacks by non-state armed groups along the Sokoto–Kebbi border.

Between 17 and 19 August 2026, more than 5,000 people reportedly fled eight communities in Jega LGA following attacks attributed locally to banditry groups, with the majority moving to Jega town. More than 2,500 displaced people were initially accommodated at Jega Model Primary School, while others sought shelter with host families in Jega. The continued use of the school as a temporary displacement site is an immediate concern, as schools are expected to reopen on 12 September 2026, creating an urgent need for an alternative site and coordinated relocation planning.

Subsequent field-level assessment in Kanya Community identified 6,430 displaced persons originating from five villages—Dpindu, Dkwala, Kundurku, Rafin Gora and Gwazawa. The assessed population comprises 3,879 children, 450 pregnant women, 197 lactating women, 850 adult males, 984 adult females and 70 unaccompanied persons, highlighting significant humanitarian and protection needs among particularly vulnerable groups.

The wider NRCS assessment has also documented the impact of population movement and conflict-related incidents across Bagudo, Jega, Koko-Besse, Shanga and Yauri LGAs, covering 18 affected communities. The assessment recorded deaths and injuries, alongside displacement and damage to homes and livelihoods. The available structured assessment data records 73 deaths and 177 injured persons across the reported incidents.

The evolving situation has resulted in significant needs for food assistance, emergency shelter and non-food items, safe water and sanitation, health and nutrition services, protection and PGI support, assistance to unaccompanied children and other vulnerable groups, population registration and tracking, and community engagement and accountability.

The Nigerian Red Cross Society, in coordination with SEMA, MSF and other relevant authorities and humanitarian actors, continues to assess the situation and support affected populations. Population figures are being further consolidated and verified across the different assessment locations to establish the overall caseload and avoid double counting as the displacement situation continues to evolve.

title: DSWD DROMIC Report #66 on the Combined Effects of Enhanced Southwest Monsoon and Tropical Cyclones “Luis”, "Maymay", and “Neneng” as of 04 September 2026, 6AM
content:
I. Situation Overview

On 30 July 2026 at 4:00 PM, the trough of a Low Pressure Area (LPA 07f) affected the eastern sections of Visayas and Mindanao. On the same day, the trough of the LPA brought continuous heavy rainfall, resulting in flash floods in Zamboanga City.

On 01 August 2026, the LPA located east of Infanta, Quezon developed into Tropical Depression (TD) Luis.

On 02 August 2026, TD Luis brought moderate to heavy rainfall, strong winds, and rough sea conditions across Northern and Central Luzon, resulting in flooding in low-lying and flood-prone areas, particularly in the Cagayan Valley Region. Continuous moderate to heavy rainfall was also experienced in parts of La Union and Pangasinan.

The effects of TD Luis also extended to the Bicol Region, where a Yellow Rainfall Warning was raised over Camarines Norte due to the risk of flooding in low-lying areas and communities near river channels. Moderate to heavy rainfall also affected parts of Masbate, Camarines Sur, and Sorsogon. Meanwhile, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) suspended sea travel for all types of vessels in the Province of Catanduanes and the eastern portion of Camarines Norte due to hazardous sea conditions.

On 03 August 2026, TD Luis brought rains accompanied by gusty winds over the Province of Aurora, while the rest of Central Luzon experienced cloudy skies with scattered rain showers and thunderstorms associated with the tropical cyclone (TC). At 11:00 PM on the same day, TD Luis weakened into a LPA while in the vicinity of Peñablanca, Cagayan.

On 04 August 2026, the LPA west of La Union developed into TD “Maymay”. The TD remained over the sea west of La Union, intensified into a Tropical Storm (TS), and gradually moved northward and east-northeastward toward the Ilocos area on the following day.

On 06 August 2026, “Maymay” made landfall near Magsingal, Ilocos Sur, traversed Northern Luzon and then moved over the Philippine Sea while weakening into a TD. By 07 August 2026, “Maymay” had weakened into an LPA over the Philippine Sea.

On 08 August 2026, the effects of the Southwest Monsoon (SWM) continued to affect the country, bringing heavy rains, flooding, and strong winds in several areas. In Western Visayas, flooding and strong winds were reported in Antique, Aklan, and Iloilo City, while sea trips were cancelled, leaving passengers stranded in several ports. A tornado also struck parts of Iloilo City, damaging roofs, power lines, and trees. Flooding was likewise reported in several areas in the National Capital Region (NCR).

On 18 August 2026, the LPA located 1,025 km East of Extreme Northern Luzon (20.4°N, 131.8°E) developed into TD “Neneng”.

On 19 August 2026, TD “Neneng” slightly intensified as it moved northwestward over the sea east of Batanes.

On 20 August 2026, TD “Neneng” weakened into a LPA and exited the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).

On 28 August 2026, an LPA was estimated based on all available data at 720 km East of Itbayat, Batanes (21.9oN, 128.7oE).

On 29 August 2026, SWM continued to affect Luzon and Visayas.

In response, the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), through its Field Offices (FOs) Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR), I, II, III, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, V, VI, VIII, IX, and NCR, is in close coordination with the affected Local Government Units (LGUs), to monitor the situation and ensure the provision of necessary assistance to the affected population.

Meanwhile, the DSWD FOs NCR, CAR, I, II, III, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, V, VI, VIII and IX have already provided relief assistance to address the immediate needs of the affected families and individuals. Additionally, the DSWD ensures the protection of Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) through Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) and dedicated IDP Protection mechanisms, while continuously working with affected LGUs to support response and recovery efforts.

title: UNICEF Afghanistan Humanitarian Situation Report No. 7, 1-31 July 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Flash floods affected 1,168 families across 14 provinces, damaging or destroying 1,164 homes. In Parun, Nuristan, 23 people were killed and water services for around 1,000 families disrupted.
  • UNICEF supported essential health services through 2,393 static and 16 mobile facilities and responded to 245 disease outbreaks. Some 183,000 children under five were vaccinated against measles.

title: UNHCR-IOM Pakistan Flash update # 109 on Arrest and Detention/Flow Monitoring, 15 Sep 2023 to 29 Aug 2026
content:
INTRODUCTION

In response to the Ministry of Interior's (MoI) decision of 26 September 2023 to enact an “Illegal Foreigners' Repatriation Plan”, UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency and IOM, the UN Migration Agency, have collated their data on the arrest, detention, and deportation of Proof of Registration (PoR) holders, Afghan Citizen Card (ACC) holders, and undocumented Afghan nationals as well as on the outflows of Afghan nationals at the Torkham, Ghulam Khan, Chaman, Badini and Bahramcha border crossing points, to better understand the protection environment and movements of Afghan nationals returning to Afghanistan from Pakistan.

In 2025, the Government of Pakistan (GoP) issued several directives impacting Afghan nationals. In January, the GoP announced that Afghan nationals should relocate from Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT) and Rawalpindi, or else face deportation. In April, further announcements indicated the implementation of the second phase of the “IFRP”, targeting ACC holders, in addition to undocumented Afghans. In July, the GoP issued a Statutory Regulation Order (SRO) directing the repatriation/deportation of PoR card holders following the expiry of PoR card validity on 30 June. The GoP later indicated a deadline of 1 September for PoR holders to leave Pakistan, before the start of the repatriation/deportation process. UNHCR issued a press briefing expressing concern regarding the decision and urging the GoP to exempt Afghans with international protection needs, as well as those with particular circumstances or vulnerabilities, from involuntary return.

title: WFP Nepal Situation Report on the Rasuwa Flood Response, 04 September 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• WFP has dispatched 85.8mt of food rations sufficient for 15 days to Dhading, Nuwakot and Rasuwa, along with 2.8 mt of BP-5 and 40 boxes (0.45 mt) of fortified biscuits, reaching 8,000 people.

• WFP has facilitated 101 transport movements to date, including 57 services supporting Government-led relief operations and 44 WFP dispatches delivering assistance to flood-affected communities.

• The Logistics Cluster has been activated and is consolidating partner requirements to determine common logistics services.

Situation Overview

• Relief efforts continue across flood-affected districts following the 26 August floods, as search efforts, access constraints and major needs persist. Reported fatalities have risen to 1,259, with 5,083 people still missing.

• Floods severely damaged settlements, transport infrastructure and key economic assets along the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli corridor, with major disruptions continuing on the Rasuwagadhi and Betrawati–Rasuwagadhi routes and at several critical road and bridge crossings.

• Access to affected communities remains a major operational challenge, particularly in Rasuwa, where three local governments across the Trishuli River are still cut off by road.

• Damaged transport links, unstable terrain, compound by monsoon rains and ongoing flood risks continue to constrain relief operations, and restoration of key infrastructure may take several months.

title: WFP South Sudan Country Brief August 2026
content:
• In July, WFP assisted 2.36 million people with 15,981 mt of food and USD 13.49 million through cash-based transfers. Of the reached, were 1.8 million crisis-affected people and 338,602 school children.
  • WFP will experience pipeline breaks for 400,000 refugees and IDPs after September distributions; WFP, UNHCR and IOM are engaging with the Government of South Sudan on joint actions to inform affected refugees and IDPs of the expected impact on assistance.
  • WFP achieved strong Targeted Supplementary Feeding Programme (TSFP) results in the first half of 2026, distributing 6,000 mt of specialized nutritious foods, representing 91 percent of target. The programme admitted 222,000 pregnant and breastfeeding women and girls and 341,000 children aged 6–59 months for treatment of moderate acute malnutrition

title: Nepal Landslides & Flash Floods: Situation Report #3 (September 3, 2026)
content:
Project HOPE has established three mobile medical units in Nepal, in coordination with Volunteer Corps Nepal. Located in hard-to-reach communities along the Trishuli River, health providers with VCN began providing care this week, improving access to essential, lifesaving care for flood survivors and those impacted by last week’s massive glacier avalanche, flash floods, and landslides.

Situational Context

The scale of devastation in Nepal and the enormity of the future recovery process is beginning to set in for affected communities in Nepal. Humanitarian responders and community members are navigating villages where entire stories of buildings are buried under mud. Infrastructure has been deeply impacted, health facilities have been wiped out, and access to essential services is limited. Health threats loom large and the mental health impacts of living through the disaster are becoming more and more apparent as time goes on.

Current reporting varies between local sources and connectivity remains strained, limiting the flow of information. At the time of this report, estimates show at least 1,250 dead and 1,800 missing in Nepal. Chinese authorities have also reported 21 fatalities and 541 people missing in Tibet. These numbers include tourists from dozens of countries and local community members. The affected area is a popular tourist area for hiking, trekking, and religious pilgrimage as Tibet’s Mount Kailash is a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and other religious groups.

Nepali authorities continue to proceed with mass burials as the number of deceased washing ashore is exceeding morgue capacity in some locations. This disaster left a roughly 40-mile path of destruction, but the flow of debris traveled as far as 62 miles and there are reports of bodies washing ashore up to 250 miles downstream in Nepal and 100 miles downstream in neighboring India.

An estimated 3,458 displaced people are living across 27 displacement sites in Nuwakot and Rasuwa, primarily in schools, according to OCHA reporting**.** Significant access gaps remain in hard-to-reach locations. Parts of Tarkeshwar report receiving no assistance, all wards in Aamachhodingmo remain inaccessible by road, and four rural municipalities in Dhading lack safe drinking water. UNICEF estimates that 22,000 children are without access to safe water.

Damaged infrastructure, including 41 destroyed bridges and blocked highways, is limiting the delivery of available relief supplies to remote communities. The scale of reconstruction needs is also significant as approximately 20,000 homes will need to be rebuilt, including 7,500 that were destroyed, according to Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

Access varies across the affected communities, as continued rainfall is exacerbating muddy roads and other disrupted infrastructure. In the coming months, affected communities will need support to meet nearly every basic need across the health; water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH); mental health and psychosocial (MHPSS); food; essential non-food (NFI) item; and other humanitarian sectors.

title: Situation Report on the Crisis in Haiti (July-August 2026)
content:
The humanitarian situation in Haiti continues to deteriorate amid the increasing scale and intensity of violence associated with armed gangs. More than 2,600 people were recently displaced following attacks by armed gangs on 23 August 2026 in the municipality of Kenscoff, in the West Department. In addition, approximately 6,250 people were displaced by violence that began on 6 July 2026 in the municipalities of Dessalines and Petite-Rivière, in Haiti’s Artibonite Department.

Women and girls have been particularly affected by the crisis and face heightened risks of sexual violence. Access to medical care for survivors within the critical first 72 hours remains limited, particularly in frontline and conflict-affected areas.

UNFPA continued to deliver sexual and reproductive health and gender-based violence services to affected populations where access was possible. Between July and August, UNFPA and its implementing partners reached 15,191 people with sexual and reproductive health services and 3,483 people with GBV prevention, mitigation, and response activities. In addition, 1,547 women and girls benefited from psychosocial support and 700 received dignity kits.

UNFPA requires US$32.8 million to strengthen and expand access to life-saving reproductive health and protection services in Haiti. As of August, only US$4 million—just 12 per cent of the total funding required—had been received. As humanitarian needs continue to escalate, urgent additional funding is needed to sustain and expand these critical services for women and girls.

title: Venezuela Earthquakes Situation Report #8 (September 3, 2026)
content:
FAST FACTS

  • On June 24, two earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 hit northern Venezuela less than one minute apart, impacting at least seven states—including the capital Caracas and the neighboring city of La Guaira.
  • Official figures have confirmed 6,509 fatalities, 6,462 people rescued and 226,696 people who have received hospital care following the quakes.
  • Priority needs include healthcare services, clean water, food, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), adequate sanitation and hygiene facilities, protection support and shelter.

Our Response

  • International Medical Corps has deployed three mobile medical units, which have provided 5,914 consultations since July 1.
  • On July 11, International Medical Corps opened an Emergency Medical Team Type 1 Fixed facility that has so far provided 5,617 consultations.
  • Our teams have delivered 900,000 liters of safe water across displacement sites.
  • Our teams have provided 1,157 MHPSS services.

title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #27 (28 August to 2 September 2026)
content:
Situation Report No. 27 provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 28 August to 2 September 2026.

Highlights

Between 28 August and 2 September, IOM continued its multisectoral response in planned camps and affected communities through interventions in camp coordination and camp management (CCCM), shelter, health, mental health, protection, Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), information management, and Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA). IOM maintained management of four planned camps in La Guaira, strengthened inter-agency coordination and continued supporting return and potential relocation processes for earthquake-affected populations.

During the reporting period, IOM supported the update and verification of population records in Campo de Golf, confirming the presence of 330 people accommodated in 118 tents, including 111 women, 121 men and 98 girls and boys. The updated information will support service planning and discussions related to potential relocation options.

IOM coordinated improvements to WASH infrastructure in Mare Abajo II, including greywater drainage works and installation of the structure for a new community laundry facility to improve access to basic services for camp residents.

IOM continued providing health and mental health services in temporary accommodation sites, delivering 216 consultations during the reporting period, including 142 consultations in Cesar Nieves and 74 consultations in Jose Maria Vargas Sports Complex.

IOM Activities

IOM maintained coordination and management of the planned camps at Jose Maria Vargas Sports Complex and Campo de Golf and continued co-management of Cesar Nieves, Campo de Golf and Mare Abajo II together with the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC). Activities focused on population registration, service coordination, community monitoring and support for return and relocation processes.

Population registration and information management activities continued across the planned camps. In Campo de Golf, validation exercises conducted by IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) team, together with Equilibrium and community representatives, identified 330 people accommodated in 118 tents. In Cesar Nieves and Mare Abajo II, updated records and needs assessments supported targeting and planning for future interventions.

IOM continued distributing essential household items in camps and affected communities. During the reporting period, IOM provided 550 collapsible jerry cans, 521 plastic tarpaulins, 352 hygiene items, 340 tool kits, 224 solar lamps and 205 ropes. In addition, 320 families in Carabobo received integrated shelter and basic needs kits.

In WASH, IOM continued coordinating water supply, sanitation and hygiene services across planned camps while monitoring water access, safe storage, drainage and sanitation infrastructure. In Mare Abajo II, IOM coordinated drainage improvements, greywater management works and installation of a community laundry facility. In Campo de Golf and Cesar Nieves, IOM monitored sanitation conditions and supported actions to improve access to WASH services.

IOM continued delivering health, mental health and psychological support services through mobile teams and fixed service points. During the reporting period, 216 consultations were conducted, including services in general medicine, internal medicine, paediatrics, gynaecology and psychology. IOM also led the third Health Technical Working Group meeting in Campo de Golf and supported the introduction of a unified epidemiological data collection tool.

In protection, IOM continued providing legal counselling, case management, referrals and coordination of protection services. Through its implementing organization HIAS, IOM provided services to 74 unique individuals in La Guaira and the Capital District. Activities also included strengthening protection mechanisms for children and adolescents, supporting women and girls at risk, and facilitating referrals to specialized services.

IOM continued coordinating sectoral and inter-agency meetings with authorities, humanitarian organizations and community representatives. Coordination efforts supported ongoing discussions on relocation, return processes, infrastructure improvements, education, livelihoods and community participation across the planned camps.

In PSEA, IOM continued integrating Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse principles into camp management and community activities. In Cesar Nieves, IOM and NRC implemented an entry protocol for external organizations and volunteers, including guidance on safeguarding, child protection and standards of conduct prior to carrying out activities in the camp.

IOM Planned Response

IOM will continue supporting return, relocation and temporary accommodation processes while maintaining updated population records to guide service planning and decision-making. IOM will also continue strengthening camp infrastructure, shelter conditions and service delivery in planned camps.

In WASH, IOM will complete drainage and greywater works and operationalize the community laundry facility in Mare Abajo II, while strengthening hygiene promotion, safe water storage and sanitation activities across camps.

IOM will continue providing health, mental health, psychological support and protection services, including referrals, case management and support for people with specific needs. In addition, IOM will maintain DTM registration and mobility monitoring activities, complete pending assessments and continue coordinating with authorities and implementing organizations to support evidence-based response planning, returns and potential relocations.

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 83, as of 1st September 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • More than 600 people receive health care services in Bamingui-Bangoran.
  • Haute-Kotto: Adverse weather conditions and deteriorating roads hamper humanitarian access.

GENERAL CONTEXT

Haute-Kotto Prefecture – Center

  • Humanitarian access in Haute-Kotto Prefecture continues to be affected by the deteriorating condition of roads, compounded by seasonal weather conditions, making the movement of humanitarian actors increasingly challenging. Between 20 and 28 August, several vehicles and trucks transporting humanitarian assistance were stranded for several days due to muddy road conditions, particularly along the Bria–Ouadda and Aïgbando routes. These logistical constraints caused delays in the delivery of assistance, including food supplies intended for distributions during the lean season, as well as in the implementation of protection and health activities in the affected areas. Despite these challenges, humanitarian partners continue to operate under difficult conditions, including by carrying out food distributions planned this week for vulnerable populations in Ouadda.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Health

Mbomou Prefecture – South-East

  • In the context of the Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo strain reported in Bas-Uélé Province in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), which borders Mbomou Prefecture, the World Health Organization (WHO) organized a training session from 24 to 28 August for 30 community health workers in Bangassou on case definitions, modes of transmission and prevention measures for Ebola virus disease. Following the training, the community health workers will be deployed across Bangassou’s neighbourhoods to conduct community awareness-raising activities on preventive measures and support the early referral of suspected cases to health facilities.

Food Security

Vakaga Prefecture – North-East

  • From 23 to 31 August, World Vision, a World Food Programme (WFP) implementing partner, distributed 30-day food rations to 527 households in villages surrounding Birao. The assistance included oil, salt, rice and pulses. The beneficiaries were host households that had accommodated internally displaced persons (IDPs) during 2025.
