title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 28 August 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Since the beginning of 2026, more than 1,040 Palestinians have been injured in settler attacks, with 80 settler incidents resulting in casualties or property damage in the second and third weeks of August.
  • Three families in Qusra remained isolated following the establishment of a new settlement outpost in Area B around 9 August, while humanitarian access negotiations enabled partners to reach the families with assistance.
  • On 25 August, Israeli forces forcibly entered UNRWA’s Kalandia Training Centre in East Jerusalem, which Israeli officials indicated had been seized, putting the education of 340 Palestine refugee youth at immediate risk.
  • In Gaza, 58 per cent of the population is facing severe deficiencies in shelter conditions or access to essential services and non-food items, exposing them to serious health, safety and dignity risks.
  • Preparations for the rainy season are underway but are held back by restrictions on the entry of supplies access to land within Gaza and funding shortfalls.
  • Days of intensified airstrikes resulted in civilian casualties and damage to humanitarian structures and to critical supplies.

Overview

In a briefing to the Security Council on 26 August, the UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process ad interim said that “tensions are rising and uncertainty deepens in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.” While calling for steps towards recovery and a lasting political settlement, Dr. Alakbarov – who is also the Humanitarian Coordinator – said that people’s needs remain immense and urgent. He warned that humanitarian actors, especially international non-governmental organizations, “continue to face operational constraints related to access, supplies, and funding, with the 2026 Flash Appeal only 40 per cent funded.”

Speaking on the Gaza Strip, he said that people continue to endure intolerable conditions and immense hardship. He warned that amid Israeli airstrikes, drone attacks, ground operations, and persistent humanitarian challenges, people are losing hope. “Around two-thirds of Gaza remain inaccessible or subject to severe access restrictions, leaving civilians confined to overcrowded and insecure areas… Soon, winter will descend on Gaza.” Efforts to prepare for the rainy season “must be scaled up and facilitated. Plans are in place, but stocks of shelter and non-food items are depleted, access constraints on the entry of critical humanitarian items continue, and funding remains critically low.” Dr. Alakbarov called for the restoration of electricity, including by operationalizing the Gaza Power Plant.

Speaking on the West Bank, he warned that large-scale settler attacks “continue with virtually no accountability for these crimes. Israeli security forces have frequently failed to protect Palestinians from settler attacks and, in some cases, have reportedly facilitated or participated in such violence. Israel, as the occupying power, must ensure that the civilian population is protected, and perpetrators are held to account.”

West Bank

The reporting period for this section is 11 to 24 August unless otherwise specified.

Humanitarian needs across the West Bank continued to be driven by operations by Israeli forces, settler violence, demolitions and movement restrictions. These practices have also disrupted access to essential services and constrained humanitarian operations, amid persistent funding shortages. According to the Education Cluster, on 23 August, Israeli forces entered a girls’ secondary school in Jericho, causing damage to parts of the building just weeks before the new school year is due to begin. In Masafer Yatta, community-supported clearance of rubble began at a mixed basic school partially demolished by the Israeli authorities on 4 August, while rehabilitation and alternative learning arrangements remain suspended due to the risk of further demolition.

In a significant development following the reporting period, on 25 August, Israeli forces forcibly entered the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) Kalandia Training Centre (KTC) in occupied East Jerusalem, after which Israeli officials indicated in public statements that the premises had been seized by the Israeli authorities. This marked the fifth unauthorized entry by Israeli forces into the Centre since May this year. UNRWA issued a statement condemning the unauthorized incursion, describing it as unacceptable and emphasizing that the KTC, as a United Nations facility, is protected by the privileges and immunities afforded to the agency under international law and that its inviolability must be fully respected. Later the same day, clashes erupted in the surrounding area, during which Israeli forces reportedly fired tear gas canisters and live ammunition, resulting in at least nine injuries. The UN Secretary-General condemned the actions in the strongest terms, including the unlawful entry, continued presence and unauthorized works on the premises, and reiterated that UN premises are inviolable and immune from interference. The UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process ad interim also condemned the unauthorized entry and unlawful seizure, warning that it would immediately deprive 340 Palestine refugee youth from the West Bank of their right to education, with thousands more at risk in the coming years. Established in 1952, the KTC is UNRWA’s oldest vocational training centre and has served Palestine refugees for more than seven decades, providing free vocational education and skills training to hundreds of students annually, many of whom come from refugee camps across the occupied West Bank and face significant socio-economic hardship.

Partners leading on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) continued to respond to acute and prolonged water insecurity. Following the technical breakdown at the Mekorot-operated Beit Iba well on 24 July, which disrupted water supply to communities in the northern West Bank, the WASH Cluster mobilized emergency water trucking to three communities in Nablus governorate – Tell, Qusin and Bizzariya – based on assessed needs and gaps in alternative bulk water supplies. Partners also continued water trucking to 10 communities in Masafer Yatta, more than 1,500 people displaced from Tulkarm and Nur Shams refugee camps, and over 2,000 displaced people at the Arab American University displacement site in Jenin, where sewage desludging is also ongoing. Emergency water trucking continued in 15 additional locations, primarily supporting people recently displaced due to settler violence.

Humanitarian partners continued shelter and protection assistance. Between 10 and 23 August, Shelter partners provided shelter repairs, non-food items and cash assistance to 1,475 people from 348 households, primarily in Nablus, Ramallah and Hebron governorates. During the same period, partners addressing gender-based violence (GBV) maintained specialized services across 16 service delivery points and 40 safe spaces for women and girls, including psychosocial support, case management, emergency assistance and mobile outreach. Funding shortages, which have resulted in the closure of two Women and Girls Safe Spaces, alongside movement restrictions and settler violence, continued to constrain access to and delivery of GBV services. Mine action partners provided risk education on explosive ordnance, conflict preparedness and protection sessions to more than 2,000 people across six governorates. Since the beginning of 2026, child protection partners have provided mental health and psychosocial support to more than 57,000 children, including over 2,200 children with disabilities, and nearly 25,700 caregivers.

Casualties and Settler Violence

Between 11 and 24 August, members of Israeli forces shot and killed three Palestinians, including two boys, in three incidents in Jenin, Nablus and Hebron governorates. Two Palestinians, including one child, were killed during operations by Israeli forces on 21 and 23 August in Jenin city and Askar Camp, respectively. On 21 August, an Israeli settlement guard shot and killed a Palestinian boy and critically injured another Palestinian during an attack by more than 50 Israeli settlers on the Hamrush community near Sa'ir village in Hebron governorate. In the same incident, settlers damaged four residential structures and set fire to another structure, destroying about seven tonnes of stored fodder.

During the reporting period, over 100 Palestinians, including eleven children and nine women, and one off-duty Israeli soldier were injured. More than two thirds of Palestinian injuries occurred in the context of settler attacks, including 55 Palestinians injured by Israeli settlers. Recurrent attacks were reported in and around Al Mughayyir in Ramallah governorate, including along the village's only access road, where settler attacks repeatedly injured Palestinians, damaged vehicles and disrupted movement. On 20 August alone, 11 Palestinians were injured during an attack on the village. On the same day, another 11 Palestinians were injured during a night-time settler attack on the Deir Shams community near Adh Dhahiriya in Hebron governorate, during which more than 240 sheep were reportedly stolen and homes, vehicles and an animal shelter were damaged. On 23 August, a Palestinian child stabbed and injured an off-duty member of Israeli forces traveling with his family near Al Auja, in Jericho governorate. Following the attack, Israeli forces closed the village, raided several homes and a school, and detained a 16-year-old Palestinian boy in connection with the incident.

Since the beginning of 2026, 79 Palestinians, including 19 children, have been killed and about 1,870 injured by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank. Of these, 23 Palestinians were killed and over 1,040 injured in the context of settler attacks. The frequency of injuries directly caused by Israeli settlers has risen sharply, from an average of one Palestinian injured every three days in 2020, to two per day in 2025 and more than three per day so far in 2026.

During the reporting period, OCHA documented 80 attacks by Israeli settlers that resulted in Palestinian casualties, property damage or both. Incidents included recurrent attacks on some of the same communities, affecting Palestinians' access to homes, agricultural land and roads, as well as water and electricity infrastructure. Settler attacks also resulted in the displacement of three households: one family of six, including four children, after settlers set fire to their home near Yatta town of the Hebron governorate on 20 August, and two families comprising nine people, including two children, after settlers burned their residential and livelihood structures in Burqa, Ramallah governorate, on 22 August.

Access Restrictions Linked to Settlement Expansion

The establishment of Israeli settlement outposts, previously concentrated in Area C, has increasingly extended into Area B. According to Israeli group Peace Now, settlers have established at least 26 outposts in Area B of the West Bank over the past two and a half years, including 19 since the end of 2024, most of them in recent months. Peace Now estimates that settlers have taken control of more than 100,000 dunams (24,710 acres) in Areas A and B, including 55,000 dunams (13,591 acres) in Area B, and reports that violence and threats have been used to restrict Palestinian access to land and, in some cases, pressure families to leave their homes.

In Qusra, Nablus governorate, the establishment of a new settlement outpost in Area B around 9 August, near three Palestinian households in the Ras Al Ein area, was followed by increased presence of Israeli forces and settlers, damage to water and electricity infrastructure, and restrictions on Palestinian movement and access. On 15 August, after the municipality obtained Israeli approval to repair infrastructure damaged by settlers, settlers physically assaulted and injured two members of the repair team and Israeli forces detained four electricity workers, preventing the completion of repairs. On 23 August, municipality workers delivered food to the families, following access approval by Israeli authorities.

As of 26 August, the three families remained subject to severe access and movement restrictions, with two of the four roads connecting the area to the rest of Qusra under Israeli control: one through a permanent military checkpoint and another where Israeli forces have reportedly installed a road gate. One of the affected homes had also been occupied by Israeli forces for about 10 days. Following the withdrawal of Israeli forces on 23 August, the family was able to return to their home. During the period of the takeover, Israeli forces removed most of the family’s belongings from the house, many of which were reportedly damaged. Through coordinated access, humanitarian partners were able to reach the affected families with some essential assistance, including food, water, medicines and other basic supplies.

In Hebron governorate, on 12 August, a humanitarian assessment was conducted in Surif and Halhul following an increase in settler attacks and access restrictions in areas affected by the establishment and expansion of settlement outposts in Area C. In Al Quraynat area of Surif, home to about 65 Palestinian families, Israeli settlers established two settlement outposts in 2025 and mid-2026. Since January 2025, there have been 16 settler attacks resulting in Palestinian casualties or property damage in the area, compared with eight such attacks in the preceding five years. The severity of incidents has also increased: since January 2025, one Palestinian has been killed and 20 others injured by Israeli settlers or forces during settler attacks, compared with seven injuries and no fatalities in the preceding five years. During the assessment, residents reported recurrent shootings, physical assaults and intimidation by settlers, damage to homes, agricultural land and livelihood assets, and increasing restrictions on their access to agricultural and grazing land.

In Halhul town in Hebron governorate, seven new settlement outposts have been established since May 2025. Palestinian residents reported that the establishment and expansion of these settlement outposts and associated restrictions have constrained their access to about 14,000 of 37,000 dunams (3,459 – 9,143 acres) they own, much of which is productive agricultural land. Farmers reported reduced agricultural production and income due to access restrictions, settler attacks and the designation of some farmland as “military zones.” The assessment also highlighted the impact on access to essential services and protection concerns. In Wadi Muhaisin, seven families comprising about 90 people face movement restrictions that disrupt their access to schools, health care, and other essential services. For the past eight months, Israeli forces have reportedly prevented residents from using a route near a closed road gate close to Karmi Tsur Israeli settlement, forcing schoolchildren and other residents to take a four-kilometre detour along narrow agricultural routes to reach schools and other essential services. Residents also reported settler harassment while travelling along these routes, alongside psychosocial distress among children, women and families exposed to recurrent violence and intimidation.

Operations by Israeli Forces and Access Disruptions

During the reporting period, OCHA documented at least 22 raids, search operations and other operations by Israeli forces involving detentions, temporary home evacuations and movement restrictions, including in Jenin, Nablus, Tulkarm and Hebron governorates. On 13 August, amid the reported return of Israeli settlers to the former Ganim settlement east of Jenin city, which was evacuated in 2005, Israeli forces established checkpoints and closed sections of Road 60, cutting off direct access to Jenin city for about 10 villages comprising more than 20,000 Palestinians. On 17 August, Israeli forces temporarily evacuated for seven hours about 10 families from Jabal an Naser neighbourhood in Tulkarm, due to military activities near the adjacent Nur Shams refugee camp. Israeli military bulldozers excavated part of a road, damaging water and sewage networks, and carried out excavation works on Palestinian land before withdrawing. Families reportedly returned to their homes, and municipal crews repaired the damaged infrastructure once Israeli security forces withdrew from the area. A separate 10-hour operation in Qabatiya, in Jenin, involved searches of about 100 homes and the detention of more than 60 Palestinians. On 19 August, Israeli forces imposed a curfew for more than 12 hours affecting an estimated 40,000 Palestinians in Adh Dhahiriya town in Hebron governorate, where they detained and interrogated about 40 Palestinians and took over seven homes for use as interrogation sites, confining the affected families to single rooms.

Demolitions and Forced Evictions

During the reporting period, OCHA documented 22 incidents in which 79 Palestinian-owned structures were demolished across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, five of which had been provided as humanitarian assistance following previous demolitions. The demolitions displaced 16 households comprising 73 people, including 34 children, and otherwise affected more than 280 people, including about 100 children. Three structures were demolished in Kafr Sur, in Tulkarm, in proximity to the Barrier and 76 structures were demolished for lacking Israeli-issued building permits, including 66 in Area C and 10 in East Jerusalem. Demolished structures included 15 residential structures and 64 livelihood-related, agricultural, and water and sanitation structures.

More than half of those displaced – 45 Palestinians, including 22 children – were in Beit Hanina, Jabal al Mukabbir and Silwan in East Jerusalem, following demolitions of residential structures carried out by Israeli forces or by owners following the receipt of demolition orders. In Jabal al Mukabbir, 22 people, including 13 children, were displaced in two incidents on 12 and 14 August; in Silwan, 13 people, including five children, were displaced in two incidents on 12 and 17 August; and in Beit Hanina, three refugee households comprising 10 people, including four children, were displaced on 19 August when the Jerusalem Municipality, accompanied by Israeli forces, demolished a two-storey residential building. Some affected families reported losing belongings and furniture during the demolitions, including in Beit Hanina, where residents reported being prevented from retrieving most of their belongings before the building was demolished.

Separately, on 18 August, Israeli forces forcibly evicted two Palestinian households comprising eight people from parts of their three-storey residential building in the Batn al Hawa area of Silwan, East Jerusalem, in favour of the Israeli settler organization Ateret Cohanim. The families had built and inhabited the building prior to 1967. Following Israeli court proceedings over claims that parts of the building stand on land owned by Jews prior to 1948, settlers took over the second-floor apartment and parts of the third-floor apartment rendering it uninhabitable, as well as the main entrance and part of a ground-floor apartment inhabited by two elderly women, one of whom has mobility challenges. The women were left without independent access to their home and now require coordination through the settler-controlled section to enter or receive visitors.

Since the beginning of 2026, 24 Palestinian households comprising 93 people, including 30 children, have been forcibly evicted from their homes following Israeli court decisions, most of them in Silwan. Approximately 200 Palestinian households of about 900 people across East Jerusalem remain at risk of forced displacement due to ongoing eviction cases before Israeli courts, the majority initiated by Israeli settler organizations.

For key figures and additional breakdowns of casualties, displacement, and settler violence between January 2005 and July 2026, please refer to the OCHA West Bank July 2026 Snapshot. For key figures on the impact of settler attacks, please refer to the West Bank – The Impact of Settler Attacks, January 2023 – April 2026.

Gaza Strip

The reporting period for this section is 10-23 August unless otherwise specified.

The humanitarian situation in Gaza remained critical as military activities continued to result in civilian casualties, displacement, and damage to civilian and humanitarian infrastructure. Recent incidents affecting humanitarian facilities and warehouses have disrupted humanitarian operations and damaged critical infrastructure and supplies, while aid organizations continue to face severe access and security constraints.

According to the Ministry of Health (MoH) in Gaza, which operates under the de facto authorities, 47 Palestinians were reported killed, including those who died of wounds and had their bodies retrieved from under the rubble, and 176 people were injured between 12 and 26 August. This brings the overall reported casualty toll since the announcement of a ceasefire agreement on 10 October 2025 to 1,303 fatalities and 4,336 injuries, according to MoH. Children continue to bear a disproportionate impact of the violence, with at least four children reportedly killed and several others sustaining life-changing injuries across the Strip over the past five days, underscoring the continuing risks faced by civilians despite the ceasefire framework.

On 23 August, three UN warehouses in Deir al Balah were damaged following an airstrike on an adjacent location. One warehouse sustained significant structural damage, while the other two were affected to a lesser extent. No major loss of stored supplies was reported. On 24 August, warehouses operated by Ard El Insan Palestinian Charitable Association (AEI), also in Deir al Balah, sustained extensive damage following a strike on an adjacent residential building. According to AEI's initial assessment, virtually all stored nutrition supplies – including supplements and specialized products for children, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers – were rendered unusable due to debris, dust, and blast damage. Not far from there, the windows of a guesthouse used by a humanitarian partner were shattered. Overall, at least four airstrikes hit near humanitarian facilities on 24 August – in Ash Shati’ Camp, Al Bureij, and two locations in Deir al Balah.

Meanwhile, on 24 August, severe damage to a UNICEF-supported water well and desalination facility in Deir Al Balah has disrupted access to safe drinking water for more than 4,000 people, including around 2,000 children. Emergency water trucking is ongoing. These but the incidents further undermine access to essential nutrition and safe water services for affected families.

Critical shortages of medicines, medical supplies and laboratory reagents continued to severely strain Gaza’s health system, threatening the continuity of lifesaving services. The Ministry of Health reported that central stocks of IV solutions had been depleted. While diagnostic cardiac catheterisation services have resumed, shortages of essential consumables continue to limit access to therapeutic procedures. More broadly, persistent shortages of medicines, dialysis supplies, laboratory reagents, oxygen equipment and other critical items, combined with restrictions and delays affecting the entry of health commodities, continue to undermine health care.

According to the latest classification by the Shelter Cluster, based on surveys conducted between 14 and 28 June 2026, an estimated 1.98 million people (94 per cent of Gaza's population) require shelter assistance and non-food items (NFIs). More than half of the population (58%) faces critical or catastrophic shelter needs, which means that they face severe deficiencies in shelter conditions or access to essential services and NFIs, exposing them to serious health, safety and dignity risks. Some 84 per cent of households experience severe living condition constraints, including inadequate protection from weather conditions. The findings highlight exposure to environmental hazards, deteriorating temporary shelters, and limited access to essential services and housing repairs.

While these findings stress the need for timely support in preparing for the rainy season, such efforts are held back because stocks of shelter materials and NFIs are largely depleted, due to Israeli access restrictions and funding shortfalls. Shelter response is also limited because much of the land suitable for the establishment of safer displacement sites is off limits for most Palestinians, as Israeli authorities continue imposing access restrictions on most of the Gaza Strip’s area (south, east and north of the “Yellow Line” and beyond). Without adequate support, hundreds of thousands of people, including those living in damaged homes, makeshift shelters and overcrowded displacement sites, will face heightened risks of flooding, illness, malnutrition and cold-related health complications, particularly among children, elderly people and other vulnerable groups.

Meanwhile, attempts by the de facto authorities to inspect humanitarian warehouses for alleged contraband continue. Between 27 July and 24 August, UN recorded at least four requests from the de facto authorities to search humanitarian warehouses, causing disruptions to humanitarian operations and breaching the inviolability of United Nations premises. No contraband was found.

Incoming Supplies

According to data collected by the Logistics Cluster, the UN and partners’ aid offloading rate, representing the proportion of truckloads successfully offloaded at Kerem Shalom against those authorized to be manifested each day, stood at 86 per cent, consistent with the previous reporting period. The Egyptian corridor continued to face the highest levels of truck returns and rejections, with an offloading rate of 76 per cent, consistent with the previous reporting period. The Ashdod route was the most utilized entry route for UN and partners’ humanitarian cargo during the reporting period, accounting for 45 per cent of all truckloads entering Gaza. By contrast, the use of the Jordan corridor declined compared with the previous reporting period. Kerem Shalom remained the only operational crossing point for cargo.

The UN is only able to confirm the entry of supplies tracked by UN 2720. For breakdowns of those, see the online UN 2720 Mechanism Dashboard.

For a detailed account of the latest humanitarian operations in Gaza, see Annex 1 below.

title: UNRWA Situation Report #233 on the Humanitarian Crisis in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem [EN/AR]
content:
All information updated for 12 - 25 August 2026 [1]
Days 1039 - 1052 since the start of the war in the Gaza Strip

Highlights

The occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem

  • Israeli forces forcibly entered the UNRWA Kalandia Training Centre in occupied East Jerusalem on 25 August. UNRWA subsequently released a statement on the Kalandia Training Centre.
  • Two Palestinian children were killed in separate incidents in the occupied West Bank between 21 and 23 August, one by Israeli settlers during an attack on Khirbet Hamrush and another by Israeli forces during a search operation at Askar Camp.

The Gaza Strip

  • Airstrikes by Israeli forces continued to affect areas where civilians reside, hindering humanitarian operations and increasing risks to personnel and infrastructure. Over the reporting period, temporary evacuation orders affected several UNRWA installations in Gaza City and the Middle Area, resulting in temporary displacement and shelter-in-place measures.
  • UNRWA and other humanitarian actors continue to face mounting operational challenges including the prolonged shortage of lubricant oil, spare parts, and other critical supplies required to maintain generators, vehicles, and operational equipment. Just one third of generators and half of UNRWA vehicles remain operational.
  • On 20 August 2026, an UNRWA school was reportedly impacted indirectly by Israeli forces fire in the vicinity of Beit Lahiya Project Area, north of Gaza City. One internally displaced child was reportedly seriously injured in the incident and later pronounced dead the same day, while receiving medical treatment at hospital.
  • Two new UNRWA Temporary Learning Spaces opened during the reporting period, in Southern Gaza City and in Rafah area respectively, further expanding access to learning for nearly 2,500 children. UNRWA’s summer learning activities also continued, reaching over 47,000 children over the reporting period.

title: UNICEF Cameroon Cholera Outbreak Flash Update No. 3, 23 July-24 August 2026
content:
Situation Update

• During epidemiological week 34, two additional health districts, Maroua II and Mokolo, reported laboratory-confirmed cholera cases, bringing the total number of confirmed affected districts to 10: Mada, Makary, Kousseri, Fotokol, Kolofata, Mora, Maroua I, Maroua II, Maroua III and Mokolo. In addition, Mozogo and Gazawa health districts remain under suspected cholera status. This expansion reflects the continued geographic spread of cholera across the Far North Region and underscores the need for sustained surveillance and response efforts in affected and at-risk areas.

• Children and adolescents remain particularly at risk, with a median age of 12 years among reported cases. The age of affected individuals ranges from 3 months to 87 years, highlighting that the outbreak is affecting all age groups, while placing a significant burden on children.

• UNICEF continues to support the government-led response across key sectors, including Health, Water, Hygiene, and Sanitation (WASH), Social and Behavior Change (SBC), Accountability to Affected Population, Child Protection, Youth participation, Nutrition and overall response coordination.

title: IOM Colombia Earthquake Response - Situation Report #6 (28 August 2026)
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

On 10 August 2026, at 7:34 a.m., a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck, with its epicenter in San José del Palmar, Chocó Department. Given the scale of the emergency, the National Government declared a national disaster and an Economic, Social and Ecological Emergency. Since then, Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Risaralda and Caldas have remained priority departments due to the extent of the impact.
In Colombia, emergency response is led by the National Government, within the framework of the National System for Disaster Risk Management (SNGRD) and under the coordination of the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD). At the territorial level, departmental and municipal authorities, together with UNGRD local staff, guide the identification of needs and response priorities.
The international humanitarian community complements the Government-led response by aligning its capacities with the priorities identified by the authorities. Coordination takes place at the national level through the Humanitarian Country Team (EHP) and, at the departmental level, through the Local Coordination Teams (ELCs), in coordination with territorial authorities.

title: Nepal Flash Floods: UN Women Gender Alert #1 (29 August 2026)
content:
On 26 August 2026, severe flooding along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers affected communities across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan districts, causing loss of life, displacement and damage to homes, infrastructure, agricultural land and livelihoods. An estimated 157,050 women and girls living in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts have been impacted directly and indirectly.

The differentiated impacts on women and girls are not yet fully known. Initial information points to heightened risks associated with displacement and protection, access to safe WASH and essential health services, food and nutrition insecurity, loss of livelihoods and increased unpaid care responsibilities, and barriers to accessing humanitarian assistance and participating in recovery.

This Gender Alert draws on available emergency information, initial reporting from women’s rights organizations, pre-crisis gender data and evidence from previous disasters in Nepal to identify emerging gender risks and priority actions for the humanitarian response.

title: IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 15 (17-23 August 2026)
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Angola, Burundi
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

According to the World Health Organization, as of 22 August 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported 5,514 confirmed cases and 198 suspected cases of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease (BVD), with a case fatality ratio of 48 per cent and 1,200 recoveries. The outbreak remains a significant public health concern due to continued transmission in affected areas. The evolving outbreak continues to unfold in a complex humanitarian context characterized by population displacement, insecurity and constrained access to health services in affected areas. Continued armed-group activity and localized security incidents in parts of Ituri Province pose operational challenges for response activities, underscoring the need for sustained access, coordination and risk mitigation measures to support implementation of critical public health interventions. These challenges, coupled with ongoing transmission across multiple provinces, reinforce the importance of sustained investments in disease surveillance, early detection, infection prevention and control (IPC), community engagement and case referral systems to support timely response measures and reduce the risk of further spread. Population mobility and cross-border movements remain key considerations for outbreak preparedness and response efforts. During the reporting period, neighbouring countries continued to strengthen preparedness measures through disease surveillance, health screening, population mobility mapping, risk communication and community engagement (RCCE), cross-border coordination and capacity-building activities. These efforts support early detection and preparedness in areas at heightened risk of crossborder disease transmission. In the DRC, surveillance and mobility monitoring activities continued to support early detection and inform preparedness and response efforts in outbreak-affected areas. In line with the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) systemwide scale-up activation for infectious disease events, IOM continues to support outbreak response activities in Priority 1 countries, DRC and Uganda, while strengthening preparedness and readiness measures in neighbouring and at-risk countries.

title: Regional Situation Report: Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak 1 - 31 July 2026
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda
content:
While Uganda declared the end of its Ebola outbreak on 28 July 2026, the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to escalate rapidly, becoming the second-largest Ebola epidemic on record.

The outbreak is triggering a catastrophic secondary reproductive health emergency. Widespread fear of health facility transmission, coupled with stigma and misinformation, is causing pregnant women to abandon facility-based antenatal care and deliveries, leading to a concerning increase in maternal deaths.

At the same time, contraceptive uptake has declined sharply, with use of short-acting oral contraceptive pills falling by 62.5% and injectable contraceptives by 54.3%. This is particularly concerning in an area with more than 360,000 women of reproductive age, where access to contraception plays a critical role in enabling women to avoid unintended pregnancies at a time when pregnancy carries heightened risks.

To address the rising number of maternal deaths, UNFPA is working closely with partners to scale up risk communication and community engagement, improve the quality of care for pregnant women, and ensure continuity of essential sexual and reproductive health services. In July, UNFPA reached 82,291 people with reproductive health services through operational support provided across 130 health facilities and four Ebola treatment centres. UNFPA also distributed reproductive health kits to 34 health facilities in the affected area, which will support an additional 11,240 people.

UNFPA also scaled up gender-based violence prevention and response activities, as the socio-economic disruptions caused by the outbreak have adversely affected livelihoods and further heightened vulnerability to gender-based violence, including sexual exploitation and abuse. In July, UNFPA and its partners reached 129,380 people with prevention and response interventions.

As the Ebola outbreak continues to escalate in the DRC, with other countries remaining at high risk, urgent funding is needed to sustain life-saving reproductive health and protection services while strengthening prevention and preparedness efforts. UNFPA requires a total of US$20.8 million for the Ebola response, but as of 31 July, only 17 per cent of this amount had been funded.

title: Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus - Democratic Republic of the Congo
content:
Since the last Disease Outbreak News was published on 14 August 2026, the outbreak has spread from 54 to 60 health zones. The number of affected provinces stands at six out of 26 provinces of the country: Bas-Uélé, Haut-Uélé, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, and Tshopo. Six additional health zones reported cases since the last update - Ganga and Viadana health zones in Bas-Uélé province, Biena, Manguredjipa, and Mutwanga in North Kivu, and Tshopo health zone in Tshopo province. As of 26 August 2026, a total of 5794 confirmed cases, including 2786 deaths, have been reported, corresponding to a crude case fatality ratio (CFR) of 48.1%. These figures demonstrate a substantial increase in the scale and geographic extent of the outbreak over the past three months. The crude case fatality ratio of 48% underscores the severity of the disease and ongoing challenges related to timely case detection, access to and quality of clinical care, and effective interruption of viral transmission. Delays in recognizing cases increase the likelihood of onward transmission within households, communities and healthcare facilities. The outbreak remains a public health emergency of international concern, following the advice of Emergency Committee meeting convened on 18 August.

Since the previous Disease Outbreak News was published on 14 August 2026, additional confirmed cases and deaths of BVD have been reported only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Cumulatively as of 26 August 2026, 5815 confirmed cases have been reported: 5794 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (including two cases diagnosed in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and subsequently treated in Germany), 20 in Uganda and one in France. A total of 2788 deaths have been reported, including two in Uganda. As of 26 August, at least 1314 patients have recovered, including 1293 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, 18 in Uganda, two in Germany and one in France.

As of 27 August, the 42-day enhanced monitoring period, as per international guidance, has been completed in both France and Uganda.

The continuing intensity of transmission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo means that the risk of further exportation across international borders remains. Entry and exit health screening and surveillance measures are in place at airports, ports and official land border crossings; however, movement through informal border crossing routes may occur, presenting an ongoing risk of virus exportation, importation and onward transmission. Therefore, cross‑border collaboration, and sustained surveillance and preparedness are essential to prevent further regional spread and ensure an effective public health response.

On 27 August, vaccination of health care workers using the Ervebo vaccine was initiated in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in some areas, including in Kisangani, Tshopo province. Although Ervebo is a safe vaccine, and effective against Ebola virus disease, it is not known whether it provides protection against the Bundibugyo virus in humans. Thus, starting a clinical trial of the vaccine, alongside this wider use, is key to provide important new evidence and inform future use of the vaccine.

The second IHR Emergency Committee meeting regarding the epidemic of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo took place on 18 August. Following the advice of the Committee, the Director-General agreed that the ongoing outbreak remains a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, and issued updated temporary recommendations to countries.

Figure 1. Distribution of cumulative confirmed cases of Bundibugyo virus disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as of 26 August

Democratic Republic of the Congo

Since 14 August 2026 when the last Disease Outbreak News was published, an additional 1129 confirmed cases, including 602 confirmed deaths, have been reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Although part of this increase likely reflects expanded surveillance, enhanced laboratory testing, improved diagnostic capacity, and periodic data backlog reconciliation, the sustained rise in number of cases and deaths are the result of continued transmission and substantial outbreak expansion. As of 26 August 2026, a total of 5794 confirmed cases, including 2786 deaths (CFR 48.1%), have been reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. To date, 1293 patients have recovered.

Cases have been reported from 60 health zones (HZ) across six provinces. Ituri has 28 health zones affected out of 36, followed by North Kivu (15/34), Haut-Uélé (6/13), Tshopo (7/23), South Kivu (1/34) and Bas Uélé (3/11). The most recently affected province, Bas-Uélé, started reporting cases since 12 August. The most recently affected health zones are Biena and Manguredjipa in North Kivu province. As of 26 August, of the 60 affected health zones, 81 new confirmed cases were reported in the last 24 hours from 19 health zones in Ituri, North Kivu, Haut-Uélé, and Tshopo provinces. Ituri remains the epicentre of the outbreak, with 4802 confirmed cases reported since the start of the outbreak, including 52 new confirmed cases reported in the last 24 hours, as of 26 August. Nord-Kivu is the second most affected province, with a cumulative number of 775 confirmed cases, including 22 reported in the last 24 hours, as of 26 August. The highest CFR (68%) in this outbreak has been reported from North Kivu province; the reasons for this high CFR are under investigation.

The number of individuals requiring contact monitoring has also increased substantially as the outbreak has expanded. As of 26 August, the proportion of contacts followed up in the last 24 hours is at 82.3% (22 091 seen out of 26 850 to follow up). The large number of contacts reflects the scale of potential exposure within affected communities.

The outbreak is unfolding in a conflict-affected humanitarian context marked by insecurity, armed violence, and large-scale displacement. More than 26 million people face acute food insecurity, and an estimated one million internally displaced people live in Ituri Province alone. Insecurity and displacement disrupt access to health care and essential services, restrict access for response teams, and impede surveillance, case investigation and contact follow-up. Overcrowding, limited water, sanitation and hygiene services, and restricted access to healthcare in mining communities, informal settlements and sites for internally displaced people further hinder early detection, infection prevention, and appropriate care. These conditions also make it harder to implement response measures consistently and to reach affected populations.

Figure 2: Number of confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, by date of notification, as of 26 August 2026

Figure 3: Number of deaths among confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo by date of notification, as of 26 August 2026

Between 18 May and 28 August 2026, enhanced public health intelligence conducted by WHO identified 76 Ebola-related signals across 23 countries and territories, supporting rapid verification, risk assessment and information sharing with national authorities through IHR National Focal Points. Most signals, 92% (70/76), including suspected cases among travellers and health-care workers and reports circulating in public sources, were subsequently ruled out through investigation and laboratory testing. The remaining six were confirmed as Ebola events.

Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) is a severe Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, one of the Orthoebolavirus species. It is a zoonotic disease, with fruit bats suspected to be the natural reservoir.

Human infection is thought to occur through close contact with the blood or secretions of infected wildlife, such as bats or non-human primates, and it subsequently spreads from person-to-person through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs, or other bodily fluids of infected individuals or contaminated surfaces and materials. Transmission is particularly amplified in health-care settings when IPC measures are inadequate and during unsafe burial practices involving direct contact with deceased individuals.

The incubation period for BVD ranges from two to 21 days, and infected individuals are not infectious until symptom onset. Early symptoms such as fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache, and sore throat are non-specific, which complicates clinical diagnosis and can delay detection. These symptoms then progress to gastrointestinal symptoms, organ dysfunction, and, in some cases, haemorrhagic manifestations.

CFRs in the past two BVD outbreaks, reported in Uganda and in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2007 and 2012, were 30% and 50%, respectively.

Differentiating BVD from other endemic febrile illnesses such as malaria is challenging without laboratory confirmation using PCR or antigen- or antibody-based assays. Outbreak control relies on rapid case identification, isolation and care, contact tracing, safe burials and strong community engagement, as no approved vaccines or specific treatments currently exist for BVD.

Since first detected in May 2026, this BVD outbreak has rapidly evolved into a large and geographically expanding epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with sustained transmission, high mortality and an increasing risk of further international spread. The current outbreak is the second documented Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the country, after the 2012 outbreak, and the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo irrespective of Ebola virus species. The population at greatest risk of exposure is concentrated in communities living in and moving through areas with active transmission.

For detailed information about the ongoing public health response actions by the Ministry of Health, WHO and partners please refer to the latest situation reports published by the WHO Regional Office for Africa: Ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo | WHO | Regional Office for Africa

Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in collaboration with WHO and partners, are continuing to implement and coordinate extensive public health measures, including disease surveillance, laboratory testing, infection prevention and control, clinical care, community engagement, research, logistics and support for response interventions and essential health services, engaging donors and mobilizing additional resources to address critical funding gaps and sustain response operations across affected and at-risk areas. A substantial scale-up is ongoing across all response pillars to get ahead of the outbreak.

On 14 August 2026, WHO reassessed the risk of the outbreak of BVD to incorporate newly available information. The risk for countries sharing land borders with the Democratic Republic of the Congo was separated from the risk for other countries in the African Region.

The risk in the Democratic Republic of the Congo was assessed as very high due to ongoing transmission and the continued expansion of the outbreak into new health zones, increasing the potential for further national and regional spread. The main considerations supporting this assessment include the substantial increase in the number of cases and considerable geographic extension of the outbreak since the previous risk assessment, and potential further increase in CFR as additional deaths are investigated and outcomes are established. In addition, reported transmission among healthcare workers, ongoing conflict and insecurity, laboratory capacity constraints, and absence of licensed vaccine or specific antiviral treatment were also considered as factors maintaining the very high risk.

The risk for countries sharing land borders with the Democratic Republic of the Congo was again assessed as high due to sustained population mobility linked to cross-border trade and mining activities, variation in capacities and experience of BVD response, and variable levels of readiness. Uganda, the Central African Republic and South Sudan are of particular concern for importation given their proximity, high population mobility and connectivity with areas of the Democratic Republic of the Congo currently experiencing intense transmission. For the Central African Republic and South Sudan, these risks are further compounded by high humanitarian needs, population displacement, insecurity and underlying limitations in health-system capacity.

The risk for the rest of the African region and at the global level was again assessed as low.

Based on the currently available information, WHO advises against any restriction of travel to, or trade with, affected countries. WHO continues to closely monitor and, where necessary, verify travel and trade measures in relation to this event.

The updated Temporary Recommendations issued to States Parties on 24 August 2026 underscore the importance of coordinated outbreak control, strengthened cross‑border collaboration, and sustained surveillance and preparedness to prevent further regional spread and ensure an effective public health response. Rapid recognition of cases, testing and optimized supportive care can reduce mortality, and improve community perceptions and acceptance of health care within the response.

On 7 August, the WHO Technical Advisory Group on candidate vaccine prioritization released a report regarding possible candidate vaccines for Bundibugyo virus disease. The members recommended that Ervebo, the only licensed Ebola vaccine (previously known as ebolavirus Zaire), be prioritized for inclusion in a randomized clinical trial in the context of the ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

In addition, WHO is sponsoring a clinical trial to find effective treatments against BVD. The trial began enrollment on 2 July. The trial, known as the PARTNERS trial, is now open in three different clinical management facilities in Ituri province and has enrolled over 250 people who are confirmed cases.

title: Situation Report on Mpox Multi-Country: Outbreak Response - Region of the Americas, Issue 3/2026, published 28 August 2026
content:
01 Summary

Global and regional snapshot of the mpox outbreak

Between 2022 and 30 June 2026, a total of 185,565 confirmed cases of mpox have been reported globally from 145 countries and territories. The Region of the Americas accounts for the largest proportion of cases (39.7%), followed by the African (37.3%) and European (17.9%) Regions [1]. In the Region of the Americas, as of 31 July 2026, a cumulative total of 74,888 confirmed cases of mpox, including 166 deaths, have been reported across 31 countries and territories between 2022 and 2026. In 2026, 11 countries have reported a combined 1,203 mpox cases and three deaths: Argentina, Bolivia (Plurinational State of), Brazil, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Mexico, Peru, and the United States (Figure 1). Over the past three months, Costa Rica, and Chile each confirmed their first case of mpox clade Ib, while the United States, Canada, and Colombia reported additional clade Ib cases during the same period. To date, nine countries in the Region have reported a cumulative total of 77 clade Ib cases: the United States (50)1, Canada (8), Brazil (5), Colombia (5), Mexico (3), Argentina (2), Costa Rica (2), Ecuador (1), and Chile (1). Most clade Ib cases reported in the Region to date have occurred in individuals with recent travel to areas with documented clade Ib transmission, or in individuals with an identified epidemiological link to a traveler or confirmed case. However, the United States has recently reported a clade I case without a history of international travel or identifiable epidemiological link to a traveler or confirmed case in July 2026. The most recent mpox clade Ib case in Canada, reported in July 2026, was confirmed to be locally acquired, with no history of international travel or contact with confirmed cases.

title: Nepal: Rasuwa Flood Flash Update #3 (As of 28 August 2026)
content:
This report is produced by the Office of the United Nations Resident Coordinator in Nepal, in collaboration with humanitarian partners and the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA). It covers the period from 26 to 27 August 2026.

HIGHLIGHTS

  • Flash floods swept down the Trishuli River corridor into Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Gorkha districts on 26 August, damaging homes, roads, schools, health posts and farmland.
  • Families are sheltering at five known displacement sites in Nuwakot district. The whereabouts of people displaced in other districts are still being confirmed.
  • Damaged roads and landslides continue to block humanitarian access, delaying assessments and slowing relief to some of the worst hit communities.
  • Health, nutrition, protection, shelter and WASH partners are scaling up support alongside Government led search and rescue operations.
  • Women, children, older people and people with disabilities face heightened protection risks, including gender-based violence and family separation, in areas where services were already limited before the floods.
  • The National Emergency Operations Centre (NEOC), Ministry of Home Affairs, reports 539 people confirmed dead and 977 missing as of 28 August, alongside 73 injured. Search and rescue operations continue, and these figures are expected to change as verification proceeds.
  • Government-led search and rescue operations have mobilized 12,249 security personnel and 15 helicopters, rescuing 3,742 people to date.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Two days after flash floods swept down the Trishuli River corridor from Rasuwa into Nuwakot, Dhading and Gorkha districts on 26 August, families across the affected districts are still taking stock of what they have lost. Search and rescue teams continue to work through damaged and cut off communities, while broken roads, landslides and disrupted communications are slowing relief and a full accounting of needs.

The scale of casualties from the floods is becoming clearer. NEOC reported 538 bodies recovered as of 28 August: 221 in Chitwan, 134 in Nuwakot (east), 46 in Gorkha, 37 in Kavrepalanchok, 34 in Dhading, 28 in Tanahun, 27 in Nuwakot (west) and 12 in Rasuwa. NEOC also reported 977 people missing: 105 personnel from the Nepal Army, Nepal Police, Armed Police Force and customs and immigration offices, 228 reported by District Emergency Operations Centres in Rasuwa (161), Kavrepalanchok (66) and Nuwakot (1), and 644 foreign or overseas resident nationals, comprising 517 foreign nationals and 127 Nepali nationals normally resident abroad. A further 73 people were reported injured, in Rasuwa (43), Nuwakot (27) and Dhading (3). These figures are based on initial Government reporting and are likely to change as search and verification efforts continue.

Search and rescue operations have rescued 3,742 people to date. The Government has mobilized 12,249 security personnel, including 4,243 from the Nepal Army, 4,348 from Nepal Police and 3,658 from the Armed Police Force, alongside 15 helicopters, 6 from the Nepal Army and 9 from the private sector, to support search, rescue and relief delivery to hard to reach areas.

The Government of Nepal is leading the response, with clusters activated for camp coordination and camp management, shelter, health, nutrition, food security and water, sanitation and hygiene. Humanitarian partners are providing technical and operational support under this national leadership. Thirteen municipalities across the four worst hit districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Gorkha have been identified as most affected, and several are likely to be declared disaster crisis zones.

Displacement figures are still preliminary. Five known sites in Nuwakot district are together sheltering more than 1,000 displaced people against a combined capacity of 1,350. The whereabouts of people displaced from other districts are not yet known. Food security partners estimate that at least 20,000 households across Rasuwa and Nuwakot, with impacts also reported downstream in Dhading, Gorkha, Chitwan and Tanahun, may need immediate food assistance. Around 18,000 households, more than 50,000 people, need emergency water, sanitation and hygiene support. Sixty-nine schools with almost 19,000 enrolled students sit within 500 metres of the affected riverbanks, and at least 23 will need to be rehabilitated. Nutrition partners estimate that some 17,000 children, 1,500 pregnant and breastfeeding women and 9,000 adolescents need immediate nutrition support.

Protection concerns are growing for the women, children and other vulnerable people caught up in this crisis. Displacement and the disruption of search and rescue are raising the risk of gender-based violence, family separation and trafficking, particularly for women, girls and unaccompanied children. These risks are more serious because protection and referral services were already limited or absent in several affected areas before the floods struck.

The damage to infrastructure and livelihoods is still being verified. Early estimates point to around 45 kilometres of damaged transport corridors and more than 11,000 hectares of damaged land, including some 2,732 hectares of lost agricultural land. Working alongside the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, humanitarian partners are scaling up distributions of food, shelter materials, non-food items, dignity kits and health supplies, while preparing more detailed assessment and response plans as access improves.

In addition the Cabinet of Ministers lifted the tax duties related to relief items entering the country and lifted the One Door policy where all humanitarian relief items had to be centralized and delivered by the government only.

title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #26 (25 to 27 August 2026)
content:
Situation Report No. 26 provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 25 to 27 August 2026.

Highlights

Between 25 and 27 August, IOM continued its multisectoral response in temporary camps and affected communities through interventions in Shelter and Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM), Health, Protection, Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), information management, and Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA). During the reporting period, IOM maintained the co-management of four temporary camps in La Guaira, supported preparedness actions for heavy rainfall, strengthened inter-agency coordination, and accompanied ongoing food assistance transition processes.

IOM provided 314 health and mental health consultations in the César Nieves and José María Vargas Sports Complex temporary camps, covering general medicine, internal medicine, paediatrics, gynaecology, psychiatry and psychology. Since the beginning of activities, IOM-supported health services have reached a cumulative total of 9,004 consultations in César Nieves and 5,225 consultations in the José María Vargas Sports Complex.

Through its implementing partner HIAS, IOM provided protection services to 191 people in La Guaira and the Capital District, including legal counselling, psychosocial support, case management and referrals. In addition, IOM coordinated the distribution of 200 personal hygiene kits and 200 cleaning kits in Campo de Golf and supported a nearby spontaneous settlement through the delivery of 50 mattresses, 50 pillows and 50 bed sheets.

IOM Activities

IOM maintained the management of the José María Vargas Sports Complex and Campo de Golf temporary camps and continued the co-management of the César Nieves and Mare Abajo II sites together with the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC). Across the sites, IOM continued population monitoring, service coordination, infrastructure improvements and support to food assistance transition processes. In César Nieves, camp signage was completed and two vulnerable families received shelter support, while voluntary departures and the start of housing rehabilitation activities were observed at the José María Vargas Sports Complex.

IOM’s Non-Food Items (NFI) teams conducted assessments to identify additional needs in temporary camps. During the reporting period, through its implementing partner Fundación Vivienda Popular, IOM distributed 146 tarpaulins, 73 kitchen sets and 65 hygiene items. To date, IOM has distributed 9,622 tarpaulins, 6,478 collapsible jerrycans, 4,815 shelter tool kits, 5,960 kitchen sets and 3,677 personal hygiene items. IOM also organized a Camp Coordination and Camp Management workshop in Ezequiel Zamora (La Zamorera) temporary camp in Miranda State, bringing together 44 community representatives, authorities and site management stakeholders.

In WASH, IOM continued coordinating and monitoring water, sanitation and hygiene services across temporary camps. In Campo de Golf, IOM led emergency preparedness measures for rainfall, coordinated the development of an emergency drainage plan, monitored water quality and maintained the operation of the water treatment plant, which has produced a cumulative 98,000 litres of safe water since installation. In Mare Abajo II, IOM coordinated mitigation measures following regional water supply disruptions linked to failures at the Punta Gorda treatment plant and supported improvements to sanitation infrastructure and waste management systems.

IOM continued delivering health and mental health services through fixed and mobile modalities. In Campo de Golf, IOM led the Health Technical Working Group and promoted the establishment of a unified epidemiological surveillance system and population profiling mechanisms. In César Nieves, IOM maintained regular medical and psychological consultations and strengthened coordination for access to medicines. In Mare Abajo II, IOM coordinated sexual and reproductive health, nutrition and psychological support activities with specialized partners.

Through protection teams and its implementing partner HIAS, IOM continued providing legal counselling, psychosocial support, case management and referrals. In Campo de Golf, IOM led the Protection Technical Working Group and supported activities focused on child protection, prevention of violence against women and girls, and community coexistence. In César Nieves, IOM advanced the development of community rules of coexistence and reinforced child safeguarding measures, while in Mare Abajo II it led protection coordination efforts and strengthened information management mechanisms. At the José María Vargas Sports Complex, IOM continued protection referrals and monitored community concerns related to rumours about camp closure and relocation processes.

IOM continued population registration and information management activities through the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) and other site management systems. During the reporting period, DTM teams updated demographic information in César Nieves and registered three newly arrived families in Mare Abajo II to facilitate access to services and assistance.

As part of its inter-agency coordination role, IOM participated in coordination spaces aimed at reducing duplication of assistance, improving service coverage, strengthening referral pathways and harmonizing distributed relief items across humanitarian actors. In addition, the Shelter, Land and Settlements Coordination Cluster, co-led by IOM and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), held its second meeting of the month to provide operational updates and strengthen coordination among partners.

In PSEA, IOM conducted capacity-building sessions for community leaders and representatives in Mare Abajo II and the José María Vargas Sports Complex and continued promoting community information mechanisms and the integration of protection and safety considerations across the temporary camps under its management.

IOM Planned Response

IOM will continue supporting return, relocation and camp transition processes while strengthening site management, infrastructure monitoring and rainfall mitigation measures in temporary camps.

IOM will maintain health, mental health, protection, WASH and PSEA activities, including epidemiological surveillance, referral mechanisms, psychological support services, water and sanitation interventions, and community protection initiatives.

In addition, IOM will continue population registration and movement tracking, information management activities, coordination with authorities and humanitarian partners, and efforts to strengthen evidence-based planning for return, relocation and camp closure processes.

title: Nepal Catastrophic Flash Flood Rasuwa-Trishuli, Nepal (26 August 2026)
content:
Snapshot of Key Concerns

Severity: A glacial collapse on the Tibet side of the border of Nepal sent a catastrophic surge down the Lhende Khola into the Bhote Koshi River. The collapse was large enough to register seismically with USGS and trigger a massive flood downstream in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and Chitwan districts.

Timing: Morning of August 26, 2026, floodwaters traveled down the Trishuli River as far as Mugling before beginning to recede. Damage spans the corridor from Timure through Syabrubesi, Betrawati, and Trishuli Bazaar.

Key Concerns: Impacted communities are in extremely remote, difficult-to-access areas. Numerous roads and bridges have been washed out, and other critical infrastructure including communications and hydropower have been severly damaged according to PDC’s AI for Humanity. This has constrained search and rescue efforts. Helicopters are the primary means of access, and adverse weather intermittently grounded flights.

title: Nepal Landslides & Flash Floods: Situation Report #1 (August 27, 2026)
content:
Project HOPE's Emergency Response Team is in Nepal, mobilizing a response to devastating landslides and flash floods caused by a massive glacier avalanche.

Situational Context

On the morning of August 26, 2026, a glacier avalanche near the border between Nepal and China sent tons of rock, mud, and ice into nearby rivers. This disaster triggered massive floods, powerful landslides, and registered a force equal to a 5.2-magnitude earthquake, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. As a result, entire villages have been wiped out and there have been significant impacts to critical infrastructure, including major roads, bridges, and electricity systems.

Initial reports put the death toll over 360, with figures expected to rise as search and rescue efforts continue. At least 1,400 people are reported missing, including tourists from as many as 27 different countries, including the United States. Many visitors in the affected area were there for the Nepali festival of Janai Purnima on Friday or on pilgrimage to Tibet’s Mount Kailash, a sacred site for Hindus.

Conditions remain dangerous in Nepal, with weather forecasts predicting three days of heavy rain and this disaster making the ongoing monsoon season even more of a threat to affected communities. Additionally, yesterday’s landslides formed a new lake, which now poses a significant risk as new bodies of water are at an increased risk of further landslides, mudslides, and flash floods.
