title: IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 13 (3-9 August 2026)
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Angola, Central African Republic
content:
According to the World Health Organization, as of 10 August, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported 4,449 confirmed cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus (BVD), including 2,061 deaths.

With the recent increase in reported cases, the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak has become the largest and fastest-growing outbreak ever reported in DRC. The rapidly escalating outbreak is unfolding against the backdrop of an ongoing triple crisis in eastern DRC, where health risks, large-scale displacement and persistent conflict intersect. Displaced populations living in camps face complex and multidimensional needs requiring coordinated, multisectoral interventions. Across affected areas, most deaths continue to occur within communities, underscoring the urgent need to strengthen contact tracing and community event-based surveillance to support earlier detection, referral and response.

The spread of the outbreak into Tshopo and Haut-Uélé Provinces underscores continued need to comprehensively address the mobility dimensions of the ongoing public health response. While no positive Ebola case has been reported on vessels arriving via riverine routes in Kinshasa, heightened transmission risks require strengthened coordination and vigilance at points of control (PoCs) along the river to prevent further geographic spread. In parallel, the rising number of cases in Haut-Uélé requires enhanced disease surveillance and cross-border coordination to prevent disease transmission into neighbouring South Sudan and the Central African Republic (CAR).

During the reporting period, key highlights include :

  • 4,449 confirmed Ebola cases and 2,061 deaths in the DRC as of 10 August 2026, making this the largest and fastest-growing Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the country.
  • Over 16.5 million health screenings supported at 225 points of entry and points of control across affected and at-risk countries.
  • During the reporting period, IOM supported 2.57 million health screenings in the DRC alone
  • More than 13.1 million individuals reached through risk communication and community engagement activities.
  • Trained 575 health workers in Rwanda on Ebola detection, infection prevention and control, surveillance, and response measures.
  • Continued to strengthen surveillance and preparedness capacities along critical mobility corridors, including riverine routes into Kinshasa and border areas near South Sudan and the Central African Republic.

The outbreak continues to unfold in a complex operational environment marked by insecurity, displacement, and population mobility. As transmission persists in eastern DRC, sustained investment in surveillance, border health measures, community engagement, and support to displaced and mobile populations remains critical to containing the outbreak and preventing cross-border spread. Learn more HERE

title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #22 (11 to 13 August 2026)
content:
Situation Report No. 22 provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 11 to 13 August 2026.

Highlights

  • IOM coordinated the distribution of approximately 1,700 non-food item (NFI) kits in Mare Abajo and surrounding communities, expanding assistance to households affected by the earthquakes.
  • IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) assessed 110 community settlements, identifying 4,733 households and 12,127 individuals in La Guaira, Capital District, Carabobo and Miranda to inform the response beyond temporary camps.
  • IOM completed the operational closure of Playa Grande, supporting the relocation of families and finalizing the removal of humanitarian infrastructure from the temporary camp.

IOM Activities

IOM continued the co-management of the temporary camps at José María Vargas Sports Complex, Campo de Golf, Mare Abajo and César Nieves, three of them jointly with the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC), ensuring service coordination, population registration and needs monitoring. In Mare Abajo, IOM coordinated the distribution of approximately 1,700 non-food item kits, following registration activities, household verification and community mobilization efforts to facilitate access to assistance.

IOM strengthened information management mechanisms through updated camp records and the rapid assessment of 110 community settlements, identifying 4,733 households and 12,127 individuals across four affected states. IOM also advanced preparations for a household survey to strengthen needs analysis and assistance planning.

In the health sector, IOM and its partner Ven Da Tu Mano continued providing mobile health and mental health services in temporary camps. During the reporting period, teams conducted 445 consultations at José María Vargas Sports Complex and 230 consultations in César Nieves, maintaining follow-up for chronic diseases and reinforcing surveillance of diarrhoeal syndromes, particularly among children.

Protection activities included coordination to facilitate access to specialized services, strengthen referral mechanisms and improve coordination among humanitarian actors. In César Nieves, IOM promoted the establishment of a technical protection coordination space to strengthen service coordination and the follow-up of individuals with specific protection needs.

IOM also facilitated inter-agency coordination spaces to strengthen distribution planning, update available services and improve referral mechanisms and needs monitoring in temporary camps. In addition, IOM completed the operational closure of Playa Grande, supporting family relocations and the progressive withdrawal of humanitarian infrastructure.

IOM Planned Response

IOM plans to:

  • Continue coordinating planned non-food item distributions in Mare Abajo and surrounding communities, preventing duplication and ensuring appropriate targeting of assistance.
  • Follow up on infrastructure gaps identified in Mare Abajo, particularly shower drainage and tent anchoring systems.
  • Maintain surveillance and medical follow-up of diarrhoeal syndromes, particularly among children and adolescents, and support continuity of treatment for hypertension, diabetes and other chronic diseases.
  • Strengthen referral pathways for mental health, protection and other specialized services.
  • Implement the household survey in IOM-managed temporary camps and expand needs monitoring and population movement tracking in community settlements and affected areas.
  • Maintain updated information on available services, operating hours and referral mechanisms in temporary camps.
  • Consolidate sector coordination mechanisms and strengthen systems for reporting and tracking security incidents and protection risks.

title: UNFPA Situation Report: Flash Floods and Landslides in Bangladesh (8 July - 10 August 2026)
content:
Heavy rains since 5 July, including renewed heavy rainfall in early August, have triggered widespread flooding and landslides across Bangladesh, affecting approximately 1.3 million people in seven districts of the Chattogram Division. Among those affected are an estimated 364,000 women of reproductive age, including 17,490 pregnant women.

Damaged roads, flooded pathways and landslides have isolated remote communities from hospitals, clinics and other essential services, further increasing sexual and reproductive health needs. Despite damage, a UNFPA-supported maternity facility remains operational through temporary arrangements and emergency referral mechanisms, helping ensure continuity of essential maternal health services.

Protection risks for women and girls increased as economic shocks drove reliance on negative coping strategies, including child labour and child marriage. For people displaced by the floods and landslides, overcrowded shelters, inadequate privacy and lighting, insufficient sex-segregated sanitation facilities, and shortages of menstrual hygiene supplies further compromise the safety, dignity and well-being of women and adolescent girls.

UNFPA continues to deploy essential supplies, midwives, community volunteers and mobile health services to affected areas. To date, 1,018 women and girls have accessed essential health services through four health camps and 15 deployed midwives at health facilities, while 6,326 people have been reached with gender-based violence risk mitigation support. UNFPA has also maintained seven safe spaces and distributed 4,500 dignity kits, 1,951 menstrual health management kits and 1,000 baby kits to affected women and adolescent girls.

UNFPA requires US$966,930 to ensure the continued delivery of life-saving reproductive health and protection services for affected women, girls and young people. To date, US$130,330 has been mobilized, leaving a funding gap of US$836,600. Urgent additional funding is needed to sustain and scale up critical interventions and ensure that reach those most in need.

content:
Global Overview: El Niño is strengthening. Abnormal heat continues to pose a threat across eastern Africa, Central Asia, Hispaniola, as well as areas of Central America and northern South America. Dryness is worsening in Central America and Venezuela.

Africa Weather Hazards

Dry conditions in Ethiopia are easing, parts of South Africa see snowfall, and aboveaverage rainfall along the Gulf of Guinea causes flooding.

Dry conditions in Ethiopia are easing, parts of South Africa see snowfall, and aboveaverage rainfall along the Gulf of Guinea causes flooding.

1) Inundation in the Sudd wetlands of South Sudan continues.

2) Severe rainfall deficits across large parts of East Africa over the past 90 days have led to abnormal dryness. As a result, conditions have been upgraded to "Drought" across the equatorial provinces of South Sudan and the eastern, central, and north-central regions of Ethiopia.

3) The southern part of Mali and central and eastern Liberia remain under abnormal dryness due to sustained below-average rainfall.

4) Persistent and forecast localized heavy rainfall maintains an elevated risk of flooding across coastal areas of Guinea and Sierra Leone, southeastern Nigeria, and the western part of Cameroon.

5) In the coming week, abnormal heat is expected in parts of Western Sahara, northwestern Mauritania, eastern Niger, Chad, Sudan, southeastern South Sudan, southwestern and eastern Ethiopia, and parts of Eritrea.

6) Moderate to heavy rainfall over the past weeks, along with forecast moderate to heavy rainfall, maintains a high alert for flash flooding in western Ethiopia.

7) Observed moderate to heavy rainfall over the past week, along with a few days of snowfall, could cause flooding in the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal provinces of South Africa, as well as in Lesotho and Eswatini. Likewise, forecasted heavy rainfall could lead to flooding in southern Mozambique and along the southern and eastern coasts of Madagascar.

title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #33 (14 August 2026, Time: 02:00 pm)
content:
Situation Report No. 33
Earthquakes in Venezuela
14 August 2026
Time: 2:00 pm

Highlights

  • Over 304,000 people affected by the earthquakes have accessed humanitarian assistance and essential services through a coordinated multi-sector response involving humanitarian organizations, United Nations agencies, communities, and national and local authorities.
  • As of 10 August, authorities reported 6,301 deaths and 73,356 people that received care at hospitals.
  • The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency to address the needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months.

Situation overview

Venezuela continues to face the consequences of the two major earthquakes (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5) that struck the north-central region of the country on 24 June at 18:00 local time, causing significant humanitarian impacts and damage to infrastructure. The first earthquake, measuring 7.2, was centered along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). According to a recent update from the United States Geological Survey (USGS), the second earthquake, measuring 7.5, had its epicenter 17 kilometers west of Catia La Mar, off the coast of La Guaira State.

As of 10 August, authorities reported 6,301 deaths from the earthquakes. They also reported that 73,356 people received care at hospitals and 53,314 homes were evaluated, out of which 9,567 are at high risk. According to national authorities, 23,26% of the total rubble has been cleared. A preliminary assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) estimates direct damage to housing and infrastructure at approximately US$37 billion, while preliminary estimates from UNDP place direct physical damages at US$6.7 billion, equivalent to 6 per cent of GDP.

More than one month after the earthquakes, the humanitarian response continues to expand across the affected states. As of 14 August, over 304,000 people (57% women and girls) had access to essential services and humanitarian assistance through the joint efforts of communities, humanitarian organizations, United Nations entities, donor partners, and national and local authorities.

title: Dengue in the Pacific: Multicountry Situation (As of 14 August 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• Since 1 January 2025, twelve dengue outbreaks have been reported across Pacific Island Countries and Areas (PICs).

• During 2025, dengue outbreaks were reported in American Samoa, Cook Islands, Fiji, French Polynesia, Kiribati, Naoero, Samoa, Tonga, and Tuvalu. A total of 21,258 confirmed cases and 21 deaths were recorded across the Pacific. Fatalities were reported in Fiji (n=8), Samoa (n=7), Tonga (n=3), Naoero (n=2), and Kiribati (n=1).

• Between 1 January 2026 and 2 July 2026, a total of 4 545 dengue confirmed cases, 175 hospitalisations and 3 deaths have been reported across the Pacific.

• The Pacific Syndromic Surveillance System (PSSS) has reported a total of 9 050 Dengue-like Illness (DLI) cases to date, a lower trend compared to the same period last year.

• In 2026 dengue outbreaks were officially declared in New Caledonia, Tonga and Shefa province Vanuatu.

• The most affected countries and areas in 2026 include: American Samoa, Cook Islands, Samoa, and New Caledonia. These account for 94% of confirmed cases.

• Dengue serotype-1 (DENV-1) and serotype-2 (DENV-2) are currently in circulation.

• The Cook Islands officially declared the end of its dengue outbreak on 25 May 2026.

• Tonga has officially declared the end of its dengue outbreak on 31 July 2026.

• As of 14 August 2026:

o The dengue outbreak remains ongoing in Shefa Province, Vanuatu, with dengue virus serotype 1 (DENV-1) continuing to circulate.

o Low levels of transmission are observed in American Samoa, Kiribati, New Caledonia, Samoa, Vanuatu and Wallis and Futuna.

content:
This Flash Update is produced by OCHA Colombia in collaboration with humanitarian partners, based on official reports (as of 13 August, 18:30 local time)

  • The scale of the emergency continues to grow. Heavy rainfall and related impacts have affected 53,816 people (25,872 families) across at least 13 departments and 401 municipalities nationwide, including 266 deaths and 11,789 homes destroyed. The most affected departments are Risaralda, Valle del Cauca, Chocó and Caldas. However, the emergency continues to expand and figures may increase due to access constraints and possible underreporting.
  • Humanitarian needs remain critical, particularly in rural areas. Challenges persist in reaching affected rural communities, limiting the full assessment of damage and needs. In addition to the loss of lives and homes, disruptions to essential services, including electricity, water, health care and telecommunications, have been reported, along with the suspension of classes in numerous educational institutions. Humanitarian partners continue to conduct rapid assessments to identify priority needs and guide the response.
  • The humanitarian response is being strengthened to save lives. While the Government continues to deploy its immediate response, humanitarian partners from the Humanitarian Country Team (HCT) and Local Coordination Teams (LCTs) are complementing efforts in the most affected areas. At the same time, implementation of the US$5 million allocation from the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) is advancing, prioritizing life-saving interventions in hard-to-reach rural areas with limited institutional presence and where assistance can provide immediate added value.

Coordination among national and local authorities and humanitarian partners remains essential to ensure a timely and effective response. We will continue to monitor the evolution of the emergency and support efforts to protect and assist the most affected populations.

title: NGA: Landslide - 08-2026 - Floods (2026-08-14)
content:
Description

Weeks of continuous, unprecedented torrential rainfall across Calabar, the capital of Cross River State, have triggered devastating landslides and severe flooding across multiple communities in Calabar Municipality, resulting in loss of life, widespread destruction of homes and property, and the collapse of critical infrastructure. The rainfall, described by observers as unprecedented in scale and intensity for the city, has caused the terrain to collapse in several locations, destroying buildings, roads, utility lines and agricultural investments, and threatening federal agencies and public infrastructure including a naval base and an inland waterways authority office.

The first major landslide struck Ikot Anwatim in the northern part of Calabar, where buildings caved into a gully, killing five persons including four siblings, Bright (18), Godswill (12), Daniel (11) and Richard (10) from one family. A fifth victim, Mr Udo, was also killed. A second devastating landslide occurred in the Anansa area of Obutong Community, Calabar Municipality, cutting off a key waterfront road, snapping high-tension electricity poles and damaging underground public water pipes. The collapse of the road has isolated residents, severed access to vehicles and disrupted power and municipal water supply across the affected axis. At least ten deaths have been reported across the full extent of the Calabar flooding and landslide disasters, with property worth hundreds of millions of naira destroyed.

The disaster has affected homes, shops, businesses, farmlands and major infrastructure. Community and traditional leaders in Obutong have appealed for urgent government intervention to save homes and livelihoods. The Member representing Akpabuyo, Bakassi and Calabar South Federal Constituency who also chairs the House of Representatives Committee on Disaster Management and Preparedness has called for a coordinated national and international response, warning that the scale of the crisis is beyond the capacity of the state government alone. Cross River State Governor Bassey Otu visited victims, extended financial assistance and pledged to strengthen flood mitigation and emergency response systems. The governor, upon visiting the site, described the scale of destruction and the loss of life as deeply heartbreaking.

On 4 August 2026, the Federal Government, acting through the South South Development Commission (SSDC) in collaboration with NEMA, the Nigerian Red Cross Society and the Cross River State Emergency Management Agency (CR-SEMA), conducted a comprehensive assessment of the flood and landslide-affected communities in Calabar. The assessment, led by the SSDC Managing Director, aimed to coordinate humanitarian interventions and formulate longer-term environmental resilience strategies. The NRCS was actively part of this coordinated assessment, and the figures in this report reflect findings from that exercise alongside verified media and official reporting.

title: South Sudan - Operation Overview, April - June 2026
content:
Background

South Sudan continues to face a complex humanitarian crisis driven by conflict, climate-related shocks, disease outbreaks, displacement, food insecurity and economic deterioration. Access to affected communities remains constrained by poor road conditions, seasonal flooding, and limited transport infrastructure. In this context, the WFP-led Logistics Cluster continues to enable humanitarian operations through logistics coordination, information management, capacity strengthening and common transport services, including air, river and road transport to hard-to-reach and priority locations.

Operational Highlights

• During the reporting period, the Logistics Cluster facilitated the transportation of 3,077 MT of humanitarian cargo, supporting 43 organizations and reaching 37 destinations across South Sudan.
• Road transport accounted for 46 percent of the cargo moved, followed by river transport at 39 percent and air transport at 15 percent.
• The Cluster coordinated eight humanitarian road convoys delivered approximately 1,417 MT of multisectoral supplies.
• The Logistics cluster completed 31 service requests, enabling partners to deliver critical assistance to priority and hard-to-reach locations.
• The Logistics Cluster supported the Unity State cholera response in Leer, Mayendit and Mayom by facilitating the transport of 30.2 MT of emergency relief cargo.

title: UNFPA Colombia Earthquake Flash Update (10 - 12 August 2026)
content:
On 10 August, Colombia was struck by a 7.4-magnitude earthquake, affecting 380 municipalities, with the most significant impacts reported in Chocó, the Eje Cafetero and Valle del Cauca. Preliminary reports indicate that 181 people have died and 2,754 have been injured, while search and rescue operations remain ongoing.

The earthquake’s epicentre was located in San José del Palmar, in Chocó Department. Characterized by remote and rural areas, Chocó relies heavily on river and air transport as the primary means of access, creating significant challenges for the delivery of essential services and supplies. Existing structural vulnerabilities in the department further exacerbate the impact of the disaster and the difficulties faced by affected communities.

The healthcare network has been significantly affected, with 1,172 health facilities reportedly impacted. At the same time, the surge in demand for medical care resulting from the large number of people injured has placed considerable pressure on already strained health services. Disruptions to essential healthcare services pose heightened risks to pregnant women and newborns.

Preliminary assessments indicate that more than 19,000 homes have been damaged and 3,971 destroyed, displacing thousands of people. Displacement, overcrowding in temporary shelters, disruption of community support systems and economic hardship are increasing protection risks, including gender-based violence, exploitation and abuse, particularly for women and girls.

UNFPA is on the ground, working with partners to mobilize resources and rapidly assess and respond to the most urgent sexual and reproductive health and protection needs of women, girls, adolescents and other people in vulnerable situations. Priority areas include maternal healthcare, emergency obstetric care, family planning, prevention of and response to gender-based violence, and the clinical management of rape.

title: Pakistan Rain Monitor - Issue Number 8 (11- 17 August 2026)
content:
Using remote sensing techniques, the seven-day forecast of total rainfall for the country is analyzed against the long-term average rainfall to highlight the areas which are expected to receive above normal, normal and below normal rainfall. The satellite data for a period of thirty years from 1993-2023 is extracted from CHIRPS (Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Station data) and analyzed to estimate deviation from normal rainfall. For the forecast of total precipitation for next seven days, the data is sourced from global model of ECMWF (European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts).

The satellite-based national rainfall forecast analysis for 11-18 August indicates below rainfall across most parts of the country with the exception of northern parts of GB, northern and central KP and northeastern districts of Punjab, Given the ongoing flood conditions in parts of north and central areas, additional rainfall may exacerbate the risk of flooding, GLOF and landslides, particularly in vulnerable locations across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Gilgit-Baltistan, Azad Jammu & Kashmir, and northeastern Punjab.

title: Colombia Earthquake: Situation Report #2 (August 12, 2026)
content:
Project HOPE's Emergency Response Team is on the ground in the Valle del Cauca and Risaralda departments of Colombia, rapidly assessing needs after a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck 150 miles west of Bogotá and caused widespread damage, landslides, and impacted critical infrastructure across a large geographic area.

Situational Context

There have been over 29 aftershocks since a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck near San Jose del Palmar, Colombia, and caused extensive damage across a wide geographic area that includes rural, urban, hard-to-reach, and low-income communities hundreds of miles from the epicenter. More than 357 municipalities across western Colombia have been impacted, with the full extent of the damage unknown due to internet connectivity issues.

The earthquake has damaged or destroyed more than 9,400 homes, killed at least 254 people, and injured at least 2,595 more — thousands of people are likely missing, and these numbers are expected to increase in the coming days and weeks.

Across the impacted region, 84 health facilities sustained damage and many have been forced to reduce or suspend services. In El Águila, San Rafael Hospital suffered near-complete destruction and, in Cali, Hospital Universitario del Valle Evaristo García suffered damage that forced it to move patients outside and reduce services, despite being one of the department's primary tertiary hospitals. Public officials have declared a “red alert” for hospitals in Cali as facilities are fully at capacity due to both the damage caused by the disaster and the subsequent surge of patient needs. Departments have established shelters across the region as impacted individuals attempt to avoid residing in damaged buildings. Shelters have noted the need for increased support for hygiene supplies and larger provisions of potable water. Damage to municipal water systems has left some communities without running water until assessments and repairs can be completed. Information remains limited on health, water, and medical needs in more rural areas — especially in Chocó Department — due to limited road access and connectivity issues.

title: Preliminary situation report: Earthquake in Colombia – August 10, 2026
content:
Executive Summary

On August 10, 2026, Colombia was affected by a major earthquake with a magnitude of 7.4, occurring at approximately 7:34 a.m., with its epicenter in the department of Chocó, near San José del Palmar. The earthquake was widely felt across the country and caused significant damage, particularly in Chocó and several areas of the Coffee Region.

The department of Chocó is facing a particularly complex situation due to the combination of earthquake-related damage, existing infrastructure limitations, historical access challenges, and limited local capacity to respond to an emergency of this magnitude.

According to reports available as of August 11, approximately 500 homes had been affected and around 20 structures had collapsed in San José del Palmar. In Quibdó, at least 40 homes were reported destroyed, with 13 people killed and 131 injured. Authorities and emergency response organizations continue to conduct search and rescue operations, damage assessments, and assistance to affected populations.

The situation remains dynamic, and figures will need to be updated as access is gained to rural and hard-toreach communities.

In response, Fundación ABBACOL is coordinating a humanitarian response with the support of local communities and stakeholders, initially prioritizing psychosocial support and needs assessments while seeking national and international cooperation to expand the response and mobilize humanitarian assistance to affected communities.

title: Attacks on Health Care in Myanmar: 22 July - 04 August 2026
content:
Using data collected by Insecurity Insight, the Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition (SHCC) identified 259 incidents of violence against or obstruction of health care in Myanmar in 2025. Health facilities, including clinics, hospitals, pharmacies, and rural health centers, were reportedly damaged or destroyed on at least 110 occasions. Most damage or destruction involved MAF military jets using rockets and cannons that hit facilities and killed and injured health workers and patients. MAF air strikes frequently damaged or destroyed health facilities, including makeshift clinics operated by CDM-affiliated health workers, particularly in Sagaing.

Five health facilities in Kachin, Kayah, Magway, Mandalay and Ta’ang were reportedly used by opposition groups as bunkers during confrontations with MAF soldiers. These are five of the rarely reported cases where damaged health care buildings were not functioning facilities at the time and therefore had lost their special protection guaranteed under the rules of war. Combatants’ use of former health care buildings as bunkers reduces access to health care for the civilian population and as such is a further example of how violence affects health care during conflict.

Documented incidents

The publicly reported incidents below are not a complete nor a representative list of all incidents that affected the provision of health care in Myanmar between 22 July-04 August 2026. The incidents have not been verified through ground investigations. There is a delay in reporting incidents due to our open-source verification protocol.

20 July 2026: In Sin Pu Hnit village, Myo Haung village tract, Launglon township, Dawei district, Tanintharyi region, a male health assistant was arrested by the Myanmar military. Source: Dawei Watch

27 July 2026: In Aye Ka Ni village, Aye Ka Ni village tract, Yebyu township, Dawei district, Tanintharyi region, a sub-rural health centre and two houses were torched by the Myanmar military. Source: Dawei Watch

Our work in the media

A recent Guardian feature on Myanmar's health system drew on Insecurity Insight's data to document the scale of attacks on health since the 2021 military coup. The article highlights how violence against health workers and facilities has contributed to the country's deepening health crisis, underscoring the importance of systematic monitoring to inform public understanding and humanitarian advocacy.

title: UNHCR-IOM Pakistan Flash update # 106 on Arrest and Detention/Flow Monitoring, 15 Sep 2023 to 8 Aug 2026
content:
In response to the Ministry of Interior's (MoI) decision of 26 September 2023 to enact an “Illegal Foreigners' Repatriation Plan”, UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency and IOM, the UN Migration Agency, have collated their data on the arrest, detention, and deportation of Proof of Registration (PoR) holders, Afghan Citizen Card (ACC) holders, and undocumented Afghan nationals as well as on the outflows of Afghan nationals at the Torkham, Ghulam Khan, Chaman, Badini and Bahramcha border crossing points, to better understand the protection environment and movements of Afghan nationals returning to Afghanistan from Pakistan.

In 2025, the Government of Pakistan (GoP) issued several directives impacting Afghan nationals. In January, the GoP announced that Afghan nationals should relocate from Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT) and Rawalpindi, or else face deportation. In April, further announcements indicated the implementation of the second phase of the “IFRP”, targeting ACC holders, in addition to undocumented Afghans. In July, the GoP issued a Statutory Regulation Order (SRO) directing the repatriation/deportation of PoR card holders following the expiry of PoR card validity on 30 June. The GoP later indicated a deadline of 1 September for PoR holders to leave Pakistan, before the start of the repatriation/deportation process. UNHCR issued a press briefing expressing concern regarding the decision and urging the GoP to exempt Afghans with international protection needs, as well as those with particular circumstances or vulnerabilities, from involuntary return.

title: Eswatini Drought - DREF Final Report (MDRSZ004)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met
30-11-2023
What happened, where and when?

The Kingdom of Eswatini persistently experienced dry spells that further exacerbated the country’s existing food insecurity challenges.

For successive years, Eswatini battled prolonged drought, whose effects on agriculture were further compounded by cumulative socio‑economic challenges the country had not overcome. As of 30 November 2023, ACAPS classified food insecurity in Eswatini as high, with 24% of the population (282,800 people) affected by food‑insecurity vulnerabilities, facing challenges in accessing food and water, with many households still reliant on welfare and social safety nets.

During the operational update in June 2024, food security had declined further, as indicated by the IPC report of 2024/25 (current period: June 2024-September 2024), where 270 000 people were in Crisis (IPC 3+), and while the projected period (October 2024-March 2025) indicated an increase to 304 000 people to be food insecure. Prolonged dry spells and other climatic conditions remained one of the main drivers of food insecurity in the country. The regions with the highest prevalence of food insecurity were the Lubombo and Shiselweni, which are the same areas mostly affected by droughts.

Despite efforts engaged by government and humanitarian actors in the country, the assessment conducted in June 2024 gathered community insights on drought impacts and food security needs, identifying a 33% gap, approximately 4,675 people, within the targeted constituencies. Consequently, the Government of Eswatini, through the National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA), relaunched a call for support from humanitarian actors and National Food Security Consortium partners, citing insufficient funds to address the needs.

However, new developments showed that in the 2024 IPC report, 243,000 people (20% of the population) were estimated to be in IPC Phase 3 (Crisis) or worse during the period June to September 2024, and for the projected period (October 2024 to March 2025), an estimated 270,000 people were classified in IPC Phase 3 (Crisis), while 34,000 people were in IPC Phase 4 (Emergency). This indicated an increase in the number of people who needed assistance to 304 000 people.

In addition, an assessment was conducted in June 2024 to gather community insights on the impacts of the drought and to understand food‑security needs among the targeted population. The assessment revealed a 33% gap (about 4,675 people) in the already targeted constituencies. Therefore, the Government of Eswatini, through the National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA), requested once again that Eswatini humanitarian actors and the Eswatini National Food Security Consortium partners intervene, as the Government did not have sufficient funds to respond to the humanitarian and food‑insecurity needs. Targeted constituencies were Hosea, Sigwe, Matsanjeni, Somntongo, Lubuli and Nkilongo. The project informed its target based on its complementarity with the ECHO PPP based in the same areas.

Between June and September 2025, 193,000 people (16 percent of the population) in Eswatini experienced high levels of acute food insecurity and loss of livelihood, classified in IPC Phase 3 or above (Crisis or worse). Although food security had improved significantly compared to the same period last year, the situation was expected to deteriorate during the projection period (October 2025 to March 2026).

title: Wildfire, Republic of Tunisia July 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRTN013)
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event
25-07-2026

What happened, where and when?

Since 1 June 2026, Tunisia has been affected by a severe wildfire season, with the situation escalating significantly from 25 July 2026 as multiple simultaneous wildfires spread across several governorates. High temperatures, dry vegetation and strong winds contributed to the ignition and rapid spread of fires, particularly in forested and agricultural areas.

The wildfires primarily affected the governorates of Bizerte, Béja, Jendouba, Le Kef, Siliana, Zaghouan, Nabeul, Manouba, Tunis, Kasserine, Sidi Bouzid, Sfax, Gafsa, Kébili, Tozeur and Mahdia. Among the most significant incidents were the Sakiet Sidi Youssef wildfire in Le Kef Governorate, which affected approximately 2,000 hectares, the Jebel Chahma fire in Zaghouan Governorate, which damaged around 1,300 hectares of forest and agricultural land, the Ghar El Melh and Rafraf fires in Bizerte Governorate, and the Cap Negro fire in Béja Governorate. Additional fires were reported across several other affected governorates.

According to official information, approximately 12,000 hectares of forest and agricultural land have been damaged since the beginning of the fire season, compared with 4,400 hectares reported by 23 July 2026 and 2,705 hectares during the same period in 2025. Historical records indicate that around 70,000 hectares of forest have burned in Tunisia over the last ten years, representing an annual average of approximately 7,000 hectares and highlighting the exceptional severity of the current wildfire season. The Director General of Forests confirmed that the fires have mainly affected cork-oak and Aleppo pine forests, which are environmentally and economically important for local communities.

The scale of the emergency has been unprecedented. Civil Protection reported approximately 900 fires within a 72-hour period between 20 and 22 July 2026, while nearly 2,800 interventions were conducted within 48 hours, covering around 600 separate fire incidents. Since the beginning of the season, the Directorate General of Forests has participated in 917 firefighting operations, compared with 620 during the same period in 2025. In response to the deterioration of the situation, the Government of Tunisia requested international assistance, resulting in the deployment of aerial firefighting assets from Italy and Algeria.

The wildfires have caused significant humanitarian, environmental and economic impacts. Evacuations were carried out in several locations, particularly in Bizerte and Jendouba, while livestock were moved from affected areas in Siliana and Ain Draham. Damage has been reported to homes, commercial premises, wooden cabins, restaurants and tourism facilities, particularly in Ghar El Melh and Rafraf. Large areas of agricultural land, fruit trees and natural resources have been destroyed, significantly affecting the livelihoods of rural and forest-dependent communities.

Firefighting operations continue to face challenges due to rugged terrain, difficult access conditions and highly flammable vegetation. As of 31 July 2026, firefighting and cooling operations remained ongoing in several governorates. While no fatalities had been officially reported at the time of writing, cases of smoke inhalation, minor burns and respiratory distress were recorded, and three Civil Protection personnel were injured. According to assessments conducted by the Tunisian Red Crescent, an estimated 27,117 people were directly affected by the wildfires. In addition, 14,362 people were affected by electricity and water supply disruptions associated with the emergency, resulting in a total affected population of 41,479 people.

title: Burkina Faso Floods Anticipatory Actions - Imminent DREF Final Report (MDRBF022)
content:
Event development

Update regarding the event’s development

The preparedness activities planned under this operation were primarily implemented in the provinces of Balé and Ioba, areas particularly exposed to flooding risks during the months of August, September, and October. This period traditionally corresponds to the season when overflow of the Mouhoun River causes recurrent flooding, especially in the provinces of Mouhoun, Balé, Ioba, Houet, and Tuy.

In August 2024, riverine flooding effectively affected the villages of Hèrèdougou and Goro in the municipality of Pâ (Balé Province), following a critical rise in the water level of the Mouhoun River. These floods affected at least 800 people, causing damage to housing, loss of household assets, and disruptions in access to essential services such as safe drinking water, healthcare, and food.

In this context, activities implemented under the DREF Imminent operation mainly focused on early disaster risk reduction actions. These included, in particular:

training 40 volunteers on flood risks and the early warning system;

training 50 volunteers (local teams) in first aid;

mobilizing 112 volunteers to conduct community awareness sessions on appropriate behaviors before, during, and after floods;

producing and broadcasting radio spots in local languages to reach a wide audience;

supporting the organization of three coordination platforms (COPROSUR) bringing together local authorities, technical services, community structures, and the Burkina Faso Red Cross (CRBF) to harmonize actions and strengthen information-sharing;

ensuring the continuous dissemination of reliable information through community radios and social media;

supporting the monitoring of early flood warning signs through the follow-up of 10 hydrological stations and the timely transmission of data to the relevant authorities.

These actions contributed to strengthening preparedness, awareness, and vigilance among exposed communities.

However, despite the mobilization and preparedness of local actors, no major flooding occurred during the implementation period of the operation. Trigger thresholds were not reached, as recorded rainfall levels were slightly below initial forecasts. Although a rise in water levels was observed in Hèrèdougou, which temporarily submerged National Road RN1, the impacts remained limited. Nevertheless, the CRBF deployed volunteers to raise awareness among road users and reinforce safety at the site.

This situation can also be explained by ongoing works in the municipality of Pâ, notably the construction of new water retention and crossing infrastructures, which helped mitigate the potential effects of heavy rainfall.

As a result, rapid response activities were not activated before the planned date of 30 September 2025, as no major flooding occurred that would have justified their implementation.

title: Venezuela | Earthquake - Operation Update #2 (MDRVE015)
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS
Description of the crisis

On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela in rapid succession; with the first one reaching a 7.2 magnitude, and a second one of 7.5 magnitude taking place approximately 39 seconds later. The epicentres were located near Morón and Yumare, in the states of Carabobo and Yaracuy, west of Caracas. USGS analysis confirmed the epicentre of the second earthquake to be approximately 17 km west of Catia La Mar, off the coast of La Guaira State1. Authorities have reported 1,463 aftershocks since the event, creating a high risk of further structural collapse2. The impact was severe and widespread, with tremors felt across much of the country, including the Capital District, La Guaira, Aragua, Carabobo, Miranda, Falcón, and neighbouring states. The earthquakes were also felt beyond Venezuela, including parts of Colombia, the Caribbean and northern Brazil, highlighting the exceptional geographic extent of the seismic event3.

The Government of Venezuela declared a National State of Emergency the same day and designated La Guaira, where the greatest concentration of damaged infrastructure and rescue operations was concentrated, as a disaster zone.

According to the Global Disaster Awareness and Coordination System (GDACS) approximately 530,000 were exposed to extreme earthquake intensity. The scale of the disaster led to a significant expansion of international humanitarian presence in the country. On 15 July, the United Nations announced an addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP), increasing financial requirements and expanding the number of people targeted for assistance for their overall humanitarian response to Venezuela (which extends beyond those affected by the earthquakes).

The event occurred during the San Juan festivities, a national celebration that attracts large numbers of people to coastal areas; and as many workplaces were closed, this also led to families having many or all members present inside their home when the earthquakes happened. In La Guaira State, a popular beachside destination to spend this festivity, this resulted in higher population concentrations in public spaces and along the coastline at the time of the event, increasing the number of people potentially exposed to the impacts of the earthquakes. La Guaira also serves multiple critical functions for the country given very close proximity to the Capital, Caracas. It hosts the country’s main international airport (Maiquetía) and one of its major ports, making it a strategic transportation, logistics, trade, tourism, fishing and service hub. Consequently, the incident impacted not only local communities and visitors present, but also essential infrastructure and activities that facilitate connectivity and the supply of goods to the capital and other regions of the country. This increases the number of people with secondary affectations and the extent of logistical capacity impacted.

As of 3 August, 6,125 people were reported dead, 16,740 injured, 6,462 rescued and approximately 17,907 had lost their homes due to severe damage to housing.4 The United Nations interagency indicated that tens of thousands of people remained unaccounted for during the response period; while many families including from those having opened tracing requests with the RCRC system have reported having been able to reunite with their loved ones in the days and weeks following the disaster. Efforts to identify and notify direct family members of persons hospitalized and persons deceased also continue. It is expected for the death toll to continue to rise as the Search and Rescue phase focused on extraction of survivors has moved towards a focus on recovery, identification and dignified return of bodies retrieved from collapsed structures to their family members.5 Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams operating under the coordination of the International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG) have now concluded their assignment. Response teams from over 29 countries deployed to Venezuela, including the United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination (UNDAC) team and multiple RCRC Movement specialized teams such as the USAR teams of the Mexican RC, Colombian RC, Costa Rican RC who deployed in support of Venezuelan RC search & rescue efforts. The initial response focused on search, recovery, debris-removal, and initial shelter provision has now shifted towards bridging emergency relief to rehabilitation and reconstruction efforts under national leadership, with a broad range of bilateral and multilateral support focused on humanitarian assistance, restoration of essential services and recovery.

According to OCHA, 2,501 infrastructure assets had sustained some degree of damage, with 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.6

On 21 July, the Venezuelan President of the Presidential Commission for the Assessment of Infrastructure Habitability reported that 6,907 buildings had been inspected in La Guaira using the traffic light assessment methodology to determine the condition of structures. Of the total inspected, 3,237 received a green tag indicating that the infrastructure poses no risk; 1,785 structures received a yellow tag indicating restricted use; and 1,885 were classified with a red tag indicating high risk. Structures assigned yellow or red classifications are now undergoing a secondary more thorough assessment7.

Disruptions of electricity, water-supply, telecommunications and transport systems caused by the earthquakes are undergoing repair to continue restoring functionality across the affected areas. Damaged roads and bridges have also affected movement to and within some affected areas; prompting authorities to relocate mobile bridges to facilitate access while repairs are finalized. Public transportation and airport operations are also under repair, with Maiquetia International Airport (which was severely damaged) expected to resume use for commercial cargo flights in the coming weeks. Commercial international passenger flights remain operating mostly in and out of Valencia airport, located approximately 2 hours out of the capital. Humanitarian cargo donated by Governments bilaterally to the Venezuelan Authorities, and through humanitarian actors, continues to flow in country through air, sea and land shipments.

In terms of essential services, healthcare capacity has been particularly including given the mass scale needs following the rapid onset emergency (trauma injuries), as well as given rates of chronic illness among displaced communities and affectations to water supply and sanitation services. More than 400 schools were also reported as affected, while some have been assigned as temporary shelters while authorities assign free permanent housing units and/or transitional single-family homes until the academic cycle resumes after the summer. To this end, Venezuelan authorities have already provided 240 permanent housing units to affected families; and while land & public housing infrastructure is evaluated and attributed for the assignment of additional seismic resistant units entirely free of charge, they have also enabled a parallel option for affected families who prefer to buy existing homes from the private market (whereby 80% of the price is subsidized by the government and the 20% remaining be granted on 25-year-loans extended by the local banking system.)

The physical impacts on affected people remain significant, with many requiring continued medical care, rehabilitation or referral services, as well as mental health and psychosocial support. Many families have experienced loss and grief, injury, displacement, separation from relatives and loss of homes, livelihoods and community support networks. The magnitude of the tragedy on human terms, continued aftershocks, displacement from damaged homes, and exposure to destroyed environments and recovery operations contributed to heightened levels of stress, anxiety and sadness among the affected population.

The earthquakes have resulted in grave humanitarian needs while exacerbating existing vulnerabilities, which increases the severity and complexity of the situation for the affected communities. This context reinforces the need for a response that addresses immediate lifesaving needs while supporting early recovery and strengthening community resilience.

title: Agrometeorological 10 days Bulletin for 11–20 August 2026 Across the Northern Tonle Sap Basin of the PEARL Project
content:
Flood Early Warning
No flood risk for the next 10 days. Keep a clean watering basin around each tree with a low earthen ring about half a palm high to slow splash; during heavy showers cut a small notch so water drains. Mulch under the canopy 10-15 cm {about a palm to a palm-and-a-half thick} using dry rice straw, chopped prunings, dried grass/leaves, leaving a hand-width gap at the trunk. Maintain diversion furrows one hand wide and one palm deep to guide rainwater away from trunks. Keep tools and bags on shelves about one palm above the floor.

title: UNICEF Afghanistan Humanitarian Flash Update No. 3 (Central and Eastern Region Flash Floods), 11 August 2026
content:
Highlights

  • On 20 July, heavy rainfall triggered flash floods across several provinces in central, northern and eastern Afghanistan, resulting in casualties, damage to homes and critical infrastructure, and disruption to essential services and livelihoods.
  • In the Eastern Region (ER), Parun district of Nuristan Province was among the most severely affected areas. Preliminary reports indicate 24 fatalities (26 per cent women, 74 per cent men), and 125 injuries (7 per cent women, 93 per cent men), with additional individuals reported missing. The floods destroyed or damaged 120 houses and affected health facilities, local markets, bridges, roads, flood protection walls, agricultural land and water supply networks, disrupting livelihoods and access to safe drinking water.
  • On 3 August, a second flash flood struck Barg-e-Matal district in eastern Nuristan, affecting 191 families through destruction or damage to their houses. This flood similarly disrupted livelihoods and damaged critical infrastructure, including bridges, roads, flood protection walls, agricultural land and water supply networks, further constraining access to safe drinking water and essential services.
  • In the Central Region (CR), flash floods across nine provinces resulted in two fatalities and six injuries. A total of 316 houses were affected, impacting 2,057 people – including 688 girls, 610 boys, 395 women and 364 men. Approximately 1.6 million square metres of agricultural land were destroyed, some 300 livestock were killed, and 17 schools sustained damage, further affecting livelihoods and access to basic services.
  • A separate flooding incident in Paktia province destroyed 11 houses and damaged agricultural land. A joint needs assessment team has been deployed to assess humanitarian needs, with distribution of assistance planned for 12 August.
  • The recent flash floods may also have displaced explosive ordnance (EO) or exposed previously buried hazards, increasing protection risks for affected communities and humanitarian personnel operating in flood-affected areas.

title: UNICEF South Asia Region Humanitarian Situation Report No.1 (Mid - Year), 30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Children and families across South Asia were affected by climate-related disasters, earthquakes, public health emergencies and conflict, resulting in significant humanitarian needs.
  • UNICEF provided life-saving health, nutrition, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), education and child protection services to 2.3 million crisis-affected people across India, Pakistan, Nepal and Sri Lanka, including 1.9 million children.
  • UNICEF strengthened national preparedness and anticipatory action capacities and promoted locally led, accountable and disability-inclusive humanitarian action.
  • By June 2026, UNICEF had received US$35.4 million against its regional Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal of US$71.4 million, limiting response, preparedness and anticipatory action efforts, including for emerging El Niño-related risks.

title: PHL: Cyclone - 08-2026 - Philippines Southwest Monsoon enhanced by Tropical Cyclones Maymay and Dolphin (2026-08-13)
content:
Description

At 8:00 PM on 4 August 2026, the Low-Pressure Area (LPA) located west of Bacnotan, La Union intensified into Tropical Depression MAYMAY, according to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA).

By 2:00 AM on 5 August 2026, Tropical Depression MAYMAY further intensified into Tropical Storm MAYMAY (international name: Kujira) while moving slowly near the western coast of Northern Luzon.

On 6 August 2026, Tropical Storm MAYMAY weakened into a Tropical Depression and made landfall over the Ilocos Sur–La Union area before traversing the mountainous terrain of Northern Luzon. As it moved inland, the system continued to weaken while crossing the rugged terrain and is forecast to emerge over the eastern coastal waters of Isabela or Cagayan. PAGASA indicated that the cyclone may further weaken into a remnant low by the afternoon or evening, although interaction with the mountainous terrain could result in an earlier weakening. The remnant low is then expected to move generally southeastward before merging with the larger circulation of Tropical Cyclone DOLPHIN.

Despite its weakening, MAYMAY, together with the enhanced Southwest Monsoon, continues to bring heavy rainfall, strong to gale-force winds, and hazardous sea conditions over affected areas. PAGASA also emphasized that localities outside the forecast track and confidence cone may still experience significant impacts, particularly heavy rainfall, strong winds, and rough to very rough seas.

Summary

PRC has supported local authorities in conducting assessments, search and rescue operations, and evacuations. Multiple ambulances have been deployed to support emergency response efforts. PRC Chapters have also distributed hot meals, drinking water, antibiotics, other essential medicines, vitamins, and information, education, and communication (IEC) materials, including to individuals in evacuation centers. Welfare Desks, Child-Friendly Spaces (CFS), and First Aid Stations have been established in affected areas to provide essential assistance and support. All PRC staff and volunteers in affected areas, as well as personnel at NHQ and warehouses, have remained on high alert and standby to provide additional support as needed throughout the week and continue to do so. The situation continues to be closely monitored by PRC Chapters and NHQ to ensure timely and appropriate response to emerging needs.

Summary

IFRC is closely monitoring the situation and ready to support PRC if requested.

Actions taken by others

Almost 500 million PHP worth of assistance has been provided. Government agencies have been on high alert and have led search and rescue and evacuation efforts. Hundreds of evacuation centers are operational. Food and Non-Food Items have been distributed across the affected areas. Roads and bridges are being cleared from debris. The situation is closely monitored on a national level, and more assistance is being provided daily.

title: Colombia: Flash Update 004 - Update on the Impact of the Earthquake in Colombia - August 12, 2026
content:
This Flash Update is produced by OCHA Colombia in collaboration with humanitarian partners, based on official reports (as of 12 August, 18:30 local time)

The emergency continues to escalate and has exceeded the local response capacity, with at least 49,214 people affected, 30,324 families impacted, 3,771 injured people, and 241 fatalities across 13 departments of the country. The damage to housing, social infrastructure, and essential services highlights a large-scale humanitarian crisis that requires a sustained and coordinated response.

Humanitarian needs are multisectoral, and significant response gaps remain, particularly in Risaralda, Valle del Cauca, Chocó, and Caldas. Damage to more than 54,900 homes (destroyed and damaged), educational institutions, health facilities, water supply systems, and roads is limiting access for thousands of people to basic services, protection, healthcare, safe water, and livelihoods.

The national and international response is underway and continues to expand to save lives and complement institutional capacity. While search and rescue operations, humanitarian assistance, and rapid needs assessments continue, the USD 5 million CERF allocation represents a critical boost to scale up the emergency response and support the populations most affected by the earthquake in Colombia.

title: Venezuela Earthquakes Situation Report #6 (August 12, 2026)
content:
FAST FACTS

  • On June 24, two earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 hit northern Venezuela in rapid succession, impacting at least seven states—including the capital city of Caracas and the neighboring city of La Guaira.
  • Official figures have so far confirmed 6,125 fatalities, 16,740 injuries and 24,477 people currently displaced.
  • Priority needs include healthcare services, clean water, food, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services, adequate sanitation and hygiene facilities, protection support and shelter.

Our Response

  • International Medical Corps has deployed three mobile medical units, which have provided 3,819 consultations since July 1.
  • On July 11, International Medical Corps opened an Emergency Medical Team (EMT) Type 1 Fixed facility to provide free medical services to impacted communities. To date, we have provided 3,263 consultations through the EMT.
  • Our teams have delivered 390,000 liters of safe water across displacement sites, benefitting an estimated 4,000 people.
  • Our teams have provided 759 MHPSS consultations.

title: Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak: Democratic Republic of the Congo | Uganda Weekly External Situation Report 13, Data as of 09 August 2026
content:
Event description

The Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo remains in a phase of intense and expanding transmission, with cumulative deaths crossing the grim milestone of 2,000 only 86 days after the outbreak was officially declared on 15 May 2026. Since External Situation Report #12, an additional 579 confirmed cases and 304 confirmed deaths have been reported, bringing the cumulative total to 4,381 confirmed cases and 2,011 confirmed deaths as of 9 August 2026, corresponding to a case fatality ratio of 45.9%. Ituri remains the epicentre, accounting for 85.8% of cumulative cases and 80.6% of cumulative deaths.
